cia-0000102961:
Work Treatment Prophylaxis Camps, Moscow, is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000102961, dated July 1, 1987. The sample covers the years 1977 to 1979 and names five or six such camps near Moscow. Each camp held several thousand people and was run by the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

Entry took a judge's order and a medical exam to show a person could perform hard labor. In practice, treatment for alcohol dependence was almost absent, beyond Antabuse or a few vitamin C tablets. A typical day meant ten hours of construction or heavy labor, plain meals, and political lessons before bed. Guards could be bribed for alcohol, and the camps failed at treating alcoholism.
cia-0000105161:
Weekly Situation Report on International Terrorism is declassified CIA document 0000105161, dated January 2, 1975 in the catalog. The sample shows the issue dated January 7, 1975. It was presented to the Working Group of the Cabinet Committee to Combat Terrorism, whose members are listed on its cover.

The contents page names the week's articles, opening with an attempted hijack in London by an unknown gunman. That single named article shows the report's mix: short items on attacks and attempts around the world. The issue is one early installment of the weekly series named in its title.
cia-0000109061: Cuban Sugar Production in 1967 and Prospects for 1968 and 1970 is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000109061, dated October 3, 1967. The heading looks backward and forward: one harvest year, then prospects for two more. Sugar is the single crop named in the title itself. The brief record is a crop production item from the autumn of 1967.
cia-0000119761: A September 1956 CIA chronology issued as a special supplement updates the master timeline of events. During that autumn, keeping the sequence current meant keeping pace with a revolution, and the supplement preserves the order of events as the agency assembled it. Supplement pages show the timeline being corrected in near real time, a working record revised as cables arrived faster than printers could reset it.
cia-0000126861: A February 1953 CIA document filed under the name John P. Hayes. The title offers no role, no charge, no context — just the name. Whatever made Hayes interesting to the agency, the answer is inside the file.
cia-0000126961: An October 1968 CIA report carries the blunt heading Haiti: Duvalier's Primitive Totalitarian State. By then the Tonton Macoute had terrorized the country for more than a decade in Papa Doc's name. The paper lays out one of the hemisphere's most brutal regimes as the agency judged it. The heading's harsh wording is itself evidence: analysts rarely wrote so bluntly about a government Washington still dealt with, which shows how far Haiti stood apart.
cia-0000132661:
The future of the Castro regime is weighed in a CIA paper dated November 4, 1960. The American election was days away, and the new president would inherit the Cuba problem at once. How long Castro could last was the question running through Washington that fall.

The agency's forecasters were split on the answer, and the paper sets out their views. For readers, it preserves a moment of honest doubt before policy hardened. Within five months the invasion at the Bay of Pigs would test every forecast in the file. The paper shows what the experts said before that test came.
cia-0000135861: With a date of 3 September 1952, a CIA routing sheet in the open files deals with a memo whose heading spells the country as Guiatemala, typo and all. Behind the paper stands PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA campaign against President Arbenz that closed with the 1954 coup in Guatemala. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000136061: From the CIA files comes a cable dated 5 March 1954, long since declassified, on the K Program, a recurring subject in the station files through the spring of 1954. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Students of the 1954 coup use such records to check later accounts against what was written at the time.
cia-0000136161: A cable dated 4 March 1954 is among the declassified CIA papers on criticisms and recommendations from headquarters, the rare cable grading the field from above. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.
cia-0000136261: Filed on 6 May 1954, this CIA cable concerns waiting until the twentieth of June for a decision before taking action, a hold order. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. A reader gets the unpolished version here, complete with code names, short titles, and gaps left by the censors.
cia-0000136961: Letters from an appropriate man are suggested in this May 1954 cable. Communist-led mass groups are rallying support for Arbenz. Unions sent sympathy messages. So did the peasant federation and student groups. They hold mass meetings against foreign intervention. They rally public sympathy with some success. Headquarters proposes a counter-move. Letters should go to conference delegates. They should also go to non-communist labor groups. The letters would decry the regime's totalitarian acts. Exile stories of arrests and tortures would be replayed.
cia-0000139161: Distribution of particularly sensitive intelligence reports is restricted in this 1985 memorandum signed for the Director of Central Intelligence. In July 1985 a sensitive source reporting format was established for highly sensitive CIA reporting concerning the well-being and possible locations of American hostages in Lebanon. The format limits distribution within the CIA and restricts dissemination to named addressees in other agencies, including the national security advisor and the directors of DIA, NSA, and State's intelligence bureau. Recipients must share it only with those having a clearly evident need to know.
un-ga-res-a-69-61:
Women belong at the center of disarmament work, argues Resolution A/69/61, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Charter itself states the equal rights of women and men. The text recalls votes of 2010 and 2012 on women and arms. It also recalls Security Council calls of 2013. Those calls seek a full part for women in the fight against the illicit spread of small arms.

Equal, full, and real roles for women and men alike are named as a core need for lasting peace. The work of women in hands-on disarmament is praised: at local, state, and regional levels, they help cut armed strife and gun deaths. The vote presses states to open that work wide.
un-ga-res-57-161:
Guatemala's peace entered its last UN phase under Resolution 57/161, passed in December 2002. The Verification Mission in Guatemala had its term stretched through 2002 by a vote of the year before. The state had restated its pledge to put the peace deals into full force. Yet core parts of those deals, the text stresses again, still waited to be done.

The follow-up team's timetable for the work now ran through 2004. Both sides had asked the UN to back the firming of peace to 2003. The mission's thirteenth report on human rights is weighed in the text. So is the seventh report on the checking of the peace deals, and the truth report on the war's crimes.
un-ga-res-161:
Congo's crisis deepened into blood in February 1961, and the vote filed here as Resolution 161 answered it. The text is in fact a Security Council vote, passed on 21 February 1961 by ten votes to one. Word had come of the killing of Congo's chiefs: Patrice Lumumba, Maurice Mpolo, and Joseph Okito. Grave fallout from those crimes, and the risk of wide civil war, hang over the text.

The UN is urged to act at once with all fit steps to bar civil war in the Congo. Truces must be set, all armed moves halted, and clashes barred, with force used if need be as a last resort. All Belgian and other foreign armed men must leave the land at once. The vote marks the UN's deepest plunge into the Congo fight.
un-sc-res-161:
Resolution 161 reacts to grave news from the Congo. Congolese leaders Patrice Lumumba, Maurice Mpolo, and Joseph Okito had been killed. The Council adopted the text on 21 February 1961. It said it learned of the killings with deep regret. Reports also pointed to a civil war taking shape.

The Council urges the UN to act at once. The aim is to stop civil war in the Congo. Steps could include cease-fires and a halt to all fighting. Force could be used if needed, as a last resort. The text also urges the removal of foreign troops and advisers. They must not serve outside UN command. Mercenaries must leave as well. States are asked to stop such people from leaving for the Congo.
un-sc-res-661: Numbered 661 in the Council's sequence, this resolution is catalogued as a 1990 entry in the United Nations official record. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1461: Holding number 1461 in the Council series, this resolution carries a 1973 date in the library catalog. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-1661: Resolution 1661, adopted in 2006, is a Security Council act preserved through English Wikisource's copy of the UN record. The Council's resolutions are how peacekeeping missions live and die, sanctions rise and fall, and demands reach governments. This entry holds one complete instance of that machinery, in the members' own formal language.
un-sc-res-1761: Adopted in 2007, Resolution 1761 is a Security Council decision preserved in official-record form. The transcription source is English Wikisource. Inside the act, the members cite their earlier texts the way courts cite precedent, then extend the line of action one step further. The entry preserves that step in its full legal dress.
un-sc-res-2361: Resolution 2361, from 2017, is a Security Council decision preserved in this collection through a transcription of the official record. Its form matches acts decades older in the same series: the institution changes slowly on paper. The entry preserves the full text at its number, so its demands can be read in the members' own durable format.
cia-0000132761:
Spring tensions run through this CIA briefing on Cuba, dated May 4, 1960. Castro's government was a year old and pressing ahead with its revolution. The United States, still weighing its options, had not yet settled on a course.

May 1960 sits in the hinge of the story: relations were bad and worsening, but the final break was still months away. Briefings from that month record an agency watching land seizures, sharp speeches, and colder diplomacy pile up. The declassified paper preserves the moment before Washington chose confrontation, and it rewards reading beside the harder papers of 1961.
plos-pone-0000061:
Andrey Rzhetsky, Tian Zheng, and Chani Weinreb tackled the errors in biology's own maps in a 2006 paper. A molecular pathway map charts how genes and proteins interact, step by step. Such maps are drawn from thousands of papers, and they contain mistakes that later work then inherits.

Their answer was self-correcting maps: pathway charts built to detect and repair their own inconsistencies as new data arrives. A map that heals itself would give systems biology, the field that simulates whole cells, a firmer base to build on. The idea treats a scientific database less like a printed atlas and more like a living document that keeps checking its facts.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d61: Ambassador W. Averell Harriman wrote to Roosevelt from Moscow on October 26, 1943, during the foreign ministers' conference. His dispatch is Document 61 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Harriman had just taken up the Moscow embassy, the post from which he would watch Stalin's government for the rest of the war. The record gives the date and the two men. His news is a matter for the printed text.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d161: Secretary Hull wrote from Moscow on October 23, 1943, addressing both the President and Acting Secretary Stettinius in one letter. It is Document 161 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. A letter to two readers at once kept the traveling secretary's news flowing to the White House and his own department together. The record names the three men and the date. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d261:
An editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume covers an informal Cairo meeting of 23 November 1943 for which no official record has been found. Its content can be partly recovered, because General Marshall described his dinner conversation with Churchill to the Joint Chiefs of Staff the following day.

From Marshall's report, Churchill had ranged over operations in the Dodecanese, the capture of Rhodes, the deployment of landing craft, and the progress of the Italian campaign. He also raised aid to guerrillas in the Balkans, how Mediterranean operations bore on the date of Overlord, and unified command of strategic air operations. Churchill took up the same subjects the next day with Roosevelt present.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d361:
Minutes kept for the Combined Chiefs of Staff record the same first plenary session at Tehran, on 28 November 1943 at four in the afternoon, in a fuller American staff version. They run parallel to the Bohlen minutes printed beside them, with the speeches set down at greater length.

Roosevelt welcomes Stalin and Churchill to the family table, Churchill speaks of the future of mankind resting in their hands, and Stalin answers, let us get down to business. Roosevelt's survey stresses three points. America bears the major part of the Pacific war and wants its forces home. Japanese shipping losses outrun replacement. And the north Burma operation under Mountbatten, with an amphibious stroke toward Bangkok's supply lines, is meant to open the road to China and keep that country fighting.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d461:
The Combined Chiefs of Staff were still meeting on December 7, 1943, a day after the Second Cairo Conference ended, and their minutes appear in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume. The joint American-British command had followed the leaders from Tehran back to Cairo. Its work did not stop when the public sessions closed.

These minutes carry the conference into its aftermath: decisions confirmed, orders framed, and business handed on to the commands that would carry it out. For readers, the record is a reminder that summits end on paper before they end in practice. The chiefs' last Cairo sessions turned three weeks of talks into instructions the war machine could follow.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d561:
Prime Minister Churchill sent another message to President Roosevelt on March 9, 1944. Two days had passed since his last, which counts as a pause in that season's correspondence. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

The Roosevelt-Churchill file for March 1944 runs thick because the decisions did: shipping, bombing, invasion security, and the politics of liberated Europe all demanded the leaders' own words. Churchill's habit of writing everything down is the reason this record exists at all. For readers, the message adds one more piece to a conversation that, read whole, is the nearest thing to a diary of the alliance.
frus-1944-quebec-d61:
H. H. Kung, China's minister of finance, addressed this letter to President Roosevelt on September 8, 1944. Kung was China's chief financial official and a brother-in-law of Chiang Kai-shek. The letter appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

China's finances were collapsing under inflation that autumn, and Kung's appeals to Washington sought the aid that might hold his government together. A finance minister writing directly to the President shows the depth of China's need and the personal nature of wartime aid. For readers, the letter brings the fourth ally's distress into a volume dominated by the two Western leaders.
frus-1944-quebec-d161:
Hopkins answered Winant's letter on September 4, 1944, with reassurance and candor. A number of people in Washington, he wrote, were greatly concerned about British participation against Japan, and he was hopeful the president would land on the right side. The hostile attitude in certain circles, he insisted, did not represent public opinion.

Some British demobilization after Germany's collapse was inevitable, Hopkins conceded, but it should be played down, with no public announcement. Ways must be found for Britain to take her full and proper place against Japan despite transport and supply difficulties. Lasting peace, he argued, required Russia, Britain, and America to see eye to eye, backed by their peoples.
frus-1944-quebec-d261:
"Rankin" planning, preparing for a sudden German collapse, is the subject of C.C.S. 684, the British Chiefs' paper of September 15, 1944. It asks approval of a directive to General Wilson for the Mediterranean. Wilson was to plan to seize immediate control of Austria with four divisions, Greece with about one British division, the Dodecanese with some 2,400 men, and Venezia Giulia with a division.

No forces would be stationed in Yugoslavia or Albania beyond supply guards, and no British troops would go to Bulgaria. British naval help on the Danube, including mine clearance, required prior agreement with the Russians. The force calculations exclude American troops, who would withdraw, and the four Indian divisions, who would not be used for Rankin duties.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d61:
Keeping the Yalta trip secret is the subject of a 20 January 1945 note from Charles Bohlen to Under Secretary of State Joseph Grew. Bohlen, an assistant to the Secretary of State, reports a White House decision on press censorship. The note is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences.

Two days earlier, Hopkins, Admiral Wilson Brown, and Stephen Early had agreed to invoke the censorship code from 19 January. It barred any speculation about the time, place, or general area of the coming meeting. Staff were also told how to answer questions about absent officials. The only allowed reply was, “He is out of town.”
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d161:
Roosevelt passed Stalin's New Year answer on Poland to Churchill on 4 January 1945. His telegram quotes the Soviet reply in full for the prime minister's information. The exchange is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

Stalin writes that he is extremely sorry he failed to convince the President of the Soviet position's correctness. Events, he hopes, will prove that the Polish National Committee has given the allies real help against Hitler's Germany. The London émigré government, by contrast, spreads disorganization and so aids the Germans. As for delay, Stalin pleads one hard fact. On 27 December the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet already told the Poles it intends to recognize their provisional government.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d261:
The Kurile Islands get a full territorial study in this paper of 28 December 1944. Written by the Division of Territorial Studies, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Its problem is stated in one line: the future disposition of the Kurile Islands.

The chain runs some 690 miles from Hokkaido to Kamchatka: forty-seven volcanic islands, thinly peopled. About 17,550 permanent residents, all Japanese, swell by tens of thousands of seasonal fishing hands in summer. Fish give the islands nearly all their economic worth. Their history is a see-saw: Russia yielded the whole chain to Japan in 1875, in exchange for Japan's withdrawal from southern Sakhalin. The paper weighs the islands' strategic value to Japan, Russia, and the United States alike.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d361:
Ships for freed Russians are the subject of a memorandum from Admiral Emory Land, the War Shipping Administrator, to Secretary Stettinius on February 5, 1945. Land reported that the American chiefs had agreed to use troopships for repatriation. The lift would match British help: 10,000 men a month across the Atlantic.

The deal held only while overland routes stayed closed. Once Germany fell, redeployment would need every troopship. Land added that Eisenhower had asked for two large troopships to move Russians gathered at Marseille. The memo turns Eden's prisoner diplomacy into tonnage, ports, and sailing dates.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d461:
Churchill edited like a proofreader, and this list of his changes to the draft communiqué, dated February 11, 1945, preserves his pencil at work. In the part on Germany's defeat, one word should become another throughout. Coordination should read as concert, launched should gain the word continuously after it, and joint should give way to combined.

On occupation and control of Germany, jointly becomes together, and coordinated becomes united. The last change is substance, not style. France, the new sentence should say, would be invited by the three powers to take a fourth zone. She would also sit as a fourth member of the Control Commission. The list shows the communiqué's final polish.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d61:
President Truman replied to Ambassador Harriman on June 14 or 15, 1945, with early word on his party for the Berlin conference. The telegram is document 61 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam, answering Harriman's question about what to tell the Russians. It gives a first picture of the American group being put together.

Eisenhower, Truman says, has orders to arrange rooms and meeting space, but has not yet been told who is coming. The President plans to bring his Chiefs of Staff, the Secretary of State with his aides, two or three other high officials, plus servants and Secret Service men. Names and numbers will follow once they are fixed. The message shows the trip still taking shape a month before departure.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d161:
President Truman answered Stalin on recognizing the ex-enemy states in a message sent through Harriman on June 18, 1945. The telegram carrying his words is document 161 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Stalin had proposed restoring diplomatic relations with Romania, Bulgaria, Hungary, and Finland.

Truman fully agrees that recognition would be a constructive step, the message says. But the two governments stand differently toward each state: nothing blocks instant American ties with Finland, while the internal situation in Romania, Hungary, and Bulgaria differs country by country. He is studying the matter further. The practical course, he proposes, is to discuss it at their coming meeting and reach a uniform agreement there. The draft was written in the State Department and approved by the President.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d261:

His whole finding is negative. There has been no reference to the free use of the Rhine and Danube rivers in Roosevelt's and Truman's messages and papers in the Map Room. The tiny memo still earned its place. Free navigation of the Danube in particular was a live question at Potsdam, pressed by Eisenhower among others. And the President's staff needed to know one thing. No past presidential word committed the United States either way.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d361:

He had asked authority on two points: filling London Munitions Assignment Board needs from stocks in Germany and Austria, and scrapping surplus enemy gear.

The report notes informal talks at government level. Some nations, it says, wanted enemy war material shared out among the United Nations. Those nations opposed the wide destruction of German equipment. The paper shows that even captured guns became a diplomatic question in the summer of 1945.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d461:
Tito's charges against Greece are answered in MacVeagh's cable from Athens of July 10, 1945. Tito had broadcast on July 8 that Greeks were firing across the border to provoke the Yugoslavs. He claimed thousands of Macedonians and Greeks were being fed in Yugoslavia after escaping terror by Greek reactionaries. Premier Voulgaris called on MacVeagh in alarm.

The Premier planned to fly to Salonika the next day, quietly, to learn the facts himself, then make a temperate factual broadcast on his return. American observers in northern Greece, MacVeagh reports, fail to confirm Tito's statements. Conditions on both sides of the border were disturbed, but the refugee figures struck him as unquestionably fantastic.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d561:
Marshal Tito and Field Marshal Alexander signed an agreed note at Duino on June 20, 1945. It is document 561 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The note covers civil rule in the part of Venezia Giulia placed under Allied military government.

The Yugoslav side would not accept the Allied plan for running the zone. It reserved the right to raise the matter through normal state channels. A Yugoslav note attached argues that the old Italian system should not come back. The zone's own wartime organs should be kept if they work well. It also states that Slovene and Italian tongues are equal, and that Rome's government should have no say in the zone.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d661:
A Soviet demand on Tangier reached Washington on July 2, 1945, and is recorded in document 661 here. The Secretary ad interim, Grew, relayed it to Ambassador Winant in London. Moscow had just learned of the three-power expert talks set for Paris on July 3.

The Soviet ambassador told Grew his government was interested in Tangier. It was surprised its opinion had not been asked and no Soviet expert invited. It asked that the experts' meeting be postponed until a Soviet expert could attend. Grew records the answer he gave in reply. The United States, he pointed out, never signed the 1923 statute and never joined Tangier's administration. Its presence rested on the interest shown by keeping a diplomatic agent there.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-61:
George Allen memoranda'd a foreign ministers' exchange on the Italian colonies, written up on July 24, 1945. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The discussion itself took place at the ministers' meeting of July 22.

Molotov recalled that Moscow had declared at San Francisco its intent to apply as a trustee power. He then turned on a Commons statement by Eden that Italy had lost its colonies in Africa and the Mediterranean. By what right, Molotov asked, had Great Britain decided this question? Who, he demanded, had found the colonies? Eden answered in kind, in a few words. Italy had lost her colonies to the British Army, he said. They sat under British military occupation pending their final disposal in the peace treaty with Italy. Molotov said his delegation had presented a paper on the subject for the next meeting.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-161:
Thompson's minutes close his conference run with a session of August 1, 1945. He had recorded Potsdam meetings since the first week. His sets, printed in the second Potsdam volume, form one of its most complete spines. This last set covers the closing day, when the final protocol was adopted.

Readers who followed Thompson across July meet a familiar, steady hand. The style stays plain to the end. That steadiness is the value: one observer's record, kept the same way throughout. The minutes let the conference be rebuilt day by day. They end where the work ended, with the deal in hand.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d761:

An opening-day letter sets the home office's tone. Grew could pass first news and steady the travelers' rear. Readers see the partnership between the two men at its start. The document pairs with Byrnes's reply of the same week. Together they frame the link that let the summit function at a distance from its own capital.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d861:
Document 861 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 20, 1945. It closes this run of the volume's papers. Staff drafted it at the end of the conference's first week. The paper stayed in the delegation files and was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

A week's-end working paper shows positions after first contact. The drafters had heard the other sides and written again. Readers can use it as a hinge in the run: behind it, preparation; ahead, the hard second week. The document ends this set where the conference itself paused to breathe, with the largest questions still open and the paper still flowing.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d961:
Secretary Byrnes handed this American proposal on German reparations to Molotov on July 30, 1945. He gave it just before the foreign ministers met that day. Russian and Polish claims would be met from the Russian zone. Two additions would come from the Ruhr, in the British zone.

The first addition is a quarter of the surplus factory equipment there. It would be traded for equal value in food, coal, potash, zinc, timber, clay goods, and oil goods from the Soviets. The second addition is a further 15 percent of such equipment. That share would pass to the Soviet government free, with no payment or exchange in return.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1061:
Secretary of State James Byrnes wrote this letter to Molotov at Potsdam on July 19, 1945. It proposes joint Allied supervision of the approaching Greek national elections. Allied duties to Greece, and the pledges made at Yalta, are given as the grounds. Responsibility to the Greek people, Byrnes argues, makes shared supervision wise.

Four governments would share the task: Britain, the Soviet Union, France, and the United States. Greece's own government has agreed to elections under their watch. That consent rests on Article 9 of the Varkiza Agreement, which provides for Allied supervision. Byrnes closes with earnest hope that the Soviet government will agree to join.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1161:

This paper is part of the American opening hand, played once the first speeches were done. Kept word for word in the record, it lets readers judge what Washington sought before the trades began.

arxiv-2606-05561: Speech can reveal mental health struggles, but screening systems that store raw voice recordings are privacy nightmares. InfoShield learns privacy-preserving speech representations for mental health screening via information-theoretic optimization — keeping the diagnostic signal while provably discarding identity. Helpful screening should not require handing over your voice.
arxiv-2606-05661: Most AI benchmarks reset the world between questions, but real deployments never do — state persists, mistakes compound. Continual Learning Bench evaluates frontier AI systems in real-world stateful environments, where agents must carry context forward across long, messy episodes. It tests whether today's AI can actually operate in the ongoing world rather than just answer isolated questions.
arxiv-2606-05761: Long-horizon AI agents must remember subtle relationships — who promised what to whom, three days ago. SubtleMemory is a benchmark for fine-grained relational memory discrimination: testing whether agents track delicate relational facts over long episodes. It measures the difference between remembering and truly keeping track.
arxiv-2606-06061: A person and a robot carrying a table together must negotiate constantly — in words. This conversational framework for human-robot collaborative manipulation uses distributed generative AI models to ground that dialogue in action. Talking through the task turns awkward co-manipulation into teamwork.
arxiv-2606-06461: Adapting a policy to a new situation usually means retraining it — expensive and slow. This paper adapts with flow-based methods and no policy updates at all: transforming the policy's outputs instead of its weights. Update-free adaptation makes deployment nimble and cheap.
arxiv-2606-06561: Quantum hydrodynamics — Madelung's fluid picture of quantum mechanics — usually assumes gentle amplitudes. This paper extends it to amplitude-dependent regimes via a coth-Madelung ansatz. The extension pushes the fluid analogy into wilder quantum waters. Strong quantum fluctuations finally get a fluid description.
arxiv-2606-06661: The nonlinear Fourier transform untangles integrable systems — but its convergence is delicate. This paper proves convergence for sparse square-summable cases. The result firms up the analysis behind soliton mathematics. Rigorous convergence grounds the transform’s practical use in applications. The proof closes a gap in integrable systems theory.
arxiv-2606-06761: Robots acting from camera images must map pixels to physical coordinates — a fragile step. AxisGuide grounds the robot's action coordinate system directly in RGB observations for robust visuomotor manipulation. Grounded coordinates make manipulation survive the real world's messiness. Robust grounding survives clutter and occlusion.
arxiv-2606-07161: Spotting text in surveillance video — signs, plates — needs trajectory-level reasoning. TraRA aggregates recognition along trajectories for video text spotting in urban surveillance. The aggregation tracks text through the city. Text tracked through busy urban scenes. Trajectory aggregation improves recognition.
arxiv-2606-00061: Markets are reflexive — predictions change the predicted. This paper asks whether prompting LLMs with that awareness improves them as financial forecasters. The reflexivity experiment tests machine self-awareness. Self-aware markets behave quite differently. The clever experiment is revealing and important.
arxiv-2606-07361: Dominating set and vertex coloring — classic hard problems — have landscapes worth analyzing. This combinatorial landscape analysis maps them. The maps guide better heuristics. Computationally hard problems have navigable energy landscapes. Careful analysis informs substantially better heuristics. Very useful.
tob-0161:
C. G. Jung published Psychology of the Unconscious in German in 1912, and Beatrice M. Hinkle's 1916 translation, the first of Jung's books in English, brought it to America. The long study of a patient's fantasies marks Jung's public break with Freud. Libido, for Jung, is general life energy, not sexuality alone, and myths are the psyche's own language.

Symbols from world mythology are read as stages of an inner transformation, a method Jung would expand into analytical psychology. Hinkle, herself an early American analyst, renders the dense argument faithfully. Readers watch a founder declare independence in real time, with consequences for a century of psychotherapy and literary criticism.
tob-10261:
Athanasius Kircher, a Jesuit scholar in Rome, published Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae, the Great Art of Light and Shadow, in 1646. He wrote on nearly every subject of his age, and optics gave him rich ground. Fine engravings fill the large volume.

Kircher treats lenses, mirrors, sundials, and light thrown through colored glass to cast pictures on walls. One device he describes stands close to the magic lantern, the ancestor of the film projector. His science mixes sound tests with wonders and errors, yet the book shows how Baroque scholars pictured light and made a show of knowing it.
tob-10361:
Johann Weyer, a Dutch physician, issued the Pseudomonarchia Daemonum in 1563 as part of his work on demons and witchcraft. Weyer doubted that accused witches had real powers. Yet he still catalogued the spirit world his age believed in.

His list names sixty-nine demons, with their ranks, forms, legions, and the hours when they may be called. Later grimoires, above all the Goetia, borrowed the list and its order. The catalogue is a master index of Renaissance demon belief, and Weyer's doubt about witch trials gives the strange book a humane core.
tob-4161:
Edward Burnett Tylor published Primitive Culture in 1871, the book that founded anthropology as a science in English. Tylor, a Quaker who never held a university post when he wrote it, worked from travelers' reports worldwide. The copy here follows the 1920 edition, in two volumes.

He defines culture, traces the doctrine of souls he calls animism, and treats magic, myth, and ritual as stages in one human development. Tylor's famous definition of culture, the complex whole of knowledge, belief, art, and custom, opens the work. The science of man begins in these volumes, complete, and every later anthropologist has argued with them.
schaaffhausen-busk-crania-ancient-races-:
Hermann Schaaffhausen first described the Neanderthal skull in German in 1858. George Busk's English translation, with his own remarks, appeared in 1861. The skull had been found in the Neander Valley in 1856 by quarry workers.

Schaaffhausen measured the brow ridge, skull shape, and limb bones in detail. Johann Fuhlrott, who first recognized the find, gives his own account here. The paper treats the bones as remains of an ancient human race. Scholars now regard it as the founding document of paleoanthropology, the study of fossil humans. Busk's notes connect the skull to other ancient remains known then.
sanderson-abominable-snowmen-legend-come:
Ivan Sanderson took up the hairy man question for English readers in 1961. Abominable Snowmen: Legend Come to Life is the first major English survey of yeti and sasquatch reports. Sanderson was a trained zoologist and a famed teller of animal tales.

Fourteen chapters gather case reports from five continents, from the high Himalayas to the woods of the Pacific coast. Appendices take up footprint casts and the wild life of the snow ranges in close detail. Sanderson argues the reports point to real, unlisted primates. His book brought the snowman debate to a wide and eager public.
brasseur-popol-vuh-1861:
The sacred book of the K'iche' Maya reached Europe in print through Brasseur de Bourbourg in 1861. Popol Vuh: Le livre sacré gives the creation epic in French, its first European edition. Brasseur had found the old manuscript in Guatemala and knew its worth at once.

His French version carried the gods, the making of man, and the Hero Twins to Western readers. The edition tied the Popol Vuh to the wide debate on American antiquity and lost lands. Every later Maya-Atlantis claim leans on the text he brought out. The book is a landmark of American studies in its own right.
du-chaillu-explorations-equatorial-afric:
Paul Du Chaillu came out of the Gabon forests in 1861 with skins, skulls, and a sensation. Explorations and Adventures in Equatorial Africa made the gorilla a household word in Europe and America. No living gorilla had yet been seen by the crowds who read him.

Du Chaillu tells of hunts, river trips, and tribes of the deep forest, with the great ape as his star. His monster ape, charging and roaring, fixed the gorilla in the public mind for good. Later travelers faulted parts of his tale, but the fame held. The book turned a rumor of the woods into a beast of science.
levi-clef-des-grands-mysteres-1861:
Eliphas Levi drew his whole creed into one book in La Clef des grands mysteres, out in 1861. The title means the key to the great riddles. He links the lore of the Jews, the cards of the tarot, and a bright force he calls the Astral Light.

Levi claims one key can unlock faith, lore, and rite at once. The book is dense, bold, and meant for keen minds. French occult groups took it as core creed. It is the ripe fruit of his thought, in his own tongue. Ranks of signs and keys crowd the last parts of the book. Keen fans used them as a map for their own rites and drills.
kardec-le-livre-des-mediums-1861:
Allan Kardec trains the seer in Le Livre des mediums, his French guide of 1861. The name means the book on mediums. Kardec had set out his faith's creed in his prior book. Here he turns to craft: how sittings should run, what kinds of seers there are, what frauds and risks to watch, and how to weigh words from the dead.

Rules, types, and warns fill the guide in calm prose. His faith took it as its chief hand book at once. In French, it is the school text of a world faith. Its order is its strength.
dircks-perpetuum-mobile-1861:
Henry Dircks, an English engineer, spent years on the hunt for self motive power, and this survey came out in 1861. Men had tried for three hundred years to build a wheel that would turn for ever with no fuel. Dircks set out to list them all.

The book walks through scheme after scheme, with drawings of wheels, weights, and fluids. Dircks shows where each one fails, in plain terms a lay reader can grasp. His survey is still the main guide to the long hunt for a machine that cannot work.
pasteur-corpuscules-organises-1861:
Louis Pasteur read this memoir in French in 1861, on the tiny bodies that float in the air. It deals head on with the claim that life can spring from dead stuff. The work grew from his prize clash with Pouchet and his school.

His famed swan neck flasks let air in but trapped dust in the bent neck. Broth in such flasks stayed pure for months, while dust let life bloom at once. The clear proof, shown in a famed talk of the time, brought the long debate to an end.
rodwell-koran-1861:
John Medows Rodwell, an English cleric and friend of Darwin, made this English Koran in 1861. The text here is from the second print of 1876. Rodwell was a sound Arabic scholar, and his aim was a clear, true text for the English reader.

His new step was the order: he sets the surahs, the parts of the Koran, by the time they were first given out. That order lets a reader trace how the word of the Prophet grew with the years of his life. The book is the Koran re-set by time, a first of its kind in English.
dircks-perpetuum-mobile-first-series-186:
Henry Dircks was an English engineer with a rage for one theme. His Perpetuum Mobile, First Series, came out in 1861. The book lists scheme on scheme for a wheel that runs for all time. Dircks dug through rolls, tracts, and tales of three hundred years.

Wheels with weights, mills with pumps, and craft with magnets all get their due. Most tales end in fraud, flaw, or a hid spring of force. Dircks meant the book as a warn to men who waste life on the dream. The pair of series is the full tale of the vain hunt.
dickens-great-expectations-1861:
Charles Dickens published Great Expectations in 1861, a late novel many call his most perfect. Pip, Miss Havisham, and the convict Magwitch anchor its tight, ironic plot of ambition. Dickens shaped the tale with care and gave it a revised, softer end in print.

Pip, an orphan smith's boy, helps a convict and dreams of a finer life. A secret fortune lets him train as a gentleman in London town and lodgings. He snubs Joe, the kind smith who raised him, and chases cold Estella in vain. The fortune's true source shocks him and teaches him where worth truly lies in men. Few novels trace shame, love, and growth with such clean, hard force.
eliot-george-silas-marner-1861:
George Eliot published Silas Marner in 1861, her flawless fable of a betrayed weaver and a foundling child. A betrayed weaver hoards gold until a foundling child redeems him,. Eliot said the tale came to her as a legend meant to show the fruits of a recovered faith.

Silas, falsely cast out by his chapel, lives alone at Raveloe weaving and counting his guineas in isolation. His gold is stolen by Dunstan Cass, and a golden-haired child crawls to his hearth from the snow. Eppie, the child of an opium-dead mother, becomes his treasure and his bridge back to church, neighbors, and human trust in Raveloe. Sixteen years later her choice of the weaver who raised her seals the fable's moral. Its symmetry and warmth make it the Eliot novel most often given to the young.
mill-representative-government-1861:
John Stuart Mill published his book on elected rule in 1861, a classic theory of how free peoples should govern. Mill argues this form is best for nations that have grown mature. It trains men and women by giving them a share in rule. He backs a wide vote, with tests he thought kept it sound.

Mill gives the first strong case for fair shares of seats by votes cast. He calls this plan a great step forward. He also weighs town rule, unions of states, and rule over subject lands. On that last point, later readers fault him. Students still read the book beside On Liberty.
spencer-education-1861:
Herbert Spencer published Education in 1861, a set of essays on how children should be taught. His famous question opens the work: what knowledge is of most worth? His answer is science, in all its forms, for health, work, parenting, and citizenship. Classical languages, the pride of old schools, rank low by that test.

Spencer urges lessons that follow the child's own growth and curiosity. He opposes rote learning, harsh punishment, and cramming for exams. The essays helped found the science-based side of modern pedagogy. Teachers still quote his central question. The book reads as fresh common sense even where later practice moved on.
boyle-sceptical-chymist-1661:
Robert Boyle's Sceptical Chymist, published in 1661, is a dialogue that demolishes the old theories of matter. Speaker after speaker defends the four elements or the three principles of the alchemists, and each defense fails. The book is counted the founding text of modern chemistry.

Boyle argues that elements must be found by experiment, not assumed from ancient systems or furnace habits. His careful trials with air, acids, and colors model a new way of asking nature questions. Later chemists looked back to Boyle's dialogue as the moment their science learned to doubt in an orderly way.
morin-astrologia-gallica-1661:
Jean-Baptiste Morin was a French royal astrologer and professor whose Astrologia Gallica appeared in 1661, after his death. The work runs to twenty-six books in Latin, the fruit of a lifetime at the art. It is the last great Latin system of judicial astrology.

Morin rebuilds the judgment of nativities on strict rules for a planet's state, place, and aspects within the whole chart. He scorns cookbook reading and demands that each chart be weighed as one living configuration. Modern traditional astrologers still study Morin in translation as the master who gave their art its firmest method.
macaulay-history-england-vol-5-1861:
Volume 5 of Macaulay's History of England from the Accession of James II appeared in 1861, after Thomas Babington Macaulay's death. Friends prepared the unfinished volume from his papers. It carries his story of William III's reign toward the end of the seventeenth century.

War with France, plots against the king, and fights over taxes and trade fill the chapters. Macaulay kept his vivid style, painting scenes and judging men with confidence. The volume stops short of the full span he had planned. Even unfinished, it closed the most popular English history of its age, a work that taught generations how to picture the Glorious Revolution and its gains.
faraday-chemical-history-candle-1861:
Michael Faraday gave the lectures printed as The Chemical History of a Candle in 1861. Faraday, the great experimenter at the Royal Institution in London, delivered them as Christmas lectures for young people. A single candle, he showed, could teach the whole of basic chemistry.

Flame by flame, Faraday explained burning, air, water, and the gases a candle makes and takes. He used simple gear and clear words, testing each claim before his audience's eyes. The lectures became a landmark of popular science writing. They still serve as a first book in chemistry, proof that deep science can be taught from the plainest object on a table.
njals-saga-dasent-1861:
George Webbe Dasent published The Story of Burnt Njal in 1861, his translation of Njal's Saga. The Icelandic saga, written in the 1200s, is often called the greatest of its kind. Dasent, a scholar of Norse tales, gave it its first English form.

Njal, a wise and peaceful farmer, tries to hold back the feuds that grip his kin and neighbors. His friend Gunnar's pride and others' envy light a chain of killings that law cannot stop. The feud ends in the burning of Njal's house, with him inside. The saga blends law, fate, and stark dialogue. Dasent's version remains a landmark English dress for a masterpiece.
mill-utilitarianism-1861:
John Stuart Mill published Utilitarianism in 1861, first as magazine essays and then as a short book. Mill defended the moral theory he had learned from Jeremy Bentham and his own father. Its rule is simple to state: the right act is the one that brings the greatest happiness overall.

Mill answered the charge that the theory is a pig philosophy by ranking pleasures of mind above those of body. He argued for liberty, justice, and rules that protect the weak as parts of happiness itself. The essay is short, clear, and argued with care against named critics. It remains the canonical statement of utilitarian ethics, the first text most students read on the subject.
maine-ancient-law-1861:
Sir Henry Sumner Maine published Ancient Law in 1861. Maine, a law professor who later served in India, compared the oldest legal records of Rome, India, and other lands. He asked how law itself began and how it changed as societies grew.

Maine's famous summary runs from status to contract: early law fixes each person's place by birth, while modern law lets persons make their own bargains. He traced property, wills, and crime from family rule toward individual right. The phrase and the book founded comparative legal history and the sociology of law. Later research corrected many details, but Maine's questions still organize the study of early law.
galileo-discourse-floating-bodies-salusb:
Galileo Galilei's Discourse on floating bodies, written in 1612, appears here in Thomas Salusbury's 1661 English translation, A Discourse Concerning Bodies in Water. Galileo wrote the work in a dispute at the Medici court over why ice floats. His opponents held Aristotelian views on shape and density.

Galileo argued that floating rests on the weight of the body compared with the water it pushes aside, not on flat shape. Experiments with wax and water backed his account of hydrostatics. Salusbury's translation, printed in London, first brought Galileo's physics to English readers in their own tongue. The short work shows Galileo's style: court debate turned into careful test and proof.
galileo-mathematical-collections-salusbu:
Thomas Salusbury published Mathematical Collections and Translations in 1661 in London, a landmark set of Italian science in English. Salusbury chose and Englished works that English readers could not otherwise reach. Galileo stands at the center of the volume.

The set gives the first English forms of Galileo's Mechanics and his early work On Motion, called De Motu. Works by Castelli and Torricelli, Galileo's heirs in the study of water and motion, stand beside them. Salusbury meant to import a whole school of science at once. It shaped how English thinkers, in Newton's age, first met the Italian founders of modern study of motion.
holmes-elsie-venner-1861:
Oliver Wendell Holmes published Elsie Venner in 1861, calling it a romance of destiny. Holmes, a professor of anatomy, wanted to test a medical idea in fiction: how far is a person responsible for traits fixed before birth? The novel is the first American work of biological determinism.

Elsie Venner's mother was bitten by a rattlesnake shortly before her birth, and Elsie grows up beautiful, strange, and half serpentine in temper. Her schoolmaster falls in love with her while a doctor watches the case like an experiment. Holmes weaves New England village life around the central question of inherited sin and free will. The idea came from his medical lectures, and readers argued about Elsie for decades.
heine-poems-bowring-1861:
Edgar Alfred Bowring translated the complete poems of Heinrich Heine into English in 1861. The volume holds the Book of Songs, the young Heine's lyrics of love and loss, and the later cycles that darkened his tone. Schubert and Schumann set many of these lyrics to music that still fills concert halls.

Heine's short poems turn on a dime from tender to ironic. A love song can end with a shrug that undoes its own sweetness. Bowring kept the meters close to the German so English readers could sing along in spirit. German schoolchildren have learned these poems for generations. Bowring's volume long gave English readers their fullest Heine in verse.
silius-italicus-punica-english-1661:
Silius Italicus, a Roman consul and rich patron of poets, spent his last years writing the Punica, an epic on the Second Punic War. At seventeen books it is the longest Latin epic that survives. Thomas Ross turned it into English verse in 1661, the first time the poem had appeared in the language.

Hannibal crosses the Alps, wins at Cannae, and slowly loses the war to Roman patience and to Scipio. Silius follows Livy for the facts and Virgil for the music, with gods and omens at work above the armies. Ross's version is a landmark of translation history. The poem itself is Rome's last full epic of its own past.
bonaventure-itinerarium-mentis-latin-186:
Bonaventure wrote the Itinerarium Mentis in Deum, the Journey of the Mind to God, in 1259. He was on retreat at La Verna, where Francis had borne the stigmata. Karl Joseph von Hefele edited the Latin text in 1861. No English version in the public domain exists, so the Latin stands here as the record of the central Franciscan ascent text.

Six steps, like the six wings of the seraph, lift the soul. They climb through the world, through the senses, and through the mind's powers, to the vision of Being and of the Good. A seventh step is rest, the peace past thought. The little book is dense and burning at once. Generations of mystics climbed by its ladder.
catcott-treatise-on-the-deluge-1761:
Alexander Catcott defended the Deluge as Earth's great agent in his Treatise of 1761. Catcott was a Bristol clergyman of the Hutchinsonian school. That school set Moses's philosophy, drawn from Hebrew scripture, against Newton's system. His treatise reads the Flood as the force that shaped the crust.

Strata, fossils, and mountains all become the Deluge's work in his hands. Remarks on the Bishop of Clogher's account of the same subject join the argument. Catcott writes as a divine who trusts scripture above the new philosophy. His book shows diluvial thought fighting on into the age of geology. It preserves a losing side argued with learning. The controversy itself is the lesson.
rousseau-julie-kenrick-1761:
Julie and Saint-Preux trade letters across a Swiss lake in Rousseau's Julie, the novel William Kenrick Englished in 1761. That first English version, titled The New Eloisa, carried a bestseller across the Channel. A tutor loves his pupil, and duty, rank, and marriage stand between them for six long volumes.

Europe wept over Julie, and the book taught a generation to feel in a new key. Love, nature, and virtue argue in every letter, with the Alps watching over all. As a founding text of Romanticism in fiction, it shaped the novel of feeling for a century.
plos-pone-0003461:
Lorenza S. Colzato, Wery P. M. van den Wildenberg, and Bernhard Hommel measured blink rates in cocaine users in 2008. Long cocaine use lowers a class of dopamine receptors in the brain. Dopamine is a chemical tied to reward and self-control. Even casual use had been linked to weaker cognitive control.

Spontaneous blink rate is a rough gauge of dopamine activity. Recreational users blinked less often than non-users in this study. That pattern fits sluggish dopamine function, called hypoactivity. A simple eye measure may thus flag drug effects on brain control systems.
plos-pone-0003561:
Wiriya Rutvisuttinunt, Peter R. Meyer, and Walter A. Scott probed HIV's copying enzyme in this 2008 paper. Reverse transcriptase turns the virus's RNA into DNA. It binds tightly at fixed spots on a primer-template pair. Those stable complexes are the enzyme's working state.

The team examined contacts between the enzyme and the downstream template strand. Such contacts guide the enzyme as it copies. Fine detail on this grip exposes weak points in the machine. HIV drugs aim to jam this very enzyme. Each new grip detail gives drug design one more place to aim.
plos-pone-0003661:
Yongliang Yang, Lakshmanan K. Iyer, S. James Adelstein, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Doctors favor blood tests for finding cancer early, since blood is easy to draw and test. The team mined combined genomic data for signs of cancer that reach the blood.

Their search aimed at markers that could flag cancer before symptoms appear, when treatment works best. By pooling data across studies, they could spot signals too weak to see in one set alone. The work offers leads for blood tests aimed at early diagnosis rather than late confirmation.
plos-pone-0003761:
Charlotte Labalette, Yann Nouët, Florence Levillayer, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2008. FHL2 is a small protein tied to several pathways that control cell growth and tissue balance. The group had shown it regulates cyclin D1, a driver of cell division.

Here they show FHL2 mediates transformation driven by Ras, a classic cancer gene. It acts through the cyclin D1 and p53 pathways together. The finding flips a normal growth regulator into a cancer accomplice, and names routes by which it helps cells turn malignant.
plos-pone-0003861:
Arie Baratt, Sergey N. Arkhipov, and Ivan V. Maly published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Killer T cells destroy infected and cancerous cells with precision. To strike, a T cell positions its centrosome near the contact point with its target, the immunological synapse. How microtubules help set that polarity was controversial.

Combining experiments with computation, the team studied the effects of microtubule stabilization on T-cell polarity. Their results clarify the cytoskeletal choreography behind the immune system's precision strikes, and which parts of it depend on stable microtubules. Aim matters, since a missed aim wastes the cell's one strong strike.
plos-pone-0003961:
Pavel Krejci, Lisa Salazar, Tamara A. Kashiwada, and co-authors tested a growth receptor's signal in cartilage in 2008. Mutations that overactivate FGFR3 cause several human skeletal dysplasias. Those disorders stunt bone growth in the limbs. Many believed the transcription factor STAT1 carried the harmful signal.

Their PLOS ONE article tested six FGFR3 mutants for STAT1 activation. The results undermine the idea that STAT1 dominates the signal in cartilage. If STAT1 is not the main route, other paths must explain stunted growth. The work redirects the search for treatments for these dysplasias. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004061:
Qingzhong Xiao, Shu Ye, Friedrich Oberhollenzer, and co-authors drew on the Bruneck population study in 2008. SDF1 is a signal that guides progenitor cells to where they are needed. Its receptor, CXCR4, helps cells home, mobilize, and mature. Such repair cells in blood are called endothelial progenitor cells.

Their PLOS ONE article links a variant in the SDF1 gene to blood levels. The variant also tracked with counts of endothelial progenitor cells. Inherited differences may set how much repair capacity a person carries. That could matter for recovery after artery injury. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004161:
Hannes Drexler published this cancer cell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cells under stress in the endoplasmic reticulum, their protein-folding compartment, pause most protein production while switching on protective genes. Part of this response works by disabling a key translation factor by tagging it with phosphate.

Drexler tested the phosphatase inhibitor salubrinal together with proteasome inhibitors, drugs that block the cell's protein shredder, on leukaemic cells. He reports that the two drug types work together, inducing far more cell death than either alone. The pairing suggests a strategy for pushing stressed cancer cells past the point of recovery.
plos-pone-0004261:
Lisa Ng and colleagues published this outbreak study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Little was known about how chikungunya virus, a mosquito-borne virus, damages the body. During the first Singaporean chikungunya fever outbreak in early 2008, the team analysed immune mediators and growth factors circulating in patients' blood. The outbreak gave them a rare, well-defined group of patients to study.

Their goal was to establish biomarkers, measurable signs, associated with infection severity. They report that IL-1β, IL-6, and RANTES stand out as biomarkers of chikungunya severity. Such markers could help doctors spot, early on, which fever patients will become seriously ill.
plos-pone-0004361:
Jing Xiang and colleagues published this drug discovery study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cyclin-dependent kinases, or CDKs, control the cell cycle. Cancers often show too much of them, or switch them on wrongly. As a result, these kinases have become extensively studied targets for anti-cancer drugs. That is why drug hunters prize them.

The team combined combinatorial chemistry, which generates many candidate compounds, with zebrafish assays to identify tumour cell growth inhibitors. Testing candidates in living fish embryos filters for compounds that work in a whole animal, not just a dish. The pipeline hunts for kinase blockers with real potential.
plos-pone-0004461:
A remedy drawn from a plant may help repair hearts hurt by heart attack, report Lei Cheng, Hao Chen, Xinsheng Yao, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Heart attack, caused by blocked arteries, remains one of the top causes of early death. Dead heart muscle is normally replaced by scar, not by new working muscle.

True repair would mean regrowing heart tissue, either from the body's own progenitor cells or from stem cells brought in from outside. The team tested a plant-derived remedy toward that ideal. Their work asks whether a natural compound can push the heart toward real regeneration rather than scar. Even small steps matter here, because any gain in working muscle after an attack can add years of life.
plos-pone-0004561:
A signaling protein in the gut lining is essential to protect the bowel during chemical injury, show Jae-Young Kim, Rie Kajino-Sakamoto, Emily Omori, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is TAK1. Earlier, the team had shown that mice lacking TAK1 only in the intestinal epithelium suffer severe inflammation and die as newborns, because a death signal called TNF kills their gut cells.

Removing the TNF receptor largely rescued those newborns. This study follows the story into chemically induced colitis, inflammation of the colon, in older animals. TAK1 signaling from the epithelium proved essential for cytoprotection, the defense of cells against injury. The work maps a pathway that gut-healing drugs for colitis might aim to support.
plos-pone-0004661:
A computer model of virus sensing predicts new features of a key immune pathway, present Mohamed Helmy, Jin Gohda, Jun-ichiro Inoue, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The sensor is Toll-like receptor 3, which plays a critical role in the innate immune response against viral attacks. It recognizes double-stranded RNA, a hallmark of many viruses, or a synthetic mimic of it.

Recognition leads to activation of MAP kinases and NF-kappaB, switches that launch antiviral defenses in macrophages. The team modeled TLR3 signaling in these immune cells to predict novel features of the pathway. Predictions from a model can be tested in the lab, turning guesswork into a checklist. That speeds the search for points where immunity to viruses fails.
plos-pone-0004761:
Diana Rigola and colleagues presented a high output method to find induced and natural DNA changes, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Reverse genetics starts from a gene change and asks what trait it causes. That needs fast screens that can spot single letter changes in pooled DNA from many plants or animals.

Older screens for such changes were slow and labor heavy. The KeyPoint method pools samples and uses deep sequencing to find rare changes. Faster finds speed up gene function studies and crop breeding. Breeders can locate useful variants in large populations with less work. Taken together, the findings mark a useful step for research in this area.
rousseau-inequality-1761:
Rousseau was born at Geneva on June 28, 1712, a watchmaker's son, a note up front records. His schooling was patchy, and he tried engraving, music, and teaching before fame found him. A prize essay for the Academy of Dijon first made his name.

The discourse printed here asks where human inequality began and what grounds it. Rousseau argues that private property and civil life warped a free and equal nature. The note calls the work unsound in places yet mighty in effect. It fed the zeal for liberty, fraternity, and equality that drove the French Revolution, and it still provokes debate.
semmelweis-aetiologie-kindbettfieber-186:
Ignaz Semmelweis was a Hungarian doctor who worked in a Vienna birth clinic. In 1861 he set out his findings in German in a long, hard-fought book on childbed fever. He had seen far too many young mothers die after giving birth.

Semmelweis showed that doctors carried the fever from dead bodies to healthy women. He proved that washing hands in a chlorine mix cut deaths at once. Most doctors of his day mocked him, and he died in disgrace. His book now stands as the first great work on clean hands and safe care.
eisenhower-farewell-1961:
Dwight D. Eisenhower gave his Farewell Address in January 1961. The old general warned against the military-industrial complex by name. No presidential warning since Washington's has been quoted so often.

Eisenhower had led the crusade in Europe and built much of the arms world. Yet he cautions that its vast sway could harm free government itself. He urges balance, thrift, and care for the nation's schools and farms. A soldier's farewell doubles as a prophecy Americans still debate. The speech gains force from the speaker's own unmatched war record in Europe. Only the supreme commander could warn so credibly against arms buildup.
kennedy-inaugural-1961:
John F. Kennedy delivered his Inaugural Address in the snow in 1961. A new generation takes power in his crisp, ringing phrases. Ask not what your country can do for you, he tells Americans.

Ask what you can do for your country, the famous line concludes. Kennedy pledges strength for liberty's defense anywhere on the globe. He calls foes to talks and friends to shared, bold ventures. Grace, vigor, and high purpose mark the speech from its first words. The address defined the New Frontier and an era's bright, brief hopes. Its balanced sentences are still quoted at graduations across the land.
cia-0000014661: Samuel Novick is the subject of an untitled CIA file dated April 3, 1957. The file draws on an article by Victor Riesel in his newspaper column. Columnists fed the files with names and claims the agency then checked. Novick was a businessman whose left wing ties drew watch in the anti Communist years.

A CIA record dated May 4, 1983 concerns the 1967 crash site of an American Air Force F-4 aircraft. The site lay in My Hao district, in the Haiphong area of North Vietnam. F-4 Phantoms flew many of the bombing missions over the north during the war years. The two-man Phantom was the workhorse of the air war, and many were lost.

The record fixes where one lost aircraft came down, sixteen years after the crash. Crash sites mattered because they often held the answer to a crew's fate. Marking this one kept open the chance that searchers could one day visit the ground and learn what happened to the men aboard.
cia-0000043361:
Cuban government reactions to current crises fill a CIA record dated December 23, 1958. The date is the story: Fulgencio Batista's regime had days left to live. Rebels under Fidel Castro were closing on power across the island.

Inside, Havana's responses to the crises around it are recorded. A government in its final week speaks in a special tone. Orders, denials, and appeals all carry the sound of an ending. Within days, the government issuing them would be gone from the palace. The file preserves that sound from inside the old order, days before Batista fled and the revolution remade Cuba for the rest of the century.
cia-0000046761: Hanoi's running count of claimed American planes downed reached 4,036 in a CIA item dated October 5, 1972. The same dispatch carried word of an F-111 lost, naming its commander. Lina Cheng and colleagues showed PP1 gamma2 and PPP1R11 form a multimeric complex in developing testicular germ cells, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mice lacking protein phosphatase 1 gamma isoforms are male sterile due to defective germ cell morphogenesis and apoptosis. Deficiency causes no obvious abnormality in other tissues, and a biochemical approach examined how output varies and partners interact during sperm cell growth.

Steady state levels of partners are reciprocally related. Complex balance controls germ cell maturation. Disruption explains tissue specific sterility. Male fertility depends on precise phosphatase control. Later work can build on these findings and test them in broader settings.
plos-pone-0005461:
Gerardo Suzán and colleagues linked rodent variety to virus spread in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Many new diseases jump from animals to people, and changes made by humans can raise that risk. The team asked whether losing kinds of rodents changes how common hantavirus is among those that remain.

In field tests where rodent variety was lowered, the share of rodents carrying the virus went up. Fewer kinds meant the remaining hosts met the virus more often. The result warns that harming wild variety can raise disease risk for people living nearby.
plos-pone-0005561:
Sujit Suchindran, Emily Brouwer, and Annelies Van Rie reviewed studies on HIV and drug-resistant tuberculosis in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Tuberculosis is a major cause of suffering and death worldwide. Forms that resist standard drugs have become a threat to disease control, alongside HIV.

The authors gathered the published evidence on whether HIV infection raises the risk of drug-resistant tuberculosis. A careful review weighs weak and strong studies together before drawing a verdict. The answer guides testing and treatment policy where both diseases are common. The review method also shows where the record is too thin to settle the question, marking what to study next.
plos-pone-0005661:
A Whitman Miller and co-authors studied oyster larvae in more acidic water in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Human activity has raised the carbon dioxide in the air, and the oceans absorb much of it. That makes seawater more acidic and changes the chemistry shellfish need to build shells.

The team raised oyster larvae in estuary water at different acidity levels. Larvae in more acidic water built shells more slowly and grew less. The results warn that oyster beds, and the fisheries on them, face a hard future as the oceans change.
plos-pone-0005761:
Mark Romanish and co-authors found in 2009 that a human gene carries its own built-in promoters made from ancient viral-like scraps. The gene, NAIP, helps guard nerve cells from death and also serves innate immunity. Scraps called Alu elements litter the human genome by the million.

Some of those scraps inside NAIP act as start switches for a new, shorter form of the protein. That variant may do a different job than the full-length form. The find shows how junk DNA can be recycled into working controls. It adds a case study in how genomes invent new protein forms cheaply.
plos-pone-0005861:
Hon Cheng Muh, Joo Chuan Tong, and Martti Tammi built a program in 2009 to judge whether a protein might trigger allergy. Allergy is a growing problem in industrialized countries. With more engineered food crops arriving, their proteins need safety checks before entering the food chain.

Their system, AllerHunter, pairs machine learning with pairwise sequence comparison to flag allergen risk and cross-reactivity. Older bioinformatics tools did well, but a sharper screen catches more hazards. Regulators and breeders can run new proteins through it early. The goal is food innovation without surprise allergies.
plos-pone-0006461:
Michelle Millington and co-authors refined gene delivery into blood stem cells for PLOS ONE in 2009. Blood-forming stem cells, especially those drawn from peripheral blood, are attractive targets for cell and gene therapy. Getting new genes into them with lentiviruses can work well. The catch is doing so without harming their ability to renew themselves and make all blood cell types.

The team worked toward a transduction protocol fit for clinical use. Their focus was primary human CD34 positive stem and progenitor cells. A clinic-ready protocol must be both efficient and gentle. Progress here brings gene therapy for blood diseases closer to routine care.
plos-pone-0006561:
Bruno Sainz, Naina Barretto, and Susan Uprichard compared liver cell lines for hepatitis C work in PLOS ONE in 2009. In 2005, the first robust hepatitis C virus infectious cell culture system was developed. It was based on a genotype 2a clone called JFH-1 and Huh7 human hepatoma cells. Different Huh7 cell lines vary in phenotype, though.

The team studied HCV infection in phenotypically distinct Huh7 cell lines. Line choice can change experimental outcomes, so documenting differences matters. Their comparison helps labs pick the right line and interpret past results. Good cell models underpin all drug testing for this virus.
plos-pone-0009461:
Olivia Masseck, Sascha Forster, and Klaus-Peter Hoffmann studied motion vision in goldfish in PLOS ONE in 2010. Seeing movement across the whole view helps animals steer through space. In fish, nerve cells in a brain area called the pretectum do much of this work. The team showed fish patterns of moving dots.

Some dot patterns moved together, and some were random noise. The fish gave behavior responses, and the team also recorded from the motion sensing cells. Comparing the two showed how faint a motion the fish can still detect. The study ties single cells to whole animal sight in a clean, direct way.
plos-pone-0009561:
Josef Krieglstein and colleagues fed guinea pigs a fat rich diet in PLOS ONE in 2010. Oleic acid is the main fat in olive oil and is often called a healthy fat. In dishes, though, it can kill blood vessel cells by switching on certain enzymes. The team tested whether that harm appears in whole animals. They fed guinea pigs a diet rich in trioleate, a form of oleic acid.

They looked for damage in the heart and arteries of the fed animals. They also treated heart cells in dishes with oleic acid for comparison. The work tests whether a dish result holds in a living body. It complicates simple claims about good and bad fats.
plos-pone-0009661:
Francisco Azuaje, Yvan Devaux, and Daniel Wagner modeled heart failure after heart attack in PLOS ONE in 2010. After a heart attack, the main pumping chamber often weakens over time. Genes do not act alone in that decline; they work in pathways. The team built a computer model centered on pathways, not single genes. They combined gene data from failing and healthy hearts.

A pathway view can reveal drivers that single gene lists miss. Their model ranks which pathways best explain the ventricle's decline. Those top pathways are candidates for treatment research. The study shows how systems modeling can guide the search for ways to protect the heart after an attack.
plos-pone-0010461:
Helen Murphy and Clifford Zeyl measured how often yeasts mate outside their own family lines in PLOS ONE in 2010. Baker's and brewer's yeasts are laboratory staples across biology. Their wild sex lives, though, were barely known. Lab work over a century mapped mating within yeast colonies. In nature, spores from different colonies may meet and mix. The team measured that outcrossing rate.

Crossing between colonies turned out surprisingly common. Frequent mixing reshuffles genes and speeds adaptation in the wild. It also changes how scientists should model yeast evolution. A lab organism's natural history often surprises those who only know the lab. This study restores yeast to its wild context.
plos-pone-0010561:
Cynthia Massaad and co-workers studied an Alzheimer's mouse model in PLOS ONE in 2010. They linked a reactive oxygen form in mitochondria to blood flow and transport problems. Alzheimer's brings memory decline plus clumps of amyloid and tau in the brain. A state of oxidation has long been noticed in the disease. The team used the Tg2576 mouse, which makes human amyloid. They focused on superoxide made inside mitochondria, the cell's power plants.

That superoxide contributed to poor blood flow and slowed transport along nerve fibers. Both faults can starve and disconnect brain cells early in disease. Targeting mitochondrial superoxide is therefore a candidate strategy. The study connects oxidation to concrete physical failures in the living brain. It moves beyond merely noting that oxidation is present.
plos-pone-0010661:
Andrew Vallely and colleagues ran a feasibility study in Mwanza, Tanzania, reported in PLOS ONE in 2010. Vaginal microbicides are gels meant to block HIV during sex. Testing them fairly requires volunteers at real risk who will stay in a long trial.

The team recruited women working in bars, guesthouses, and similar venues. They tracked attendance, retention, and HIV rates over the study period. The cohort stayed engaged and showed infection rates high enough for a fair test. That groundwork means a full trial in this population can give a trustworthy answer about whether a gel works.
plos-pone-0010761:
Sophie Smout and colleagues modeled how a generalist predator's eating changes with prey numbers, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Predators shape prey populations through their functional response: how much one predator eats as prey grows scarce or plentiful. A generalist eating several prey species complicates that curve, since it can switch targets.

The model let prey densities rise and fall together. Eating rates depended on the whole prey mix, not one species alone. Ignoring the mix can mislead forecasts of predator impact. Better curves help managers judge, for example, whether protecting a predator will truly suppress a pest species or merely shift its diet.
plos-pone-0010861:
Changnian Song, Jinggui Fang, Chen Wang and co-authors published this plant methods study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Computers can predict microRNAs, the tiny gene regulators found in plants and animals, but they cannot pin down a molecule's exact start and end. Without exact ends, predictions stay rough, so the team built a lab method to finish the job.

Their approach, called MiR-RACE, enriches a sample for microRNAs from trifoliate orange, then runs two targeted reactions that read each molecule's precise ends before cloning.
