Song and colleagues present it as an efficient route from computer guess to verified sequence. Reliable microRNA sequences matter for plant breeding and stress research, since these small molecules help control how crops grow and cope with drought or disease.
plos-pone-0010961:
Thomas Birkballe Hansen, Jesper Bertram Bramsen and Jørgen Kjems published this gene discovery study in PLOS ONE in 2010. MicroRNAs are tiny bits of RNA that help run cell growth and disease. Listing them all is a first step toward grasping either process. Rather than making new data, the authors re-mined two large published data sets of small RNAs. Those sets came from human stem cells taken from embryos.

The new look turned up more than a hundred candidate new structures. Lab checks confirmed real processing in most of the cases they tested. Adding more public data sets strengthened several further candidates. Hansen and colleagues demonstrate that yesterday's sequencing data still hides undiscovered genes. Their haul expands the known human list and makes a broad case for revisiting stored data with fresh eyes.
plos-pone-0011061:
Christofer Bang, John Sabo and Stanley Faeth published this urban ecology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Plants usually grow better in cities than in surrounding wild land, a pattern blamed on warmer temperatures, extra water, and nutrients. The authors proposed a neglected factor: buildings shelter plants from wind, and wind is known to stunt crops in farm fields.

They designed a field experiment in a desert city to test whether reduced wind speed alone explains the urban growth bonus. Comparing plants in sheltered and exposed settings while other city effects were accounted for, they found that calmer air improves growth. Bang and colleagues add wind shelter to the list of ways cities reshape nature. The result helps explain why urban ecosystems are often more productive than the deserts they replace.
plos-pone-0011161:
Chen, Xie, Zhang and colleagues explored stroke damage in PLOS ONE in 2010. When blood flow to the brain is cut, a channel in nerve cells can open too far and let cells die. The team tested whether drugs that block a fat breaking enzyme could close that harmful channel.

Those blocker drugs did stop the channel's activity and the cell death that followed. That protective route could save brain tissue if given soon after stroke. Stroke care gains from every new target, since current options are few and time bound. The result gives drug makers a defined channel and a drug class to explore.
plos-pone-0011261:
Zhang, Savelieva, Suwanichkul and colleagues studied a little known mouse protein in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, called Tmub1, appears in the brain and other tissues. Mice lacking it were tested for movement and sleep wake patterns, and its partners inside cells were identified.

Loss of the protein changed locomotor activity and wakefulness in the mice. It also interacted with a known partner protein in cells, placing it in a defined circuit. A single obscure protein thus turns out to help run daily activity and rest. The finding informs research on sleep and movement disorders.
plos-pone-0011361:
Yan-Chuan Shi and colleagues used mice in 2010 to separate the brain's control of fat from its control of bone. A brain chemical called NPY acts through receptors in nerve cells, and one receptor type had been linked to both body fat and skeleton strength. The question was which of those effects truly start in the brain.

By removing the receptor only from NPY nerve cells, the team showed that fat stores and spongy inner bone changed, while hard outer bone stayed normal. That split proves the brain steers some bone and fat traits through one narrow pathway, not all at once. The result helps obesity and bone researchers target the right circuit. A treatment aimed at this receptor might adjust fat and inner bone without disturbing the bone shell.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1261:
A second Sato cable to Togo bears the date 30 July 1945. The Moscow embassy sent its last July reports in pairs as the crisis thickened. Each tested the Soviet mood one more time and found it unchanged.

By then the pattern was fixed. Moscow gained by waiting, and Tokyo's need grew by the day. Sato's twin reports of 30 July hold that pattern at its end. Within a week the atomic bomb and Soviet entry would end the waiting by force. This cable is part of the record of the days just before, when paper was still Japan's only weapon.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1361:
Henry Villard, chief of the Division of African Affairs, wrote to the acting secretary of state on 27 July 1945. Villard's division handled American ties with Africa inside the State Department. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Africa rarely tops the Potsdam story, yet the department kept a full division on it, and its chief could write straight to the acting secretary. Questions of colonies, bases, and trade crossed Villard's desk in 1945 as empires began to loosen. This paper brings that corner of the department into the record. It reminds readers that the postwar world was being argued over on every continent, not Europe alone.
frus-1945-50-intel-d61:
Minutes dated 26 December 1945 record a meeting held in the quiet week between Christmas and the new year. The intelligence question did not rest for the holiday. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Late December meetings in Washington are usually small and pointed: the men who attend are the ones who must finish the work. These minutes belong to the final clearing of ground before the January directive. Readers can use them to date the moment when argument gave way to drafting. The volume's long autumn of rival plans ends in this season. The papers of the new year open with a president's signature instead of another committee's view.
frus-1945-50-intel-d161:
The title "Central Intelligence Group Directive No. 14" heads a text dated 19 July 1946. It survives in print as document 161 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The first peace-time setup paired the National Intelligence Authority at the top with the Central Intelligence Group below it.

Orders of this kind turned broad policy into daily rules. They name the office in charge and the work to be done. The shelf of such orders, read in order, is the true org chart of the system as it grew. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d261:
A memorandum dated 11 March 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Chief of the Special Procedures Group(Cassady). The reader was the Deputy Chief of the Special Procedures Group (Dulin). It is document 261 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. Across Washington, the new security bodies were moving from setup work to the real business of the Cold War.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d361:
A letter from Robert Blum of the Office of the Secretary of Defense reached Allen W. Dulles on 7 February 1949. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 361 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The Council had sent in an outside team to grade the CIA, and the whole town knew a blunt report was coming.

Writers chose a letter when they wanted a stance to count. The text gives the sender's side in full. Many of the big fights of these years can be followed letter by letter. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1861-d61:
Charles Francis Adams received a letter from William H. Seward dated 21 July 1861. The letter is document 61 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward wrote on the very day of Bull Run, before its result was known in full. His words to London kept the calm, firm tone of the spring. The clash of dates shows a chief guiding his envoy in one world, while a battle remade that world at home. The battle was fought on a Sunday, and Seward spent it near the telegraph office. A Sunday battle and a weekday letter frame the strange pace of that summer.
frus-1861-d161:
William Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 November 1861, the day Seward also wrote to him. The dispatch is document 161 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The same day crossing ends the Dayton run in this file. Neither man knew of the Trent seizure as he wrote. Their paired pages form a fitting close: a partnership in full working order on the eve of its hardest test. A fitting close to the run: two partners in step, the storm not yet known. The hardest test of their partnership lay just past the edge of this file.
frus-1861-d261:
Home in Washington, Seward read a fresh report from James Shepherd Pike, dated 16 October 1861. Congress received it as Document 261 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. By then, in the autumn of the war's first year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d61:
The State Department sent word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 9 May 1862, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 61 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It was written in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d161:
A second Adams report dated 10 October 1862 stands in the file as Document 161 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Like its pair, it went from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Sending two reports in one mail was normal legation practice when business was heavy. One letter might log a meeting while the other passed on newspapers, notes, or private word from officials. For the reader, the pair shows the London post working at full stretch in a week of sharp debate over British policy toward the war.
frus-1862-d261:
William L. Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 March 1862, in a report printed as Document 261 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It followed another Dayton report by a single day.

Spring 1862 was the season when France's break with its allies over Mexico became clear: Britain and Spain withdrew, France advanced alone. That split eased one fear in Washington and raised another, since a France alone in Mexico might seek friends in Richmond. Dayton's quick reports in this week belong to the file tracking that turn. Dayton's French was limited, and he leaned on his staff and on careful written notes.
frus-1862-d361:
Edouard Thouvenel wrote from Paris to Henri Mercier in Washington on 13 March 1862. In an instruction printed as Document 361 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Thouvenel was France's foreign minister; Mercier was his minister to the United States.

Mid-March brought the ironclad fight at Hampton Roads and the news that Britain and Spain were quitting the Mexican venture, leaving France alone in it. Paris had reason to rethink its American course. An instruction written that week carried the court's updated mind to Washington, where Mercier would apply it in his talks with Seward. Formal calls between the two men were frequent, and their notes followed up the talks.
frus-1862-d461:
On 18 November 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to John Lothrop Motley at Vienna. It is Document 461 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the last Austrian order in the year's file.

Seward wrote in the weeks when France was sounding out Britain and Russia on joint mediation. The subject was the American war. The Union rejected the plan flatly. His ministers needed one clear line: no foreign hand in an American quarrel. Motley in Vienna, though far from the main courts in that scheme, had to hold the same line. The letter closes the year's Austrian instructions with the war's diplomacy entering its winter test.
frus-1862-d561:
On 10 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henry Shelton Sanford, the American minister in Belgium. The instruction is Document 561 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Four days after the paired orders to Brussels, Seward was writing again. That pace tells its own story about the Belgian file that autumn. Sanford reported gossip from half the courts of Europe, and Washington answered with instructions to match. The matters between them included the watch on Confederate activity and the presentation of the Union's case after Antietam. The letter keeps up a correspondence that stands out in the volume for speed on both ends.
frus-1862-d661:
William H. Seward sent this letter to Robert H. Pruyn on 11 March 1862. Pruyn was on his way to head the American legation in Japan, succeeding Townsend Harris. The letter stands as document 661 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Written orders were the spine of a mission in the age of sail and steam. Seward used them to fix what Pruyn should say and do once he faced Japan's rulers. This letter came late in the chain of orders, close to the start of Pruyn's work in Japan. It rounds out the record of how he was briefed for the job.
frus-1863p1-d61:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 23 January 1863. Two more Adams letters share the date in the volume. Adams was the American minister in London, and the letter is document 61 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Three letters in a day mark a desk clearing a pile of London business at once. Adams wrote on the British government's temper and the acts of the South's friends in the city. Each sheet he sent fed Seward's sense of how near Britain stood to a step toward the South. This one opens the day's set of three.
frus-1863p1-d161:
Late April's run to London opens with this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, dated 20 April 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 161 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, opening a late-April run of Seward letters.

Seward wrote as the spring's ship gains settled in. His task now was to hold them: keep the claims warm, the tone right, and the envoy stocked. This letter opens a three-day run in the file. It shows Washington tending the brief with the same care in a fair week as in a foul one. That habit won the long game in Britain.
frus-1863p1-d261: An untitled paper dated 8 August 1863 stands as document 261 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It falls within the volume's long Adams and Seward sequence, the London correspondence that carried Anglo-American business during the Civil War. With no title or named author in the record, only its date, number, and setting can be stated with confidence.
frus-1863p1-d361:
A formal note dated 15 January 1863 passed from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, in Washington. It stands as document 361 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Canada, then a British colony, shared a long border with the Union. Worries about raids, plots, and smuggling across that line sit behind part of this correspondence. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d461:
The date 15 April 1863 heads a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d561:
Document 561, dated 10 June 1863, records a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d661:
The 13 November 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality.
plos-pbio-0020261:
Carsten Schnatwinkel, Savvas Christoforidis, and their team studied cargo intake in cells for PLOS Biology in 2004. Cells pull in material by endocytosis, pinching off small sacs from the surface. A protein called Rab5 manages early steps, and its partner Rabankyrin-5 helps run more than one intake route.

The study shows Rabankyrin-5 coordinates distinct mechanisms rather than serving just one. That makes it a hub in the intake system. Hubs are where a cell can tune traffic up or down with a single change. Knowing them helps explain how cells feed, sense their surroundings, and take in signals. It also matters for diseases where viruses or toxins hijack entry routes.
plos-pone-0000161:
Robert J. Greenstein, Liya Su, Vahram Haroutunian, and colleagues published this microbiology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It tests how two long-used drugs, methotrexate and 6-mercaptopurine, act on Mycobacterium avium subspecies paratuberculosis. This bacterium causes Johne's disease in cattle and has been debated as a factor in Crohn's disease.

Both drugs are used in inflammatory bowel disease, where benefit was often credited to immune suppression. The authors examine the drugs' direct action on the bacterium itself. If the drugs also kill or slow this microbe, the standard story of how they help bowel patients may need revision.
plos-pone-0000261:
A. Townsend Peterson, Brett W. Benz, and Monica Papeş published this avian flu risk paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It asks how highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza could enter North America through bird migration. The authors model the pathways that migrating birds might carry the virus along.

H5N1 had spread across Asia and Europe, and North America was watching its flyways. Mapping likely entry routes tells surveillance teams where to sample birds first. The paper is a risk assessment, using migration ecology to aim limited testing resources at the most probable doors.
plos-pone-0000361:
Faridabano Nato, Armelle Phalipon, Lan Phuong Thi Nguyen, and colleagues published this diagnostics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Shigella flexneri 2a is a bacterium that causes dysentery, a severe diarrheal disease. The authors present a dipstick test for rapid diagnosis of this strain directly in stool. The strip gives an answer at the bedside or in the field.

Dysentery outbreaks strike where labs are scarce, so a stool dipstick that needs no equipment is valuable. The authors report the test's performance on real samples. Fast identification guides treatment and outbreak control for a disease that kills many children in poor regions.
plos-pone-0000461:
Matthew N. Van Ert and colleagues traced the family structure of the anthrax bacterium worldwide, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Bacillus anthracis causes anthrax, a disease of animals and people and a feared bioweapon. The team analyzed its global genetic population structure, how its strains group and spread across regions.

Anthrax spores travel with livestock, wool, and soil, so strain patterns record both natural spread and human trade. A global structure map helps investigators match an outbreak sample to its likely origin. That matters for disease control. It also matters for forensic work after deliberate releases. It also shows how a bacterium with little genetic variety is organized across the planet.
plos-pone-0000561:
Lyubomir G. Nashev and colleagues studied an enzyme that tunes hormone strength inside cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Hexose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase modulates how 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 handles certain steroids, including 7-keto- and 7β-hydroxy-neurosteroids. The type 1 enzyme activates cortisone-like signals and is a drug target in metabolic disease.

A modulator enzyme matters because it decides how much active hormone a tissue actually sees, whatever the blood level says. Neurosteroids act in the brain, so the partnership may shape mood and cognition as well. Fine-grained control points like this are where selective drugs try to act.
plos-pone-0000661:
Fabien Lacaille, Makoto Hiroi, Robert Twele and colleagues found that a fruit fly sex signal tastes bitter to males, reported in PLOS ONE in 2007. Sexual behavior requires animals to tell the sexes apart and respond correctly to each. In Drosophila melanogaster, as in many insects, chemicals on the body surface called cuticular hydrocarbons are thought to carry sex recognition.

Direct neural proof of their role had been missing. The title names an inhibitory sex pheromone, a signal that discourages male mating attempts, and says males taste it as bitter. A taste pathway for a stop signal is a neat piece of sensory design, linking flavor to courtship decisions.
plos-pone-0000761:
Jing Tang, Jewn Giew Park, Charles B. Millard and colleagues used computer-aided design to improve a blocker of the botulinum toxin enzyme. Botulinum neurotoxin serotype A is among the most potent toxins known. Its zinc endopeptidase is the part that cuts proteins inside nerve cells. Optimizing a selective small-molecule inhibitor is a formidable challenge, because the enzyme-substrate interface is unusually large and the enzyme itself is big and complex.

Computer-aided lead optimization refines a starting inhibitor in silico before costly lab rounds. A better blocker could serve as an antidote after exposure, a long-standing biodefense goal. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study reports the improved inhibitor and the design path that produced it.
plos-pone-0000861:
Zohar Mor, Charlotte K. Kent, Robert P. Kohn and colleagues documented a paradox in HIV prevention, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Recent experimental evidence had demonstrated the benefits of male circumcision for preventing HIV infection. Studies had also shown circumcision is cost-effective and reduces risk for certain ulcerative sexually transmitted diseases. Few preventive measures arrive with that strength of trial evidence behind them.

Yet their title reports declining rates of male circumcision amid that increasing evidence of public health benefit. A proven intervention spreading more slowly than the science invites questions about culture, cost, and health system habit. The authors document the trend so policy can answer those questions with data.
plos-pone-0000961:
Tasneem Khanam, Carsten Raabe, Martin Kiefmann and colleagues tested whether repeated DNA elements can guide messages to dendrites, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Nerve cells send some RNA messages out into their dendrites, the branches that receive signals. Placement depends on signals within the RNA and on factors that read them.

A small RNA called BC1 is thought to tune protein building in dendrite zones. The team ask whether ID repetitive elements, common repeated stretches in rodent genes, can act as targeting signals themselves. They test the idea in living systems. The answer bears on how neurons place the right proteins at the right branch.
plos-pone-0001061:
Caitlin Conboy, Christiana Spyrou, Natalie Thorne and colleagues showed that cell cycle genes are the conserved targets of one factor, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Resting cells are held in a quiet state partly by a protein complex called DREAM. In human cells the factor E2F4 directs that complex to its targets.

The team found E2F4 binds a highly overlapping set of genes across contexts, and those targets are cell cycle genes. Conservation of the target set suggests the quiet state is guarded by an old, stable program. When that program fails, cells divide when they should rest, a step toward cancer. The work names the guarded genes.
plos-pone-0001161:
Blood vessel lining cells survive in part because a growth factor called VEGF blocks their self-destruction. Ling Wang and co-authors mapped part of that survival signal in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They focused on neuropilin-1, a partner protein for VEGF, and on p53 and the caspases, proteins that drive programmed cell death.

The authors report that neuropilin-1 modulates the p53 and caspase axis to promote endothelial cell survival. In plain terms, it tips a life-or-death switch inside vessel cells toward life. That pathway matters wherever new vessels grow, from healing wounds to tumors.
plos-pone-0001261:
Hospitals keep huge archives of tissue samples fixed in formalin and embedded in paraffin. These archives are a goldmine for molecular studies, if the RNA inside them can be read. Silke von Ahlfen and colleagues investigated what determines RNA quality from such FFPE samples, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Fixation and storage damage RNA, but the adverse effects of standard pathology practice were incompletely documented.

The authors set out to pin down which steps of collection and processing hurt RNA most. Their guidance helps researchers judge which archived blocks can support gene expression profiling and which cannot. The archives' value depends on exactly this kind of quality map.
plos-pone-0001361:
Obesity is a major health problem with substantial heritability, yet the genetic mechanisms predisposing to it were poorly understood in 2007. Anke Hinney and colleagues performed a genome wide association study for early onset extreme obesity, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They used a genome-wide SNP array covering the genome's common variation.

The authors report that the study supports the role of variants in the fat mass and obesity associated gene, FTO. FTO was the first gene robustly tied to common obesity, and this study extended the evidence to children with extreme, early onset obesity. The finding helped establish FTO as a cornerstone of obesity genetics.
plos-pone-0001461:
Sigal Saar and Partha Mitra wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE methods paper on how birdsong rhythms grow. Brain rhythms in young birds build up over time scales from split seconds to years. Reading that growth poses hard math problems. The team focused on song, where rhythm change can be heard and timed with care.

They offer a way to track how song rhythm takes shape as a bird matures. The method splits rhythm into layers and charts each layer's growth. Tools like this help labs link brain change to learned skill. They may also serve work on how human speech rhythms form in the young.
plos-pone-0001561:
Moisés Santillán and Michael Mackey wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE model of how body segments form in embryos. The classic clock and wavefront model had gained strong backing from fresh gene finds. Genes that pulse in the tail bud form the clock. A moving front sets where each segment locks in. The pair asked how clock and front talk to each other.

Their model sets out a way the two could mesh to lay segments at a steady pace. A clear mesh lets labs test which gene faults break the rhythm. Segment faults cause spine ills in people, so the stakes are real. The paper gives those tests a firm frame.
plos-pone-0001661:
Robert-Jan Palstra and co-authors tested whether far-apart pieces of DNA stay in contact when transcription stops, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. DNA folds inside the nucleus so that distant genes and their switches can touch. Many thought active transcription by RNA polymerase II was what held that folded layout in place.

Using 3C and 4C methods, which capture which DNA pieces sit near each other, the team blocked ongoing transcription and rechecked the contacts. The full text gives the contact maps before and after the block. Their results bear on a basic question. Is the genome's 3D layout a stable scaffold that gene activity uses, rather than a shape activity must keep rebuilding?
plos-pone-0001761:
Jianzhong Yu, John Poulton, Yi-Chun Huang, and their co-authors studied two signaling pathways in fruit fly eggs in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Setting the head-to-tail axis of a Drosophila oocyte requires talk between germ-line cells and the surrounding follicle cells. Notch signaling is one of the pathways involved in forming oocyte polarity.

The team reports that the Hippo pathway promotes Notch signaling, and together they regulate cell differentiation, proliferation, and oocyte polarity. The full text gives the fly genetics and the egg chamber images. Pathway partnerships like this are a general theme in development. Organs are built by committees of signals, not single switches, and fly eggs are where many such partnerships are first mapped.
plos-pone-0001861:
Matthew Siegel, Pavel Strnad, R. Edward Watts, and their co-authors measured the activity state of a wound-healing enzyme in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Transglutaminase 2, or TG2, is a mammal protein with many jobs, including transamidase and signaling roles. Using chosen TG2 inhibitors and tagged amine targets, the team probed the enzyme outside cells.

They show most TG2 outside cells is inactive under normal conditions in the body, but is briefly switched on upon tissue injury. The full text gives the activity readings in tissues. An enzyme that wakes only at wounds is a safe drug target in principle: blocking it should spare normal tissue while touching healing and fibrosis.
plos-pone-0001961:
Lydia Jimenez-Diaz and co-authors studied how pain fibers make their own proteins on site, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Nerve cells are long, and the far tips that sense pain sit far from the cell body where most proteins are made. Recent work had shown that local protein synthesis at the tips matters for how nerves adapt.

The team focused on the mTOR path, a known driver of local synthesis, in primary afferent fibers, the fibers that carry pain signals inward. They report that local translation in those fibers regulates nociception, the sensing of harm. That puts a local factory on the map of pain control.
plos-pone-0002061:
Roberta Schulte and co-authors shrank a classic protein test down to single beads, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Pull-down tests check whether two proteins bind by fishing one out and seeing what comes with it. Their miniaturized method uses standard affinity reagents, the same beads and columns labs already own.

Proteins are color-coded with quantum dots, tiny glowing crystals, so binding events can be seen on single beads under a scope. The name is SINBAD, for single bead affinity detection. Seeing single binding events can reveal weak or rare pairings that bulk tests wash out.
plos-pone-0002161:
Maya Dinur-Mills, Merav Tal, and Ophry Pines studied proteins that work in two places at once inside cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In complex cells, the very same protein can end up in different compartments, a trait called dual targeting. The team split a reference set of mitochondrial proteins into those that are dual targeted and those found only in mitochondria.

They compared the targeting signals that guide each group to its place. Dual targeted proteins showed lower signal scores and a lower total charge on their guide pieces. The contrast helps explain how one protein can be sent to two addresses by a weaker, more flexible signal.
plos-pone-0002261:
Michiya Kawaguchi and co-authors mapped a region of a cell-surface protein that helps cells stick together, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The protein is called Bves, short for blood vessel epicardial substance. It gives cells adhesive properties, but how it does so at the molecular level was unknown. Its sequence shows no known functional motifs outside its membrane span.

The team found a new interaction domain inside the cell that is essential for Bves to work. Partners binding that domain likely switch its adhesive role. Finding the working part of an obscure protein is the first step to learning what it does in the heart and beyond.
plos-pone-0002361:
Mathias Streitz and co-authors dissected the T cell response in one patient with virus-linked heart inflammation, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Parvovirus B19 is the virus most often found in heart muscle biopsies from patients with inflammatory cardiomyopathy, a disease where the heart muscle weakens. T cells are central to antiviral defense, yet their role against this virus in the heart was little known.

The team characterized B19V-specific CD8 T cells aimed at the viral NS1 protein. These cells showed effector function and a dominant receptor pattern in the patient. A close look at one case guides the search for immune markers in a murky disease.
plos-pone-0002461:
Giri and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Pramod K. Giri, Jeffrey S. Schorey, among others. Its subject is exosomes Derived from M. Bovis BCG Infected Macrophages Activate Antigen-Specific CD4 +. The rest of the title points to CD8 + T Cells In Vitro and In Vivo. Activation of both CD4 + and CD8 + T cells is required for an effective immune response to an M.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002561:
Dechartres and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Agnes Dechartres, Isabelle Boutron, Remy Nizard, among others. Its subject is knee Arthroplasty: Disabilities in Comparison to the General Population and to Hip Arthroplasty Using a French National Longitudinal Survey. Knee arthroplasty is increasing exponentially due to the aging of the population and to the broadening of indications.

We aimed to compare physical disability and its evolution over two years in people with knee arthroplasty to that in the general population. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002661:
In 2008, Amanda Ross and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about modelling the epidemiological impact of intermittent preventive treatment against malaria in infants. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Amanda Ross, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Trials of intermittent preventive treatment against malaria in infants (IPTi) using sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) have shown a positive, albeit variable. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002761:
David Kaplan and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of sample size and precision in NIH peer review. The catalog record names David Kaplan first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The Working Group on Peer Review of the Advisory Committee to the Director of NIH has recommended that at least 4 reviewers should be. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002861:
In 2008, Toby Leslie and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was a randomised trial of an Eight-Week, once weekly primaquine regimen to prevent relapse of plasmodium vivax in northwest frontier province, pakistan. Authorship is credited in the record to Toby Leslie and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Vivax malaria remains a major cause of morbidity in the subtropics. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002961:
Adriano Boasso, Andrew Hardy, Stephanie Anderson and co-authors linked interferon, tryptophan breakdown, and T cell failure in HIV in 2008. HIV infection shows chronic activation of T cells alongside poor function, and the causes were largely unexplained. Type I interferon is a first-line signal that fights viruses.

The team cultured blood cells from uninfected donors in lab setups that copy parts of HIV infection. Their title reports that interferon and tryptophan breakdown together drive T cell dysfunction despite activation. Published in PLOS ONE, this process helps explain a central paradox of HIV immune defense. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003061:
Daniela Pignatta, Brian Dilkes, Tadeusz Wroblewski and co-authors tested gene silencing across ploidy levels in 2008. Whole genome duplication, which creates polyploidy, is common in plant populations and recurs in flowering plant evolution. It can change gene expression and epigenetic stability.

Transgene-induced silencing was not affected by a change in ploidy level, the title reports. That steadiness is useful news for plant breeding, where doubling genomes is routine. Published in PLOS ONE, the result separates one epigenetic process from the genome-size upheaval around it. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003161:
Jorieke H. Peters, Frank W. Preijers, Rob Woestenenk and colleagues describe a clinical grade method for preparing regulatory T cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Therapy based on these cells interests many groups as a way to promote tolerance in autoimmunity and transplantation. For trials, teams need an isolation protocol that meets Good Manufacturing Practice rules and yields enough cells.

The authors cover GMP isolation, improving purity by removing CD127 positive cells, expanding the cells, and freezing them for storage. Readers get a full practical pipeline, not just a lab result. That kind of protocol is what lets a cell idea move toward real patient trials.
plos-pone-0003261:
Walter Jetz, Robert P. Freckleton and Andrew E. McKechnie examine metabolic rate in birds in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Basal metabolic rate represents the minimum maintenance energy requirement of a warm-blooded animal and has far-reaching consequences for interactions between animals and their environments. Avian metabolic rate exhibits considerable variation independent of body mass, and some long-distance migrants differ notably.

The authors test the roles of environment, migratory tendency, and phylogeny, or family history, in that variation. Readers see three explanations weighed against each other. Separating history from habitat helps predict how bird energy needs may shift with climate.
plos-pone-0003361:
Laura H. Tsang, James E. Cassat, Lindsey N. Shaw and colleagues study biofilm failure in staph mutants in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Mutation of sarA in Staphylococcus aureus results in reduced capacity to form a biofilm, but the mechanistic basis for this remains unknown. Previous transcriptional profiling experiments identified a number of genes differentially expressed both in a biofilm and in mutant strains.

The authors assess factors contributing to the biofilm-deficient phenotype of sarA mutants. Readers learn how one regulator controls the communal surface growth that makes staph infections hard to clear. Biofilms protect bacteria on implants and wounds, so their control genes are clinical targets.
plos-pone-0007461:
Atsushi Oyagi and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 creating a new research tool for brain science. Growth factors and immune signals have been linked to schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and depression. One growth factor, HB-EGF, also nourishes developing brain cells. Studying it has been hard because removing it everywhere at once distorts development. The team built a more precise option.

They engineered mice in which the HB-EGF gene can be switched off only in chosen tissues or at chosen times. Such conditional knockout mice let researchers isolate where the factor truly matters. The tool can now be used to test HB-EGF's role in brain development and mental illness. The paper reports both the construction of the mice and their first characterization.
plos-pone-0007561:
Zi-An Fang and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how a yeast called Kluyveromyces lactis responds to oxygen. Baker's yeast has an unusual, fermentation-loving lifestyle. That lifestyle may stem from an ancient doubling of its whole genome. K. lactis never had that doubling, which makes it a useful comparison. The team measured its gene responses as oxygen availability changed.

Genes tied to oxygen response showed notable patterns in the unduplicated yeast. Comparing them with baker's yeast reveals what the genome doubling changed. The oxygen-responding system was rewired along the way. Such comparisons are how evolution's experiments get read. One yeast kept the older wiring; the other rebuilt it after doubling. The study uses that contrast to trace how a metabolic lifestyle was born.
plos-pone-0007661:
Xiaomin Zheng and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the famous chromosome swap behind Philadelphia-chromosome leukemias. The swap between chromosomes 9 and 22 creates the BCR-ABL fusion gene, a known leukemia driver. Being a balanced swap, it also creates the reciprocal fusion, ABL-BCR, on the other chromosome. That second product was largely ignored. The team tested its power to cause leukemia and its effects on B cell development.

The reciprocal fusion protein has leukemogenic potential of its own. It also altered how B cells commit to their lineage. So both products of one swap can push blood cells toward cancer. That doubles the list of suspects in these leukemias. It may matter for therapy, since drugs target the famous fusion alone. The study restores the swap's forgotten half to the story.
plos-pone-0007761:
Christopher Rex and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It hunts the source of a brain wave pattern called the sharp wave. Sharp waves start in one part of the hippocampus, CA3, and spread through the region. They appear when animals rest awake or during sleep.

The hippocampus is central to memory, and sharp waves may help store it. The team used slices of rat hippocampus to find what starts these waves. They traced the factors that trigger and shape the pattern. Knowing where the rhythm begins helps explain how the resting brain replays and fixes memories.
plos-pone-0007861:
Jennifer Simpson and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests which birds a common mosquito prefers to bite. Culex pipiens is the main carrier of West Nile virus in the northeastern United States. Field evidence suggested it feeds preferentially on American robins.

If robins are favored, they may amplify the virus for human outbreaks. The authors ran experimental trials to separate innate preference from chance. Their design asks what the mosquito chooses when options are equal. The answer helps disease modelers weigh each bird species' role. It also guides surveillance toward the hosts that matter most.
plos-pone-0007961:
Vaughn Cooper and colleagues asked how a worm's last meals shape its fate with germs, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The worm, C. elegans, is a stand-in for studying how animals and bacteria meet. Worms eat bacteria, so their food and their foes can be close kin.

Worms raised on one diet fell to Burkholderia germs more readily than worms raised on another. Scents the germs give off also drew or warned the worms. The work shows that lab results with this worm hinge on what it ate, a point any study using it must heed.
plos-pone-0008061:
Junbin Hu and colleagues solved the shape of a yeast delivery protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. Some proteins anchor in cell membranes by a single tail at their end, and they need a special delivery crew. The crew's core is Get3, which ferries the tail proteins to the right membrane.

Crystal shapes of Get3, caught in several states, suggest how it grips a tail, carries it, and lets go at the target. The steps read like a loading dock in miniature. Kindred systems run in human cells, so the yeast map informs cell biology broadly.
plos-pone-0008161:
Junjie Su and colleagues sorted cancers by the activity of whole pathways in PLOS ONE in 2009. Gene activity profiles can tell one cancer class from another, but single genes make noisy guides and samples are often few. Pathways, sets of genes with one job, offer a steadier signal.

Their method infers each pathway's activity with a probability model, then classes the tumor by the pattern. The pathway-based calls proved more accurate and steadier than gene-by-gene calls. Steadier sorting matters, because the class a tumor lands in often decides the patient's treatment.
plos-pone-0008261:
Kristen Alexa and colleagues studied pancreas development in zebrafish in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Zebrafish are a standard model for watching organs form in embryos. The team isolated a new mutant that lacks a proper endocrine pancreas. In the mutant, key markers of hormone-producing cells were missing. Other nearby tissues were less affected.

They traced the fault to the aldh1a2 gene and its activity. Both maternal and zygotic copies of the gene proved necessary. The gene helps make signals the developing pancreas requires. The finding clarifies early steps in how the pancreas forms.
plos-pone-0008361:
Roderick F. Felsheim, Timothy J. Kurtti, and Ulrike G. Munderloh sequenced a tick bacterium genome in PLOS ONE in 2009. Rickettsia peacockii lives harmlessly inside Dermacentor ticks in western North America and Canada. It is an obligate intracellular bacterium, unable to live outside host cells. Where it occurs, the dangerous relative Rickettsia rickettsii becomes rarer. That pattern hints at competition inside ticks.

Comparing the two genomes helped identify virulence factors. Shared and missing genes show what makes one species harmful. Such insight could lead to ways of blocking the dangerous species. It also explains a natural control on disease.
plos-pone-0008461:
Aaron Jeffs and co-authors search for a gene signature in melanoma in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Melanoma is a skin cancer that can spread to other organs. The team use a new panel of cell lines from spread tumors. They define gene traits that track with tumor behavior. Their aim is to find new markers that predict outcome. They also seek new targets for drugs.

They find a set of genes whose activity marks invasive potential. Cells with that signature are more apt to invade tissue. Such a signature could help sort patients by risk. It gives drug research fresh leads to test.
plos-pone-0008561:
Saurabh Sahar and co-authors study stability of a clock protein in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Circadian rhythms govern a large array of body and metabolic functions. Clock proteins undergo various post-translational modifications to stay plastic. Those modifications influence their activity and interactions. BMAL1 is a core clock protein that drives daily gene cycles. The team examine how an enzyme called GSK3beta modifies BMAL1. The enzyme adds a phosphate tag to the protein.

That phosphorylation regulates BMAL1 protein stability and circadian function. Tagging changes how long BMAL1 lasts before degradation. It thus tunes the period and strength of the daily rhythm. The work adds a control knob to the molecular clock.
plos-pone-0008661:
John Cisne and co-authors link old text work to new math in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Scholars who rebuild ancient texts work from copies full of scribal errors. Long ago, they grasped that a choice between readings is a bet on odds. One old rule prefers the harder reading. Scribes tend to smooth hard lines, so a hard line is more apt to be the true one. The team restate that rule with entropy, a measure of surprise in a message.

Their method gives a math way to rank variant readings. It can refine how classic texts are rebuilt from flawed copies. Early scholars thus saw core ideas of information theory long before it had a name. The paper joins the humanities and math in one frame.
plos-pone-0008761:
Daniel Scott-Algara, Maryline Mancini-Bourgine, Hélène Fontaine, and colleagues watched killer cells change after a hepatitis B vaccine. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Natural killer cells are fast-acting immune defenders. They can help dendritic cells pick strong T cell responses. A DNA vaccine for chronic hepatitis B aimed to revive patient immunity. Whether it also reshaped killer cells was unknown.

After vaccination, the mix of natural killer cell types shifted. Certain subsets grew that cooperate well with other immune cells. Such shifts may help explain who responds to the vaccine. Future vaccine designs could aim to recruit these helpful subsets.
plos-pone-0008861:
Christian Rödelsperger and Christoph Dieterich wrote a program that lines up gene order across seventeen vertebrate genomes. Their software paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Gene order was once viewed as mostly random shuffling. Shared order was treated as a mere mark of common ancestry. That view has been revised as functional constraints emerged. Comparing order across many genomes needs progressive alignment, genome by genome.

Their tool, CYNTENATOR, performs that multi-genome alignment. Conserved blocks stand out against shuffled regions. The tool helps separate chance similarity from meaningful conservation. Evolution researchers gain a lens on how genomes reorganize over deep time.
plos-pone-0008961:
Jun Toyohara and colleagues tested two radioactive tracers for brain scanning in living animals, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The tracers aim at the alpha7 nicotinic receptor, a docking point on brain cells. That receptor is tied to schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease. A good tracer would let doctors watch the receptor with a PET scanner.

The team labelled two candidate drugs with carbon-11 so they could be tracked. They injected them into mice and into awake monkeys and followed the signal. The tests showed how each tracer entered the brain and where it stuck. Such checks decide whether a tracer deserves trials in human patients.
plos-pone-0009061:
Marc Tänzer and co-authors tested a blood test for early bowel growths, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Screening cuts deaths from colorectal cancer, yet many people skip current tests. Colonoscopy is effective but unpopular; stool tests are often missed. A simple blood draw could win wider acceptance.

The team measured two methylated DNA markers, SEPT9 and ALX4, in blood plasma. They judged how well the pair flagged precancerous lesions, not just cancers. Catching growths before they turn malignant is screening's real prize. Their performance figures show what such a test can and cannot yet do.
plos-pone-0009161:
Fu-Shi Quan and co-authors built a vaccine from empty flu shells and tested it in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The 2009 H1N1 pandemic exposed worldwide shortages of flu vaccine. Virus-like particles mimic a virus's shape without its genes. They cannot cause infection, yet look real to the immune system.

The particles were built from the pandemic strain A/California/04/2009. Vaccinated mice were protected against that 2009 H1N1 virus. Protection came without growing live virus in eggs for months. Faster platforms like this could blunt the next pandemic's first wave.
plos-pone-0009261:
Nyresa Alves and co-authors published this brain development study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Attention deficit disorder is far more common in boys than girls. Yet little was known about sex differences in how attention circuits develop. The prefrontal cortex, a seat of attention, relies partly on nicotine-sensitive receptors.

The team recorded nicotinic currents in layer VI neurons of the prefrontal cortex. They compared mice and rats as the animals grew up. Males and females showed different patterns in those currents during development. Such early wiring differences may help explain why attention disorders strike the sexes unequally.
plos-pone-0009361:
Elke Braun, Bart Geurten, and Martin Egelhaaf published this study of animal behavior in PLOS ONE in 2010. To learn how animals solve tasks, scientists must first split behavior into parts. The key step is spotting the moves that repeat again and again. Doing that by eye is slow, and two watchers may not agree.

The authors let a computer do the sorting instead. Their program groups like moves into sets, finding the stock parts of an animal's act on its own. A clean parts list makes studies easier to repeat and to compare. It also helps tie what an animal does to the brain paths that steer it.
plos-pone-0011461:
S Lee Hong and Melissa Beck measured in 2010 how people quietly adjust their attention when the world becomes hard to predict. Attention feels steady, but it must trade sharp focus against wide monitoring as uncertainty rises. The team used tasks in which timing and gaze could be recorded while the predictability of events changed.

Response times and the length of time eyes lingered both shifted as uncertainty grew, revealing a compensation pattern in how focus is spent. People hold their gaze longer and answer differently when the next event is unsure, as if the mind pays a tax to stay ready. Mapping that tax matters for any job built on vigilance, from driving to screening scans. The study turns a vague feeling of strain under uncertainty into timed, measurable behavior.
plos-pone-0011561:
Chelsee Hewitt and co-authors mapped in 2010 how Down syndrome disrupts brain building in a mouse model even in adulthood. Down syndrome stems from an extra copy of one chromosome, which unbalances hundreds of genes at once. The team used the Ts1Cje mouse, which carries a similar extra segment, and examined adult brains, where new neuron production continues in a few regions.

They found disrupted gene networks and defective neurogenesis, the birth of new neurons, in the adult model brain. The network view moves beyond single genes to show how the extra chromosome rewires the brain's construction crew as a system. Adult defects matter because they suggest some features of Down syndrome remain active and potentially treatable after development ends. Interventions aimed at network balance, rather than one gene, follow naturally from this framing.
plos-pone-0011661:
Israt Jahan and co-authors studied how the inner ear builds its sound-sensing cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A small set of related genes directs whether young ear cells become neurons, hair cells or supporting cells. One of them, Neurod1, was known to interact with its relatives, but its precise duties were unsettled.

The team found Neurod1 holds back hair cell formation in ear nerve clusters, while in the cochlea it guides which hair cell subtype develops. That dual role, suppressing in one place and refining in another, makes Neurod1 a key switch for hearing cell identity and a clue for future hearing repair.
plos-pone-0011761:
Cheng Hu and co-authors tested four blood-sugar genes in a Chinese study group, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Variants in the genes GCK, GCKR, G6PC2 and MTNR1B had been found to shift fasting glucose levels. The team aimed to confirm those links in Chinese subjects and to look deeper at effects on insulin release.

They measured how each variant relates to glucose handling and to the two phases of insulin release. The four-way test sorts out what each gene adds to the body's sugar control. Confirming gene findings across ancestries is a must before they can inform diabetes forecasting or care.
plos-pone-0011861:
William Swindell, Andrew Johnston, and Johann Gudjonsson created in 2010 a reference tool for reading gene activity in fat-fed mice. Earlier microarray studies had found that a high fat diet raises the activity of many immune-linked genes. Part of that signal may come from white blood cells moving into tissues rather than from the tissues themselves.

To separate those sources, the team profiled distinct white blood cell populations and recorded each one's gene activity pattern. With those profiles in hand, other researchers can judge how much of a diet-linked pattern is explained by arriving immune cells. That makes past and future diet studies easier to interpret, including work on how fatty food stirs up body-wide inflammation.
plos-pone-0011961:
Delilah Zabaneh and David Balding ran in 2010 a whole-genome search for gene variants tied to the metabolic syndrome in men of Indian Asian stock. That group bears a heavy load of the syndrome, the cluster of blood pressure, blood sugar, and fat traits that raises the risk of heart disease and diabetes. The search ran in two stages, with the first stage reading more than three hundred thousand DNA markers.

Scanning men from a high-risk group that studies often skip looks for common variants where the need is most sharp. Most gene hunts of the time used white European samples, so their finds may not hold for all. A search built for this group both serves its health needs and tests which gene effects are shared by all peoples.
plos-pone-0012061:
Amandine Gasc and co-workers showed in 2010 that invasive predators harm island lizards in a way headcounts alone would miss. Introduced predators on islands are famous for eating native species toward extinction. The genetic consequences for the survivors, however, had never been examined.

Populations hunted by invasive predators carried depleted genetic diversity compared with uninvaded ones. Low diversity is a slow emergency: it leaves lizards less able to adapt to disease or climate shifts long after the killing slows. Conservation that counts only bodies will underrate the damage predators do, because the gene pool is part of what is being lost.
plos-pone-0012161:
Kaori Shiojiri, Rika Ozawa, Soichi Kugimiya, and co-authors studied the alarm scents plants release when insects chew them, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Attacked plants give off chemicals that summon predatory insects to eat the attackers. The heavier the attack, the more scent the plant releases, and predators judge by the dose whether help is truly needed.

The question was whether those signals stay honest, scaling with real danger, or can mislead like a false alarm. Honest dose-based signals keep the plant-predator alliance working for both sides. The answer matters for farming ideas that would use plant scents to draw pest-eating insects into fields as a natural defense.
plos-pone-0012261:
Cedar Chittenden, Carlo Biagi, Jan Grimsrud Davidsen, and co-authors separated nature from nurture in coho salmon, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hatcheries breed salmon to boost wild runs, yet hatchery fish survive poorly after release, casting doubt on the whole enhancement strategy. The team crossed the two questions: does being born in a hatchery matter, or being raised there, or both?

By raising hatchery-born and wild-born fish in both settings, they could split genetic effects from rearing effects on the young salmon's traits. The answer decides whether hatcheries should change their fish or change their tanks. For managers spending public money on salmon recovery, that distinction is the difference between a fix that works and one that cannot.
plos-pone-0012361:
Intawat Nookaew, Britt Gabrielsson, Agneta Holmäng and fellow scientists fed mice a herring-rich diet and mapped body-wide effects in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Obesity-linked diseases are rising fast, and diet is a main lever for prevention. Rather than test one gene at a time, the team used systems biology to watch many pathways at once.

The herring diet shifted sterol handling and protein turnover in the mice, among other pathways. Seeing the full pattern shows how a single food change ripples through metabolism. Such maps can help design diets that prevent disease and can reveal early signs that a diet is helping or harming before illness appears.
plos-pone-0012461:
Buris Christiansen, Natalia Muguerza, Atheline Petersen and colleagues gave broccoli sprouts to people with high blood pressure, in a 2010 PLOS ONE trial. Sprouts are rich in glucosinolates, plant compounds that improved blood vessel function in hypertensive rats, possibly by raising nitric oxide. Whether the benefit reaches humans was untested.

In the human trial, eating the sprouts did not improve endothelial function, the vessel lining behavior that predicts heart risk. Negative results like this prevent hype from outrunning evidence. The rat-to-human gap also warns researchers that promising food compounds need human trials before any health claims are made.
plos-pone-0012561:
Karen Denzler, Robert Waters, Bertram Jacobs and colleagues exposed human blood immune cells to plant preparations, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Hundreds of botanicals are sold as immune boosters and antimicrobials in complementary medicine, with centuries of use but thin modern testing. The team asked how such immunostimulatory botanicals change inflammatory gene expression in PBMCs, the mixed immune cells of blood.

The botanicals tuned inflammatory genes in distinct patterns rather than simply switching immunity up. Distinct signatures mean products differ in real action, whatever their labels claim. Gene-level testing gives regulators and consumers a factual basis in a market long run on tradition alone.
plos-pone-0012661:
Law, Li, To and co-authors designed a decoy molecule that slows breast and prostate cancer cells. The target is YB-1, a protein that helps cancer grow once a chemical tag switches it on. Their 2010 paper built a fake version of YB-1's docking site to soak up the switch signal.

In their tests the decoy curbed cancer cell growth while leaving normal cells largely unharmed. Sparing healthy cells is the hard part of most cancer drugs, so that contrast stands out. The approach offers a fresh way to attack a protein long called undruggable.
plos-pone-0012761:
Prasad, Goel and Krishna used computer searches to find likely helper proteins for the cell's main folding chaperones in two plants. Hsp90 and Hsp70 are essential chaperones that fold and guard other proteins. They rely on co-chaperones, many of which carry a clamp-shaped part that grips the chaperone.

Their 2010 scan of the arabidopsis and rice genomes listed proteins with that clamp design. Each candidate is a lead for lab work on how plants handle heat and stress. Knowing the helper cast helps breeders and biologists alike.  Both plants are major models and food crops.
plos-pone-0012861:
Burgess and Braver scanned the brain to see how people handle interference while holding things in mind. Working memory must protect its contents from distractions, a core part of executive control. Past work showed a left frontal area switching on after interference appears.

Their 2010 study varied whether people expected interference and how high their fluid intelligence scored. Both factors changed how the brain mounted its control response. The results show interference control is not one fixed reflex but a flexible process tuned by expectation and ability.  Brain scans were paired with standard memory tasks.
pmc-2736161:
Damschroder, Aron, Keith, and co-authors build a consolidated framework for implementation science. Health studies often prove a treatment works, yet that success fails to reach routine patient care in many settings. Researchers increasingly judge not only final outcomes but also how change happens along the way.

Their framework gathers the many factors that help or block new practices, from leadership to local culture. It gives teams a shared language for planning and judging rollouts. Hospitals and clinics use it to find why a proven practice stalls in one place and thrives in another.
pmc-2984261:
Reuter and Mathews describe RNAstructure, software for predicting and analysing RNA secondary structure. To understand how an RNA sequence works, its folded structure must be known. Structure also matters when designing small interfering RNAs and antisense tools that target a specific RNA.

The software predicts folding using thermodynamics, estimating which pairing pattern is most stable. Predictions guide experiments before costly lab tests begin. RNAstructure gave researchers a shared, tested workbench for RNA folding, used in basic studies and in designing RNA-targeting therapies and research tools.  Designers of gene-silencing tools use its folds to avoid self-pairing traps inside constructs.
pmc-3375761:
Scallan, Hoekstra, Angulo, and co-authors estimate foodborne illness from major pathogens in the United States. Their figures attribute millions of episodes each year to a set of thirty-one known pathogens. Those illnesses lead to tens of thousands of hospital stays and more than a thousand deaths annually.

Counting the burden pathogen by pathogen shows which germs cause most harm. That ranking guides food safety rules, inspection effort, and outbreak response. The estimates became the standard reference for United States foodborne disease, cited whenever agencies weigh new controls on farms and processors.
pmc-4204661:
Cruz-Jentoft, Landi, Schneider, and their colleagues reviewed sarcopenia in 2014 for the International Sarcopenia Initiative. Sarcopenia is the loss of muscle mass and strength that comes with aging. The review asked how common it is and what nutrition and exercise can do about it.

The authors gathered clinical studies that used the agreed European definition of the condition. They examined both prevalence figures and trials of food and training interventions. Such pooled evidence helps doctors spot the condition early and act before frailty sets in. The report gave health systems a shared base for care of older adults losing muscle.
pmc-4352761:
Nott, Petsalaki, Farber, and their team reported in 2015 on a protein that forms droplets inside cells. Cells keep molecules apart in compartments to control their reactions. Besides membrane-bound parts, cells also build membraneless organelles, such as stress granules, from protein and RNA.

The team studied a disordered protein from nuage, a germ cell structure. It can shift phase and form droplets that respond to their surroundings. That behavior shows how cells create order without membranes, on demand. Such droplets are now a major topic, since their failure is linked to diseases of the brain and muscle.
pmc-6602461:
Uku Raudvere, Liis Kolberg, Ivan Kuzmin, and coauthors described g:Profiler in its 2019 form. Gene lists pour out of modern experiments, and each list needs interpretation. g:Profiler tests which biological categories appear more than chance would predict.

It also converts between gene identifier systems and maps genes to their counterparts in other species. Data sources are refreshed often so results reflect current knowledge. Care is taken to use sound statistics that correct for testing many categories. The tool is a staple for turning raw gene lists into readable biology. A public server handles lists of many thousands of genes within seconds.
pmc-7759461:
Charles Harris and many co-authors introduced in 2020 the ideas behind NumPy, the array programming library at the heart of scientific computing in Python. Array programming lets a user describe operations on whole grids of numbers at once, in compact and readable code. NumPy supplies that machinery for vectors, matrices, and arrays of higher dimensions.

The authors explain the design choices that made the library fast, flexible, and easy to build on. They also describe the large community and ecosystem that grew around it, from physics and biology to machine learning. Few papers describe a tool so many scientists use daily without thinking about it, which makes this account a useful piece of computing history as well.
pmc-9287161:
Felix Teufel and co-authors introduced SignalP 6.0 in 2022, a predictor for signal peptides, the short tags that direct proteins to be secreted or moved across cell membranes. Every living organism uses these tags to route its proteins. Earlier prediction programs could not detect all five known types of signal peptide, leaving gaps in genome annotation.

SignalP 6.0 is built on protein language models, systems trained on huge numbers of protein sequences that learn the patterns of the code. The authors show it recognizing all five peptide types in one tool. Correctly spotting these tags matters because a protein's destination shapes its function, and annotation pipelines process millions of sequences that no human will inspect.
pmc-9997061:
Justas Dauparas and co-authors described ProteinMPNN in 2022, a deep learning method that designs protein sequences to fold into a chosen shape. Predicting structure from sequence had just been transformed by deep learning. Designing the reverse, a sequence for a desired structure, still relied mostly on physics based tools such as Rosetta, which produced nearly all proven experimental designs.

ProteinMPNN takes the backbone shape as input and proposes sequences likely to fold into it. The authors show its designs solving in the laboratory at strong rates. A fast, reliable design method widens the door to custom proteins built for medicine, materials, and research, rather than only borrowed from nature.
plos-pone-0336561:
Thomas Wilkinson and seven colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about tuberculosis in South Africa. Some TB germs resist the usual drugs, a form called multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. Children who live with such patients can be given preventive treatment, and the authors ask what delivering that treatment costs.

The study counts costs on two sides: what the health system spends and what households themselves pay. Shan Xu leads a team of eight testing a protein destroying drug against bladder cancer in PLOS ONE in 2026. The drug, a peptide based chimera the group developed earlier, does not merely block its target, a growth promoting kinase called PAK4; it tags the protein for disposal by the cell. First the team confirmed the kinase runs high in bladder tumor tissue, then compared cancer cells genetically stripped of it with cells treated by the drug, in dishes and in animals.

Both routes told the same story. Without the kinase, a key growth pathway went quiet, cells stalled before copying their DNA, and a self destruct program switched on. Tumors grew significantly more slowly in mice under both the knockout and the drug. Because a degrader removes the whole protein rather than one activity, the authors argue it may outflank resistance that defeats ordinary kinase blockers.
plos-pone-0358761:
Ryoga Hayashi, Hayato Kawaji, and Satoru Kojima check whether ultrasound can reliably measure a knee gap that matters for injury assessment, in PLOS ONE in 2026. When a sideways force stresses the knee, the inner joint space widens slightly. Therapists would like to measure that widening without an X-ray. Seventeen healthy men offered thirty-four knees. Two physical therapists of different experience measured each knee resting and under a standard stress load, on separate days.

Stress widened the space by roughly a millimeter and a third, a consistent and significant shift. Agreement within each therapist across days, and between the two therapists, both rated good. The smallest change the method can certify sat well under a millimeter, and error analysis found only random noise, no systematic drift. The authors conclude ultrasound is trustworthy enough for tracking this measurement in clinics and injury studies.
plos-pone-0356761:

They looked at sexual health problems in women who had undergone the practice, and asked how those problems relate to the type of cutting, past trauma, and mental health conditions.

Lock and Ades drew on patient records in a cross-sectional study, comparing women across those factors. plos-pone-0357961:

Backes and her colleagues classified acts such as sitting, strolling, and climbing stairs from the insole's signals. Good accuracy from the feet alone matters because insoles need no wristband or phone and work all day unnoticed. plos-pone-0358261:

In skeletal Class III malocclusion, the thin bone holding the lower front teeth limits how far orthodontics can safely move them. Nguyen's measurements show orthodontists how much room they truly have. Moving a tooth beyond its bone housing risks gum and root damage that cannot be undone. plos-pone-0357661:

Li's census-based approach offers public health a cheap, wide net for finding at-risk youth before crisis. It cannot diagnose any single teen, and the authors say so plainly. Used well, it tells services where to add screening and support. Used badly, area labels could stigmatize, which is why the team's own reflections matter. plos-pone-0355961:

Into the mix go recycled concrete powder and steel fibers pulled from waste tires, replacing part of the cement and factory fibers. Bend tests with camera-based strain tracking and microscope imaging watched cracks form and bridge, while a life cycle assessment tallied climate and resource impacts from cradle to factory gate.

The greener mixes stayed competitive in bending strength, with the tire-fiber version topping the table. Life cycle results showed lower climate impact and fossil use than the conventional recipe. Manan and colleagues argue the swap supports circular building practice without surrendering the toughness that makes this composite special.
plos-pone-0356461:
Cavide Ali and colleagues measured a fat-related signaling protein, CTRP-1, in the blood of ninety-six women. Half had polycystic ovary syndrome, and half did not. All were seen at a Turkish center. Their 2026 case-control study took fasting samples in the same cycle phase. It recorded hormone and metabolic measures. It tested whether the protein separated the two groups once age and body mass were accounted for.

Women with the syndrome carried about double the protein level of controls. The protein also tracked with body mass, insulin, and blood fats. It tracked with a key ovarian hormone too. It stayed tied to the diagnosis after adjustment. The authors are careful: the sample is small, and the design cannot prove direction. Still, CTRP-1 joins the list of metabolic signals worth testing as a syndrome marker.
plos-pone-0356261:
Bo Hu and Wei Li examine how soil chemistry changes as forests recover in Huize County, in China's Yunnan Province, in work reported in 2026. They focused on the balance among carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus in the soil, which governs how well a restored forest cycles nutrients. Samples came from three forest types that represent different stages of recovery, from pine plantation to mature broadleaf forest.

Soil carbon and nitrogen turned out to be the strongest controls on the nutrient balance overall, but the details shifted with each stage. In young pine stands, potassium and aluminum mattered most for some ratios, while in mature forest total phosphorus and nitrogen took over. Environmental factors explained more as restoration advanced. The pattern shows recovering forests moving from limits set by soil's physical traits toward tighter links between trees and soil nutrients.
plos-pone-0355561:

The survey, running across all Indian states and union territories, will interview more than a quarter of a million people, making it one of the largest psychiatric surveys ever attempted. With numbers that large, keeping methods consistent is the central challenge.

The framework layers several safeguards: careful selection and translation of instruments, structured training for field workers, pilot testing, and a custom digital platform with built-in logic checks and live dashboards. A share of participants is re-interviewed, data pass through standard cleaning rules, and state and central teams review progress regularly. The authors intend the design, informed by the first survey, as a reusable model for large mental health surveys anywhere.
plos-pone-0353661:

The otter, a top river predator and a sign of healthy waterways, has lost ground as land use changes across the basin. Records were too scattered to plan protection, so the team surveyed thousands of kilometers of river by boat over several years and combined their sightings with existing records.

Feeding twenty-six environmental factors into an ensemble of habitat models produced an accurate suitability map. Two factors dominated: distance to protected areas and distance to rivers. The sobering result is how little top-quality habitat remains, well under one percent of the basin. The authors intend the hotspots to guide planners toward the stretches of river where protection would help otters most.
plos-pone-0356061:
