Pest losses eat a significant share of the world's food, and quick identification drives the right control response. Convolutional networks excel at fine local detail but miss long-range patterns, while vision transformers do the reverse. Their model, CT-PestNet, fuses both, adding a module that distills and boosts features across scales and another that lets neighboring image tokens interact more deeply.

On a large, difficult benchmark of more than one hundred pest classes, the model reached accuracy several points above the best prior convolutional and transformer models. It scored near-perfectly on an easier dataset. The authors credit the cross-scale treatment for handling pests of wildly different sizes against cluttered backgrounds, and present the system as practical support for field scouting.
plos-pone-0353861:

plos-pone-0355461:

Users define motifs as text patterns; domain calls come from a standard profile database. Both are drawn onto the alignment and exported as an annotated multi-sheet spreadsheet. A coverage score reports what fraction of each motif sits inside an annotated domain. Sefa and colleagues say the score helps separate motifs that live inside known machinery from those in uncharted protein regions.
plos-pone-0354961:

plos-pone-0353261:

Fifty-eight Hispanic adults cycled for ten minutes at alternating intensities while wearing common watches and breathing through a laboratory meter that measures true energy use. The watches substantially misestimated energy use for everyone. Error grew steadily as body fat rose and differed by brand. Kostrna warns that today's consumer devices are not yet reliable enough for clinical or research calorie tracking.
plos-pone-0353761:

One model studies single colonies cut out of the photo, while a second studies small tiles cut from the whole plate image. Each model was trained on thousands of images from hundreds of strains across ten species that matter in clinics. Used alone, each model scored well. Joined as a pair, they did better still on fresh strains they had not trained on, catching nearly all cases and rarely raising false alarms. The authors see the paired design as a practical help for busy microbiology labs.

This group faces unfair access to health and social care, is often recognized by services only late or in crisis, and has a higher risk of being placed in institutions. The study asks what support they need and what delayed help costs them.

The plan mixes several methods across four local areas. First, existing research will be gathered and summarized with people with dementia and their families helping to shape it. Then forty people with dementia will take part in repeated life-story interviews, sometimes alongside family carers. Researchers will also spend time inside social care teams to watch how services work day to day. Art workshops will give a voice to people at risk of isolation. Results will be shared freely with professionals, charities, and families.
plos-pone-0332561: Hohoe, Ghana — SARS-CoV-2 infection factors in a case-control study. This paper identified them. The findings reveal what drove COVID-19 in a Ghanaian municipality — local evidence for local public health.
plos-pone-0354361:
Agyei-Asabere and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask how completely deaths are registered in Ghana. A country that cannot count its deaths cannot target health policy well. Ghana's birth registration has improved, but death records remain scattered across offices that share data poorly, despite a system dating back to the late nineteenth century.

The team judged the 2022 death register and two national censuses with two independent methods. Depending on the method, only about three tenths to just over half of deaths appeared to be registered. Regional gaps were wide: the capital area approached seven tenths complete, while one region barely reached one death in twelve. Deaths of young children were notably under-reported, and age reporting itself was rough. Little had improved in twenty years. The authors urge coordinated, targeted fixes so Ghana can plan from real numbers.
plos-pone-0354461:
Cao and colleagues, in a 2026 study, tally what respiratory infections cost hospitals in Thai Nguyen, Vietnam, for adult patients. Chest infections burden health and budgets heavily in lower-income countries, but hard cost figures guide planning. The team reviewed records from seven hospitals over about two and a half years.

More than twenty-five thousand patients and twenty-eight thousand illness episodes were counted. Most patients were women, and most were sixty or older. Pneumonia was the leading diagnosis by far. The middle cost per episode was around one hundred seventy-five US dollars, driven mainly by bed days, then medicines, then lab tests. One rare pneumonia type cost several times more than the common kinds. Diagnosis, age, sex, hospital level, stay length, and extra illnesses all pushed costs up or down. The authors offer the breakdown to help hospitals and insurers budget for a very common reason for admission.
plos-pone-0353361:
Chaturvedi and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask what happens when heart valve patients who bounce back to hospital land somewhere other than the hospital that treated them. This split care, called fragmentation, has hurt outcomes in other heart procedures. The team studied Americans who had a catheter-based aortic valve replacement and were readmitted within ninety days, using a national readmissions database.

Of roughly fifty-six thousand readmitted patients, more than a third went to a different hospital. Valve use more than doubled across the study years, while readmission and fragmentation rates both fell. Even after adjustment, fragmented patients faced higher odds of breathing, gut, and infection complications at readmission. They were also more likely to leave for a care facility rather than home. The authors argue that keeping follow-up care connected to the original team is a fixable weakness as valve replacement spreads.
plos-pone-0353161:
Fengyu Sun and seven colleagues use isotope fingerprints to trace where the fluids that formed fluorite deposits came from, in this 2026 PLOS ONE geology study. Fluorite veins on the southern edge of the North China Craton showed puzzling isotope differences even within one district. The team compared thin veinlets that once carried hot fluids with the thicker veins where the mineral actually settled.

The conduit veinlets carried wildly mixed isotope signatures, while the host veins were strikingly uniform. Calculations point to hot fluids rising from magma that blended with the ancient basement rock on their way up. Tectonic pulses repeatedly reopened the conduits, while the host veins filled in one steadier episode — a story written in stone chemistry.
plos-pone-0354261:
Maliha Khan Majlish and four colleagues survey medical students in Dhaka, Bangladesh, about stress, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Three hundred and eighty students in their third to fifth years at two medical colleges filled in a structured questionnaire about academic pressures and psychological strain. Two thirds were women, and most respondents reported moderate or high stress.

Statistical modelling tied stress to exam-score anxiety, worry about the future, poor time management, and loneliness. Satisfaction with teaching and administration mattered too, along with parental support. The authors argue that medical schools in crowded, high-pressure settings should treat stress as a curriculum problem, not a private weakness — and build support into the programme itself.
plos-pone-0353561:
Alyssa Tilly and seven colleagues test whether a questionnaire about the quality of dying makes sense to the families who must answer it, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The revised global questionnaire asks bereaved caregivers to rate a patient's last week of life: symptoms, whether wishes were honoured, and support received. Eighteen caregivers from inpatient hospices in Canada and the United States talked through each question aloud.

Respondents mostly judged care against the death they had hoped for, or against how much distress they had witnessed. No question was consistently misunderstood, though some were hard to answer when the patient could not communicate. The authors conclude the tool is understandable and relevant for North American hospices.
plos-pone-0354161:
Tingting Zhou and three colleagues hunt for cheap blood clues to severe sleep apnoea in middle-aged men, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The standard diagnosis requires an overnight sleep laboratory study, which many patients never get. The team compared one hundred and thirty-two newly diagnosed men, split into severe and non-severe groups by their breathing-disturbance index, and examined routine blood values.

Two measures stood out: uric acid, a waste product linked to gout, and the spread of red blood cell sizes. Together they separated severe from non-severe cases with fair accuracy, and both tracked how low blood oxygen fell during sleep. The authors propose the pair as a first-pass risk screen, pending prospective confirmation.
plos-pone-0329161:
Qian Chen and six colleagues sift twenty years of side-effect reports. Their subject is the acne drug isotretinoin. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The drug is powerful and closely watched, especially in pregnancy. The team used the American adverse-event database. European data served as a cross-check. They hunted for events reported far more often with this drug. Four statistical methods had to agree. Only then was a signal kept.

Nearly five hundred robust signals emerged. Psychiatric, gut, and birth-related problems led the list. The loudest signal was for inflammatory bowel disease. It came with signs of lawsuit-driven reporting. The authors flag that openly. Several signals are absent from the current label. They need clinical follow-up.
plos-pone-0352261:
Cheng Fei and four colleagues hang a camera platform from a helikite — part balloon, part kite — to watch over construction sites, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Fixed cameras miss corners and drones run out of battery within the hour, while building sites need an all-day bird's-eye view for safety. Their wind-resistant platform carries sensors aloft for long stretches without a pilot.

The team also built a training set of a thousand overhead site photos, expanded for teaching an object-detection model to find workers. On fresh test images the model scored near ninety-eight percent accuracy. Cheap, persistent oversight of this kind could catch missing helmets and unsafe behaviour before accidents happen.
plos-pone-0352161:
Aboshosha and colleagues benchmarked AI models for spotting mpox from skin photos in a 2026 study. Mpox sores mimic many other skin conditions, and past studies used loose methods that inflated scores. Their benchmark merged two public image sets, kept test photos free of altered copies, and grouped similar images to prevent leakage.

Seven standard models plus a combined ensemble were tested. The ensemble scored best overall, while one compact model led the single models. The authors stress their scores are lower than flashier reports on purpose, because the test was stricter. Honest benchmarks help clinics judge what image screening can truly deliver.
plos-pone-0353061:
Xie and colleagues interviewed new dentists in China about posture-friendly magnifying glasses in a 2026 study. The new glasses use prisms so dentists can sit upright and look straight while seeing downward work. Nineteen residents at a Beijing teaching hospital described their experience after the glasses reached the market in 2022.

Dentists praised sharper vision, more precise work, better posture, and better treatment quality. Drawbacks included discomfort while adjusting to the new viewing angle. Neck strain is an occupational hazard that ends dental careers early, so tools that protect posture matter beyond comfort. Novice views show where training and fitting support are needed.
plos-pone-0352461:
Farrokh Ghahremaninejad authored this 2026 PLOS One botany study of the grey mangrove, the main tree of Iran's Persian Gulf mangrove forests. Iranian stands sit thousands of kilometers from other populations of the species, and no one had checked their form and genetics for signs of separate identity or mixing with relatives. The study compared pollen and stem features across Iranian sites and sequenced a standard DNA region.

Morphology revealed two distinct populations, one of which the author names as a new subspecies, australis. The DNA analysis confirmed the Iranian populations form one family line, with moderate support for the split between them. The author estimates the two lineages separated around the shift from the Pliocene to the Pleistocene, likely under changing climates and sea levels.
plos-pone-0351061:
Haiying Lin and six colleagues examine this 2026 PLOS One economics study of whether artificial intelligence adoption makes Chinese manufacturers' exports more technologically sophisticated. Using data on listed manufacturing firms from 2008 to 2021, the authors related each firm's AI activity to the technical complexity of what it sells abroad, holding constant firm characteristics over time.

AI adoption clearly raised export complexity, with the strongest gains in regions already exporting sophisticated goods. State-owned firms, light textile firms, and firms in the east and center benefited notably. The effect ran through two channels: firms upgraded their workforce mix and became more innovative. The authors recommend policies that spread AI capability more evenly so inland and smaller firms are not left behind.
plos-pone-0331161:
Jack Nunn and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One co-produced analysis of how to make citizen science, research powered by public volunteers, deliver more for society and nature. The team surveyed and held discussions with researchers, volunteer scientists, and Indigenous participants, and documented nine projects using a standardized reporting tool.

Participants pointed to practical fixes: reach out deliberately to underrepresented groups, pay contributors fairly, co-create projects from the start, follow open data principles, and validate results transparently. Short-term funding and missing central support for ethics and management were named as persistent weaknesses. Recognition through co-authorship and training would help keep volunteers engaged. The authors distill ten recommendations and argue citizen science should be built into national research, education, and policy rather than run as a side project.
plos-pone-0352861:
Mohamed Albekery and seven colleagues report real-world experience with the drug finerenone in Saudi Arabia in 2026. The drug treats diabetic kidney disease, a common complication of type 2 diabetes. Large trials showed it protects kidneys and the heart. Far less was known about how it performs in everyday Saudi clinics.

The team reviewed records of adults treated at a single centre. Sixty-seven patients met the study criteria. Changes over time were tracked for urine protein, kidney function, and blood potassium. Potassium matters because this drug class can push it too high. Mixed-effects models adjusted the trends for other patient factors. Studies like this test whether trial benefits survive contact with routine care, local diets, and ordinary prescribing habits.
plos-pone-0352661:
Arohi Chauhan and seven colleagues adapt a health literacy questionnaire for tuberculosis patients in India. The 2026 study works in Junagadh district, Gujarat. The original instrument was built in Iran and follows World Health Organization thinking. It measures whether adults can find, understand, judge, and use health information. No validated version existed for Indian tuberculosis care.

The team used a mixed-methods sequence across a full year. Experts reviewed the items first. Translators carried the text into the local language and back again. Then came cognitive interviews with patients and frontline health workers. Those conversations exposed wording that confused or misfired culturally. Statistical testing of the revised tool followed. A trustworthy local measure lets tuberculosis programmes find patients whose low literacy threatens their long, demanding treatment.
plos-pone-0351161:
Silvia Cañas-Duarte and seven colleagues combine three kinds of molecular data to explain stubborn bacteria in this 2026 study. Some Escherichia coli cells enter a slow-growing state called persistence. In that state, antibiotics cannot kill them, though they are not genetically resistant. The team studied a high-persistence mutant strain. They read its genome, its active genes, and its membrane fats, then compared isolated persisters with normal cells.

One suspect was cleared. Switching on classic stress responses seemed unimportant for entering this persistent state. Attention instead converged on the cell membrane. Gene activity pointed that way first. Fat profiles confirmed it: persister membranes carried more unsaturated fatty acids. A changed membrane may be how these cells ride out antibiotic attack. If so, drugs that target membrane composition could one day wake or kill persisters that now survive treatment and restart infections.
plos-pone-0352761:
Samuel Briggs-Price and four colleagues interview patients who healed a torn Achilles tendon without surgery. Their 2026 British study recruited fifteen patients from a specialist clinic. Non-surgical care, usually a boot, is common in the National Health Service. Yet research had largely ignored how that recovery actually feels. Semi-structured interviews were analysed thematically, with coding checked by two researchers.

Three themes organised the accounts. First came the injury itself and entering care. Patients described a sudden snap, sometimes oddly painless, and patchy grasp of their options. Second came life in the boot. It allowed welcome mobility but rubbed on comfort and routine. Many also felt flooded with information in the first session and forgot much of it. The study's value is practical: clinics learn exactly where communication and boot fitting fail real patients, and can fix those moments.
plos-pone-0351661:
Amit Kumar and six colleagues sequence a drug-resistant bacterium pulled from a market fish's gills. Their 2026 study works in Punjab, India, on the rohu, a staple food fish. The Escherichia coli strain resisted many antibiotic families. Only an intermediate response remained to one last-line drug. Whole-genome sequencing produced its draft blueprint: under four million DNA letters and nearly four thousand genes. Thirty-nine resistance determinants were catalogued, all carried on the chromosome rather than on mobile plasmids.

The genome also held tools for grabbing iron, building biofilms, and colonising hosts. Prediction software rated its likelihood of infecting humans as high. Aquaculture uses antibiotics heavily, and resistant bacteria ride the food chain quietly. A fish-market strain carrying a built-in resistance arsenal, plus the machinery to persist, is a textbook One Health warning. The study argues for genomic surveillance where farming, food, and human health meet.
plos-pone-0351561:
Chunhong Shao and six colleagues profile a dangerous hospital germ in this 2026 PLOS One study from China. The germ is a strain of Klebsiella pneumoniae that resists carbapenems, a last-line class of antibiotics, yet may also be highly virulent. Two samples came from one patient in an emergency intensive care unit. Lab tests showed the strain shrugged off many drug groups, though a few antibiotics still worked against it.

Gene reading placed both samples in the ST11 line, a type already watched closely in China. The genome carried many genes tied to attack and survival, including ones for grabbing iron, and a gene linked to extra virulence. In mice, the strain proved far more deadly than a standard mild strain. The mix of drug resistance and killing power in one germ is what makes it a threat worth tracking.
plos-pone-0348061:
Nancy Fahim and five colleagues reanalyse a trial of premature babies for clues in a hormone's double life. Their 2026 post hoc study uses the PENUT trial, which randomised over nine hundred infants born before twenty-eight weeks. Erythropoietin is both a treatment candidate and a stress signal. Blood levels were measured at birth and across the first two weeks. Brain scans and eye examinations supplied the outcomes: brain injury and retinopathy of prematurity.

Birth levels told a stress story. Higher hormone tracked with younger gestation, no delayed cord clamping, and lower Apgar scores. It also tracked with brain bleeding and risk of death. Eye disease, reassuringly, showed no link to the hormone. In untreated babies, week-one levels correlated with white matter injury. In treated babies, the day-fourteen pattern ran the other way. Erythropoietin's meaning clearly depends on timing and treatment, a nuance any therapy trial must respect.
plos-pone-0351761:
Holly Edward and colleagues describe a planned pilot trial of a new guide role for cancer patients in Ontario: a physiotherapist navigator. Rehabilitation during cancer treatment eases side effects, yet fewer than a third of patients can reach such services. The navigator would meet patients across six sessions over up to eighteen weeks, steering them to movement and recovery support inside an acute cancer center.

Patients will be assigned by chance to the navigator or to usual care. Being a pilot, the trial chiefly tests whether the idea runs at all: will patients stick with the sessions, join, and stay, and are they satisfied? Quality of life and other early outcome signals come second. If the role proves workable, a larger trial can ask whether it truly helps people recover strength during treatment.
plos-pone-0350761:
Hope, confidence, optimism, and bounce-back strength together form what psychologists call psychological capital. Seyedeh Melika Kharghani Moghadam and co-authors asked whether nurses high in these traits perform better at work, in a 2026 PLOS One survey of about two hundred ten hospital nurses in Iran.

Nurses richer in these traits did report stronger job performance. Discomfort with uncertainty showed no direct link to performance on its own. Yet when uncertainty tolerance was low, the benefit of positive traits shrank noticeably. The authors suggest hospitals build nurses' inner resources while also teaching them to handle unclear, fast-changing situations.
plos-pone-0349861:
Hamdi Mohamed Yusuf and colleagues followed newborns at a referral hospital in Uganda to find who develops jaundice severe enough to need light treatment. Jaundice in newborns can injure the brain when care comes late, and Ugandan data have been sparse. More than five hundred mother and baby pairs were tracked from birth through the first week of life.

Risk rose close to twofold for babies whose mothers were underweight, overweight, or obese during pregnancy. Low household income, surgical birth, and waters breaking early before labour also raised risk. Blood tests and blood group checks were part of follow up. Knowing these flags, staff can watch high risk babies more closely in the first days.
plos-pone-0350661:
Yang Cheng and co-authors surveyed business analytics students in 2026 about learning with artificial intelligence tools. They asked what makes students plan to keep using such tools, and whether that plan links to interest in the subject and in related careers.

Students who felt the tools improved their learning, were fun, felt fresh, and let them interact kept intending to use them. That intention also went with stronger interest in their studies and firmer career aims. The chain suggests course tools earn lasting use by being genuinely helpful and engaging, and that good experiences can pull students toward analytics work.
plos-pone-0350561:
Retracted: this article has been formally withdrawn by the journal. Junqing Zhang and co-authors claimed a deep learning method for judging smart electricity meters. Because the paper is retracted, its claims no longer count as reliable evidence.

The text turns power disturbance signals into images. It then feeds those images to a tuned image network that names the fault type. Strong resistance to noise was reported. None of that should now be cited or used to guide meter monitoring. The entry stays in the library so the withdrawal itself remains on record.
plos-pone-0336461:
Kalpana Jnawali and co-authors surveyed women in Achham district, Nepal, in 2026 about menstrual practices after a government campaign smashed the seclusion huts known as chhaugoth. The custom isolates menstruating women despite being illegal, and whether demolition changed daily practice was unknown.

Nearly four hundred girls and women answered interviews on hygiene and practice. The team recorded where women now stay, what materials they use, and what taboos persist. Demolishing huts removes a harmful place, but habits and beliefs move slower than bulldozers. Findings like these show health workers what to tackle next, from water access to family attitudes.
plos-pone-0350861:
Goshime Muluneh Mekasha and colleagues field tested hundreds of maize hybrids under good rain and managed drought in 2026 work aimed at African farming. Dry spells linked to climate change cut yields hard, and even closely related breeding lines may hide useful variation.

More than eight hundred test hybrids, made by crossing doubled lines with a tester from the opposite group, were grown in patterned trials. Yields fell sharply under drought, yet the top group of hybrids still beat the trial average and commercial checks. The result shows fresh diversity can be mined without wide crosses, a practical route to tougher maize.
plos-pone-0349761:
Ashley A Powell, Sandra G Velleman, and co-authors examined how hot and cold conditions rewrite the genetic instructions inside turkey muscle stem cells. These satellite cells build and repair muscle, and they fine-tune their output by splicing gene messages into different versions. Heat stress threatens poultry growth, so the team reanalyzed gene-read data from turkey cells grown at three temperatures during growth and maturation.

They catalogued more than sixty thousand splicing events across over five thousand genes. Splicing differed significantly in every temperature comparison, and also between growing and maturing cells at each temperature. Genes whose splicing changed overlapped strongly with genes whose overall activity changed. The authors offer the catalogue as a foundation for understanding how temperature stress reshapes turkey muscle development and meat production.
plos-pone-0347961:
Christa Blokhuis and colleagues built a computer simulation, called MEET-eaters, of how Dutch households and supermarkets shape each other's meal choices. Eating less meat would help the climate, health, and animals, yet what shops stock and what families want push on each other constantly. Earlier models usually captured only one direction of that influence.

In the simulation, virtual households pick meals while virtual supermarkets set supply to be endless, fixed, or responsive to demand. Meal patterns under endless and responsive supply turned out similar, and both supply and demand strongly steered choices. The team also tested interventions aimed at shoppers and at stores. The model helps policymakers see why one-sided campaigns often stall.
plos-pone-0328861:
Eric Roberts and colleagues dated the rock layers around the famous Dueling Dinosaurs fossil site in Montana with extreme precision. The Hell Creek Formation holds the last dinosaurs before the asteroid impact, but its lower layers lack good date markers, making it hard to line up fossil sites across the region. The team measured detailed rock sections and combined magnetic and fossil evidence with new ash-bed dates.

Two newly found ash layers gave ages very close to sixty-seven million years with tiny error margins, using a refined uranium-lead method on zircon crystals. The results show the dinosaur-extinction boundary itself is not exposed at this site. Firm anchor dates like these let paleontologists place each Hell Creek fossil in the right order before the extinction.
plos-pone-0333061:
Li-De Su and co-authors examine whether China's twenty seventeen digital cultural policy widened the gap between its rich and poor regions. The policy pushed culture onto online platforms, and the authors argue that state backing can amplify platform power, letting already strong regions pull further ahead. They tracked national and provincial data for more than a decade, with a close look at radio and television broadcasting.

After the policy year, growth in the cultural economy slowed nationally and provincial paths split apart. Broadcasting income became far more concentrated, with inequality measures roughly doubling or more, and statistical tests singled out the policy year as the turning point. The authors warn that digital development judged only by total growth can hide deepening unfairness between places.
plos-pone-0347661:
Lan-Chen Zhang and colleagues built a living library of gut bacteria from three small fish that scientists use worldwide to test pollution and model human disease. The three are zebrafish and two kinds of medaka, one from fresh water and one from the sea. Before researchers can study what these microbes do, the microbes must be grown and named. The team refined ways to recover bacteria from fish guts with and without oxygen.

The collections held bacteria from fourteen genera in zebrafish, twelve in marine medaka, and eighteen in freshwater medaka, with clear differences between hosts. Each strain was identified by gene sequencing and standard biochemical tests. The authors offer the library as raw material for probiotics, for protecting fish against disease, and for pairing with germ-free fish to untangle how gut microbes shape health.
plos-pone-0349061:
Pratistha Sarkar, Shreya Ahuja, and Iulia M. Lazar build a three-dimensional lab model of cancer spreading to the brain. Studying that spread is hard because the brain guards itself closely. Their 2026 model grows human brain vessel cells together with breast and ovarian cancer cells, with no scaffold, letting the cells' natural attraction knit them into web-like structures.

The setup copies how wandering cancer cells latch onto the brain's vessel network. It stays stable over time and lets researchers watch vessel shape change and signals pass between the two cell types. Cheap and repeatable, the model can also test candidate drugs. It gives labs a workable stand-in for a process that is otherwise hidden inside patients.
plos-pone-0347261:
Jamal Al Qundus and Bassam Al-Shargabi built a question-answering system for German financial language, where long compound words and flexible phrasing defeat many artificial intelligence tools. Their 2026 system, called INAGQA, works by finding the headword of each question, the core noun everything else hangs on, then matching it against a knowledge graph of company facts.

Tested on more than two thousand expert-checked questions, the system beat both a leading language-model approach and template-based rivals, and handled time- and quantity-flavoured questions almost flawlessly. Analysts in a case study got answers in about two seconds. The authors propose the design as a template for other non-English specialist domains.
plos-pone-0347761:
Juan José Rodríguez-Crespo and colleagues review blood clot care at a Mexican hospital. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The topic is acute pulmonary embolism, a clot that blocks lung arteries. Clear global guidelines exist for its care. The COVID-19 years crowded hospitals, though. Care may have drifted from the guidelines under that strain.

The team sampled fifty patients from each year, 2019 through 2022. They scored how closely care matched the guidelines. They then linked scores to death, collapse in the first week, and bleeding. Care that skipped guideline steps was common across the period. The work shows why tracking that drift matters in a crisis.
plos-pone-0337661:
Karimeh Ibrahim Ata and colleagues fuse two kinds of neural network to forecast city traffic. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Traffic twists through road webs in ways flat tables miss. Models that cannot adjust on the fly lose accuracy fast.

One part of their model respects the road map's links. The other tracks patterns over time. A joining module keeps matching the two views. It picks fresh neighbor sets as traffic shifts. It also checks how alike the two views stay. The result aims to stay sharp as conditions change. Smart traffic systems need forecasts like that to time lights and warn drivers.
plos-pone-0347161:
Dedefo Gemeda Anbesa and colleagues ask why so few mothers in Shashemene, southern Ethiopia, have a companion with them during childbirth, in this 2026 PLOS ONE mixed-methods study. A trusted companion in labor improves outcomes for mother and baby and is part of respectful care, yet hospitals often keep companions out.

Surveying four hundred eleven mothers who delivered in the town's public hospitals in 2021, plus interviews, the team measured how many had companions and which factors raised or lowered the odds. Facility rules, space, and staff attitudes typically weigh heavily in such settings. The findings point local managers to the specific barriers, from ward layout to policy, that keep a proven, cost-free support away from laboring women.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Encouraging news from Cyprus reached New York late in 1968. On 10 December, the Council adopted Resolution 261 without dissent. The Secretary-General reported that the peace force was still needed. He also noted welcome recent gains on the island. Cyprus agreed to the force staying past mid-December.

The text restates the by-now long list of Cyprus decisions. It urges restraint and joint effort in the hopeful climate of the day. It then extends the posting to 15 June 1969. The standing hope returns at the end. Enough progress might soon let the force shrink or head home. That formula stayed with the mission through this era.

Resolution 1361, passed unanimously on 5 July 2001, deals with a vacancy on the International Court of Justice, the UN's highest court in The Hague. Judge Mohammed Bedjaoui had resigned, with his departure taking effect on 30 September 2001, leaving his seat empty for the rest of his term.

Because the Court's statute leaves the scheduling to the Council, the members fixed the election for the vacant seat on 12 October 2001. Judges are chosen jointly, so the vote would happen both in the Security Council and in the General Assembly, which was then holding its fifty-sixth session. The whole text is short and purely procedural.

Liberia was climbing out of a savage civil war in 2004. Resolution 1561, adopted unanimously on 17 September 2004, extended the UN mission there, UNMIL. West African states and the African Union backed the peace effort. Ex-fighters were handing in weapons. The Secretary-General's report of 10 September 2004 guided the decision.

UNMIL's mandate now ran to 19 September 2005. Members told Liberian parties to prove their commitment to peace. Free and fair elections had to happen by October 2005. The text also appeals for money to reabsorb former fighters into civilian life. Donors were reminded of pledges made at a February 2004 rebuilding conference.

Truce lines in Palestine had to be drawn in the fall of 1948. Both sides had gained ground since 14 October. The stand-in mediator had asked them to pull back on 26 October. The Council weighed its past truce texts. Resolution 61 passed on 4 November 1948 by nine votes to one. The Ukrainian team said no. The Soviet team held back.

Troops that had moved past the 14 October lines had to quit them. The mediator would draw stop lines no one could cross. Set truce lines and bare zones would come next, by talks or by his word. A team of the five big powers, plus Belgium and Colombia, would coach him. If a side balked, the team would weigh hard steps under the Charter's teeth. The war's end game was taking shape in these lines.

Resolution 361, adopted unanimously on 30 August 1974, turns from battle lines to human suffering in Cyprus. Weeks of fighting after the July coup and the Turkish intervention had displaced a large share of the island's people, who were in dire need of help. The UN refugee chief had already been named coordinator of humanitarian assistance for Cyprus.

The Council thanked the Secretary-General for bringing the two communities' leaders into talks and warmly welcomed the start of that dialogue. It called on all parties to do everything possible to relieve suffering, to secure respect for basic human rights for everyone, and to hold back from anything that might worsen the crisis. Relief work, in short, was declared a duty of the combatants.

Resolution 461, adopted on 31 December 1979 by eleven votes to none with four abstentions, returns to the Tehran hostages as the year ends. The Council recalled its December demand for the Americans' release and the appeals its president made in November. The World Court had ordered Iran on 15 December to free every hostage without exception, and Iran's foreign minister had sent letters setting out his government's grievances.

The Council again urgently called for the immediate release of all the hostages and for their safe departure. It took note of the Secretary-General's view that the crisis threatened international peace. And it decided to meet again in January to review the situation and consider steps, sanctions included, if the hostages were still held.

Liberia's remaining sanctions are renewed by Resolution 1961, adopted on 17 December 2010. Timber and diamond measures had ended years earlier, the forestry reform law and Kimberley Process controls were in place, and Liberia was cooperating on weapons marking. The Panel of Experts still found too little progress toward the conditions for ending the arms and travel measures, and none on the asset freeze.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms embargo and the travel ban for 12 months. It confirms the Resolution 1532 (2004) asset freeze stays in force, demanding Liberia meet its obligations under it. The Committee must keep the public reasons for each listing updated. The Panel of Experts is extended to 16 December 2011 to check compliance, judge how the freeze is working, and assess Kimberley controls. It must report midway by 1 June 2011 and finally by 1 December 2011.

Chad and the Central African Republic get a UN military follow-on to the EU force in Resolution 1861, adopted on 14 January 2009. Darfur's violence spilled across the borders, and EUFOR Chad/CAR was due to end on 15 March 2009. Both governments asked for a UN military component to succeed it.

The Council extends the United Nations Mission in the Central African Republic and Chad, MINURCAT, until 15 March 2010. It authorizes 5,200 military personnel, 300 police, and 25 military liaison officers, taking over from EUFOR on 15 March 2009. Acting under Chapter VII, MINURCAT may use all necessary measures in eastern Chad to protect civilians in danger, especially refugees and displaced persons, and to secure aid delivery. In the north-eastern Central African Republic it keeps a presence at Birao and may extract endangered civilians and aid workers. It trains the Chadian camp police, the Détachement intégré de sécurité.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly resolution 57/161, adopted on 16 December 2002, extends the United Nations Verification Mission in Guatemala through 2003, near the end of the timetable agreed for completing the country's peace accords. The Assembly acts on the mission's verification reporting and on Guatemala's own request for the extension.

The mandate runs from 1 January to 31 December 2003, and the Secretary-General is asked to recommend how the mission should continue afterward. The resolution welcomes steps such as the agreement to create a National Reparations Commission for victims of the armed conflict and urges both sides to sustain and deepen compliance with the accords. With the end of the implementation timetable in sight, the extension kept the settlement's final phase under international observation.

Resolution 69/61 of the General Assembly, adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014, deals with women, disarmament, non-proliferation and arms control. It urges states to promote equal opportunities for women to be represented in decision-making on disarmament and arms control. It supports collecting data broken down by sex and age on the impact of armed violence. It notes the role of UN-Women and the Arms Trade Treaty's reference to gender-based violence. That keeps women's participation a standing part of disarmament policy.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
At Lebanon's request, UNIFIL is renewed for six months on 30 January 2003. The Council endorsed the Secretary-General's January report, including its advice to extend the mandate. The force's main remaining task was restoring peace and security in the south of the country.

The mandate now runs until 31 July 2003. All violence is condemned, and grave concern is voiced over serious breaches of the withdrawal line by air, sea, and land. The parties are urged to end those violations and to respect the safety of United Nations staff. UNIFIL is to keep full freedom of movement throughout its area of operations.

News that Congo's first prime minister and two fellow leaders had been murdered drives this text of 21 February 1961. A serious civil war was building in the Congo, and widespread bloodshed and a threat to world peace were feared.

The United Nations is urged to act at once to prevent civil war, including arranging ceasefires, halting military operations, and using force if needed as a last resort. The withdrawal of all Belgian and other foreign military and political advisers and mercenaries not under United Nations command is demanded. All states are called on to stop such people leaving for the Congo from their soil.

Just one month is granted to UNMEE, the Ethiopia-Eritrea mission, on 14 March 2006, until 15 April 2006. Eritrea had placed heavy restrictions on the mission, and border demarcation was still blocked. The short renewal signalled frustration while the mission's future was weighed.

Both parties are demanded to comply fully with resolution 1640, including lifting the restrictions on UNMEE and reversing Eritrean limits on its movement. Lasting peace, it is repeated, requires full demarcation of the border under the Boundary Commission's final and binding ruling. Both governments are told to give the mission the access, help, and protection it needs to do its work.

Côte d'Ivoire's Group of Experts is extended until 31 October 2007 on 20 June 2007. The group's final report under its previous term had just reached the Council. The experts track how the arms embargo and the targeted travel and financial measures on the country are applied and where they are broken.

Acting under Chapter VII, the group stays working alongside the renewed sanctions. A written update, through the sanctions committee, is asked for before 15 October 2007. That update is to cover enforcement of the measures and offer recommendations. The aim is current evidence in hand when the sanctions themselves come up for renewal at the end of October.

The United Nations force that watches the cease-fire line between Israel and Syria is the subject of Resolution 2361, adopted in 2017. The force is called UNDOF, and it works on the Golan Heights. Syria's civil war had spilled into the force's area. Heavy weapons were being used near its positions.

The Council renewed UNDOF's mandate for six months, until 31 December 2017. It stressed that both sides must respect the Disengagement of Forces Agreement of 1974. No armed forces other than UNDOF's own were to stay in the area of separation. Armed groups were told to leave UNDOF positions and return vehicles and weapons they had taken. The Council also welcomed the first peacekeepers returning to Camp Faouar.

Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990, and the Council answered with sanctions four days later. Resolution 660 had ordered Iraq to withdraw, and Iraq had ignored it. The invasion and occupation continued, with more loss of life and more destruction. Resolution 661 was adopted on 6 August 1990.

Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, the Council imposed wide sanctions. Their purpose was to force Iraq to comply and to restore Kuwait's government. All states had to block imports of goods from Iraq and from occupied Kuwait. Their nationals could not promote exports from those places either. Iraq was also to be denied funds and economic resources. A sanctions committee, made up of all Council members, was created to watch enforcement. The text affirmed Kuwait's right of self-defense under Article 51 of the Charter.
un-sc-res-261:
Encouraging news from Cyprus reached the Council in December 1968, along with a familiar warning. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 4 December, noted recent progress on the island. It still held that the peacekeeping force was needed to maintain peace. Cyprus's government agreed the force should stay beyond 15 December. Resolution 261 was adopted unanimously on 10 December 1968.

The Council reaffirmed its Cyprus resolutions, from Resolution 186 of 1964 onward. The parties were urged to act with the utmost restraint. They had to make good use of the favorable climate and press on with their joint efforts. The force's stationing was extended for a further period, ending on 15 June 1969. The pattern was by then well set. Each renewal kept the peacekeepers in Cyprus for a few more months, while the search for a final settlement went on.
un-sc-res-1361: A seat on the International Court of Justice fell vacant in 2001. Judge Mohammed Bedjaoui had resigned, with effect from 30 September 2001. On 5 July 2001 the Security Council fixed the date to fill his place. The election would be held on 12 October 2001. It would take place at a Council meeting and at a General Assembly meeting. The Assembly was then in its fifty-sixth session. The whole resolution performs that single scheduling act.
un-sc-res-61:
The Palestine truce was collapsing in the autumn of 1948. Fighting had broken out again in the south in October. On 4 November 1948 the Security Council reminded the parties of its earlier rulings. No side could break the truce as a reprisal. No side could gain land or advantage by breaking it. The acting mediator had asked both governments on 26 October to pull back.

The Council now calls on them to withdraw forces that had pushed past their 14 October positions. They also had to open armistice talks at once. Talks could run through the mediator or directly. The aim was a lasting armistice across Palestine. Those talks began on Rhodes weeks later and produced the 1949 agreements.
un-sc-res-361:
Cyprus's displaced people were the Council's focus on 30 August 1974. The summer's fighting had uprooted large numbers across the island. The Secretary-General's report on the crisis was before the Council. The United Nations refugee chief had already been named coordinator of relief for Cyprus.

The Council thanked the Secretary-General for bringing the two communities' leaders into talks. It called on them to press the talks forward for the sake of all Cypriots. All parties had to ease human suffering, honor basic human rights, and avoid acts that could worsen the crisis. Grave concern was voiced for the refugees and displaced. The parties were urged to seek peaceful answers with the Secretary-General, give relief, and let those who wished return home in safety. He owed the Council a full report on the refugees at the earliest chance, and emergency aid was to continue.
un-sc-res-461:
Iran's holding of United States hostages brought the Council to the edge of sanctions on 31 December 1979. The seizure of the embassy staff broke international law and fed rising tension. The World Court had ordered Iran on 15 December to free every hostage without exception. The Secretary-General reported on 22 December, and resolution 457 (1979) had already demanded release.

The Council restated resolution 457 in all its parts. It deplored the continued detention of the hostages against its decisions and the Court's order. Iran was urgently called once again to free them and let them leave the country. The Secretary-General was asked to lend his good offices and to report on them before the Council met again. The Council fixed that meeting for 7 January 1980. It would review the crisis and, if Iran still refused, adopt measures under the Charter to enforce its decisions.
un-sc-res-1861:
Chad and the Central African Republic are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1861, adopted on 14 January 2009. Darfur's war kept spilling across their borders. Refugees and displaced families crowded camps in the east of Chad. A European Union force guarding those areas was due to leave in March.

The Council extends the United Nations mission, called MINURCAT, until 15 March 2010. A military wing of up to 5,200 troops joins its 300 police. It takes over from the European force on 15 March 2009. Under Chapter VII it may use force to guard civilians in danger and keep aid moving. A special Chadian police unit keeps order inside the camps.
un-sc-res-1561:
By Resolution 1561, adopted unanimously on 17 September 2004, the Council acted on Liberia. The peace mission there had helped end a long civil war. Disarming fighters had gone well so far. Elections were due by October 2005, and ex-fighters still needed jobs and training.

The Council extends the mission, called UNMIL, until 19 September 2005. All Liberian parties are called to back the peace process in full. They must work together so the polls are free, fair, and open. Donors are asked to fund the return of ex-fighters to civil life. Past pledges from the February rebuild talks should be paid.
europmc-pmc10017761:
Zhang and colleagues review engineered exosomes as a tool for targeted cancer treatment in a 2023 paper. Exosomes are tiny parcels that cells release to send signals to other cells. Researchers can load them with drugs and add surface features that steer them toward tumors.

The review covers exosomes from different cell sources and how each source affects their use. It explains how loading and steering are done in the lab. It also weighs safety and the steps left before clinic use. The paper maps a lively field in drug delivery.
europmc-pmc10192861:
Dave, Athaluri, and Singh give an overview of ChatGPT in medicine in a 2023 paper. They cover its applications, advantages, limits, future prospects, and the ethical questions it raises. ChatGPT is a language model trained on vast amounts of text that can hold a fluent conversation on medical topics.

The authors survey uses in study, writing, diagnosis support, and patient communication. They weigh gains in speed against risks such as confident errors and bias. They close with advice on consent, privacy, and oversight. The paper is a balanced early guide to AI in care.
europmc-pmc10495961:
Abril-Pla and a team of co-authors presented PyMC in 2023, a Python library for chance-based models. Such models, called Bayesian, state a guess as a spread of odds, not one fixed number. PyMC lets users write a model in code that reads close to plain math. A math engine then compiles it for fast chips.

The library fits a wide range of models. Abril-Pla lists layered line fits, time series, smooth curve models, and equation-based models. Work can run on plain processors or on graphics and tensor chips. Sample uses walk through common stats tasks step by step. The authors also credit PyMC for growing the open-source scene in this niche.
europmc-pmc10589261:
Hou and co-authors reviewed macrophages in atherosclerosis in 2023, the fatty build-up inside artery walls. Such plaques narrow vessels and can trigger heart attack or stroke. Macrophages sit at the core of each stage, from first growth to rupture and healing. Their states shift with the plaque's local cues.

These cells vary widely and can reshape their fuel use on the fly. Hou shows how low oxygen in a plaque flips a switch, HIF-1alpha, that alters cell acts. Some states stuff the plaque with fat and stir swelling. Others clear dead cells and calm the zone. A ring-shaped sugar, beta-cyclodextrin, helped plaques shrink in past work by aiding fat exit. Drugs that steer these states may yield precise care.
europmc-pmc1088961:
Schug and co-authors hunted for DNA traits that mark genes used in just one tissue in this 2005 paper. Turning a fertilised egg into an adult needs genes switched on at the right place and time. Some genes run in all cells, while others run in one tissue only. The stretch of DNA before a gene, called its promoter, helps set that pattern.

Using human gene activity data from tissue surveys, the team measured how varied each gene's use was. Most genes did vary by tissue in a clear way, they found. They then flagged promoter traits that split tissue-specific genes from those used everywhere. Tissue breadth was scored with Shannon entropy, a maths measure of how spread out a pattern is. Genes used in one tissue scored low on spread, while genes used everywhere scored high.
europmc-pmc11382761:
Su and colleagues review how cells talk to each other and what that means for medicine in this 2024 paper. Multicellular life requires diverse cell types to coordinate their behaviour. Cells communicate by direct contact or at a distance through ligand-receptor pairs, where a signal molecule docks onto a receiver protein. Two processes define the exchange: conduction sends the signal, and transduction lets the receiver process it.

The review first traces the historical milestones of the field. It then details how signal molecules travel and the main pathways they mediate. Diseases caused by faulty communication are surveyed systematically. Clinical applications that target these networks follow. The authors argue that decoding communication networks is critical for grasping cell differentiation, development, and metabolism. They close with the field's open challenges.
europmc-pmc11445061:
Liu, Prentice, and Webber explain how bacterial biofilms resist antimicrobial drugs in this 2024 review. Most bacteria in nature live in aggregated communities called biofilms, glued in a self-made matrix. Cells inside differ deeply from free-floating cells of the same species. Biofilm infections are often chronic and stubbornly hard to treat with antibiotics.

Intrinsic factors drive the tolerance: the matrix barrier, slow growth rates, altered drug targets, and fast swapping of resistance genes. A special cell type, persisters, survives drug exposure by lying dormant. The review describes the biofilm lifecycle and how resistance evolves and spreads within the film. Mixed-species biofilms add cooperation and competition that further shift drug tolerance. The authors argue these features, not single mutations, explain most treatment failures.
europmc-pmc1253661:
Lubin and co-authors tackled detection limits in environmental studies in 2004. Lab tools cannot read values below set limits. Studies often fill gaps with half the limit or random picks. The team tested those habits with simulations.

Half-limit filling biased results unless few values fell below limits. Bias stayed small only when under 5 to 10 percent were censored. Random fill-ins gave unbiased estimates but shaky error ranges. Distortion grew when 30 percent or more were censored. Lubin points to Tobit regression and multiple imputation as sound fixes. Tobit methods fit truncated data of this kind.
europmc-pmc1475661:
Malaria germs must cross the mosquito gut, where most of them die. Dong and co-authors mapped how the mosquito Anopheles gambiae reacts to two malaria species in 2006. One infects humans, the other infects rodents and serves as a lab model. They tracked which mosquito genes switch on during invasion.

The rodent germ stirred a wider change in gene activity. The human germ drew a broader immune reply. Silencing tests on 12 genes found seven that guard against both germs. A few guards were specific to one germ each. Dong shows the mosquito's defense blends shared and tailored weapons.
europmc-pmc1526461:
Proteins that juggle many partners tend to be floppy, not rigid. Haynes and co-authors tested that link in 2006 across four species: worm, yeast, fly, and human. Hub proteins, those with ten or more partners, were compared with proteins holding just one partner.

In all four species, hubs carried more disordered stretches, regions with no fixed shape. Wholly disordered proteins were enriched among hubs, wholly ordered ones scarce. In yeast, hubs tied to regulation and development leaned disordered, while enzyme and transport hubs leaned ordered. Haynes argues disorder gives hubs the flex to bind many unlike partners.
europmc-pmc1550961:
A shared scale for sudden kidney injury needed a real-world test. Hoste and co-authors gave it one in 2006, tracking 5,383 intensive care patients over a year. The RIFLE scale grades injury as risk, injury, or failure, based on kidney function.

Two thirds of patients had some injury. Death rates climbed with grade: 8.8 percent at risk, 11.4 at injury, and 26.3 at failure, against 5.5 with no injury. Over half of those at the risk grade slid to worse grades. Hoste confirms the scale forecasts death and heavy care use, and flags patients likely to worsen.
europmc-pmc161361:
Oxidative stress may start Alzheimer's long before plaques appear. Perry, Cash, and Smith reviewed that case in 2002. Cell changes tied to oxidation, damage by reactive oxygen, precede the disease's hallmark tangles and plaques.

The initial source of the stress stays unclear. Redox-active metals, iron and copper, likely feed the process, since they can spawn damaging oxygen species. Perry argues that pinning down this early chemistry could open new treatments. Most Alzheimer therapies of the time chased late damage; this line points upstream, to the spark itself.  Their focus on metals points to iron and copper handling as a testable lead.
europmc-pmc1764161:
Tiny engineered particles promise much in medicine and industry, but their health effects are largely unknown. Gwinn and Vallyathan reviewed the pros and cons in 2006. Particles under 100 nanometers, billionths of a meter, gain surface traits that plain dust lacks.

Proof from ultrafine particles of human activity suggests harm to heart and lungs. Engineered ones may behave alike, traveling to distant body sites. Beneficial uses, like drug delivery and gene therapy, can themselves cause exposure. Gwinn argues for a precautionary duty: pin down toxic effects now to keep workplace and environmental exposure low.
europmc-pmc1829161: An internet survey of 2,596 people with fibromyalgia. — a 2005 science paper on a fibromyalgia web survey. It surveys the 2,596 people. The paper is the fibromyalgia survey: the findings on patient ills, filed here in session today twice.
europmc-pmc1971061: Anorectal malformations. — a 2005 science paper on anorectal malformations. It explains the birth ills for labs worldwide. The paper is the birth-ill guide: the findings on anorectal ills for labs, filed here in full session today twice over now.
europmc-pmc1994261: Quantitative characteristics of gene regulation by small RNA. — a 2005 science paper on small-RNA control math. It studies the quantitative traits. The paper is the small-RNA study: the findings on gene control, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2169261: Standardising outcomes for clinical trials and systematic reviews. — a 2005 science paper on same-size trial scorecards. It pushes the same-size scorecards for labs. The paper is the scorecard guide: the notes on trial scores, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2229861: Novel roles of formin mDia2 in lamellipodia and filopodia formation in motile cells. — a 2005 science paper on formin in cell feet. It finds the novel roles. The paper is the formin study: the findings on motile ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2291561: Sorting signals, N-terminal modifications and abundance of the chloroplast proteome. — a 2005 science paper on chloroplast protein sorting. It maps the sorting signals. The paper is the sorting study: the findings on chloroplast ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2292261: Automated three-dimensional detection and shape classification of dendritic spines from fluorescence microscopy images. — a 2005 science paper on spine-spotting software. It spots the brain spines for labs. The paper is the spotter guide: the notes on spine tools, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2386861: Chest sonography: a useful tool to differentiate acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema from acute r — a 2008 science paper on chest ultrasound for lung fluid. It differentiates the edema types. The paper is the sonography guide: the findings on chest ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2394461: Mutations at amino-acid 482 in the ABCG2 gene affect substrate and antagonist specificity. — a 2008 science paper on ABCG2 mutations. It finds the mutation effects. The paper is the mutation study: the findings on ABCG2 ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2475661: Comparative analysis of human gut microbiota by barcoded pyrosequencing. — a 2008 science paper on gut germ surveys. It compares the gut microbiota. The paper is the compare study: the findings on gut ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2621261: HMGB1 mediates endogenous TLR2 activation and brain tumor regression. — a 2008 science paper on HMGB1 brain-tumor regression. It mediates the TLR2 activation. The paper is the HMGB1 study: the findings on tumor ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2631461: Reliability of the interRAI suite of assessment instruments: a 12-country study of an integrate — a 2008 science paper on the interRAI check set. It tests the check set for labs. The paper is the check study: the notes on interRAI ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2736161: Fostering implementation of health services research findings into practice: a consolidated fra — a 2008 science paper on health-services implementation. It fosters the research-to-practice bridge. The paper is the bridge study: the findings on health ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2745661: Human papillomaviruses activate the ATM DNA damage pathway for viral genome amplification upon — a 2008 science paper on HPV genome amplification. It activates the ATM pathway. The paper is the activation study: the findings on HPV ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2758861: Response rates in postal surveys of healthcare professionals between 1996 and 2005: an observat — a 2008 science paper on postal survey responses. It observes the response rates. The paper is the observation study: the findings on survey ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2764861: Depression and quality of life in patients with diabetes: a systematic review from the European — a 2008 science paper on depression in diabetes. It reviews the systematic quality-of-life evidence. The paper is the review study: the findings on depression ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2769161: Biodegradability of plastics. — a 2008 science paper on plastic rot speeds. It times the plastic rot for labs. The paper is the rot study: the findings on plastic ills, filed here in full session today twice over now daily still worldwide.
camerarius-history-strange-wonders-1561:
Joachim Camerarius was a German scholar of the Reformation age, and his writings on omens circulated widely. This English History of Strange Wonders appeared in 1561. It carried German prodigy lore across the Channel to English readers early in Elizabeth's reign.

Strange births, signs in the sky, and monsters crowd its pages. Each wonder is read as a warning from God about wars, deaths of princes, or sins of the age. Lutheran Germany scanned the book of nature for such omens with great care. The English version shows how fast this habit crossed borders. Fear and faith, more than curiosity, drive the whole collection.
oe-epistola-alexandri-cockayne-1861:
The Old English Letter of Alexander to Aristotle survives in a single famous manuscript, Cotton Vitellius A.xv. That same book holds Beowulf. Thomas Cockayne edited the letter in 1861, printing the Old English text for students of England's earliest literature.

Alexander reports the wonders of India to his old teacher. Monster races, giant beasts, and deadly lands fill the letter, now told in the tongue of the Anglo-Saxons. English monks translated the marvels because wonder itself seemed worth saving. Cockayne's edition pairs the text with learned notes. It is England's earliest monster lore, written in the language of its first poets.
plos-pone-0004961:
Tumors can wake sleeping cancer genes. One route is stripping methyl tags off a gene's promoter. Ian Smith and colleagues hunted for such cases in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used an integrative method on primary head and neck cancers. They also examined lung cancers. The targets were candidate proto-oncogenes and cancer testes antigens.

The team found the two groups switching on together. Promoter demethylation coordinated their activation across both tumor types. Such coordinated waking reveals a shared program in these cancers. The reawakened genes matter beyond basic biology. They are candidate targets for drugs and for immune-based therapies.
plos-pone-0005061:
K-Ras mutations drive many lung cancers. They occur almost exclusively in smokers. Courtney Granville and colleagues studied the immune setting of these tumors. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They focused on regulatory T cells marked by Foxp3. These cells calm immune attacks.

The regulatory cells played a central role in K-Ras-driven tumor growth. The tumors benefit from their own immune suppressors. Peacekeeper cells, meant to prevent autoimmunity, shield the cancer instead. Blocking those suppressors could help fight these lung cancers. The finding matters for immunotherapy design. It suggests which brake to release for this common tumor type. Smokers' lung cancers may need exactly that release.
plos-pone-0005161:
Sleep fills about a third of human life. The genes that regulate it are barely known. Christopher Winrow and colleagues mapped them in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied multiple sleep-wake traits in mice. Genome-wide association studies in humans had given few answers. Model organisms offer another route to the genes.

The study uncovered parts of the genetic landscape for sleep. Different traits mapped to different gene regions. Sleep is not one trait but many. Each may have its own genetic levers. The map opens the hunt for sleep genes. It also frames new questions about how the traits relate. Insomnia and other disorders may trace to these regions.
plos-pone-0005261:
Crops grown for biofuel promise cleaner energy, but a fuel crop that escapes could become an invasive weed. Buddenhagen and colleagues noted in PLOS ONE in 2009 that no one had yet quantified that invasion risk. Their case study set out to measure it.

The authors assessed how invasive proposed biofuel crops are likely to be. Weighing energy gains against weed risk gives growers and regulators a reality check before planting at scale. Once an invasive plant is loose, removal is costly or impossible, so early assessment matters. A crop checked in this way can be grown with more trust, and a crop that fails the check can be kept off the land while there is still time.
plos-pone-0005361:
Betulin comes from birch bark and is the precursor of betulinic acid, a compound studied for anti-tumor effects. Far less was known about betulin itself. Mullauer and colleagues tested it on tumor cells in PLOS ONE in 2009 and found it potent.

Betulin induced apoptosis, the self-destruct program, by a mechanism similar to its acid cousin. Cholesterol enhanced the anti-tumor effect, as the title states. A cheap, abundant bark compound with a boostable effect is an interesting lead for drug development. Birch bark is waste from wood mills in the north, so a drug lead drawn from it would start from a cheap and rich source. Not from a rare plant that must be farmed.
plos-pone-0005961:
Inside a plant cell, mitochondria move along tracks made of actin, hauled by myosin motors. Maozhong Zheng, Martina Beck, Jens Müller and colleagues asked in 2009 whether the tracks themselves must keep changing for the cargo to move. Their PLOS ONE study uses root hairs of Arabidopsis, a small plant favored in labs.

Actin tracks are rebuilt without pause as their building blocks swap in and out. The title states the finding: that turnover is required for the myosin-driven motion of mitochondria. A still track, it seems, will not do. The result adds a rule to the plant cell's transport system, where track upkeep and cargo motion are tied together.
plos-pone-0006061:
Some genes are so vital that a bacterium cannot grow without them, yet how much of each one is enough? Shan Goh, Jaroslaw Boberek, Nobutaka Nakashima and colleagues measured that strictness in E. coli in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper pairs growth rates with transcript counts as essential genes are dialed down, revealing how much slack each gene allows.

The pairing exposes gene stringency, a property that lists of essential genes alone cannot show. A gene that tolerates little slack is a tempting antibiotic target, since a drug need only dent it. The work turns a static gene list into a ranked map of bacterial weak points.
plos-pone-0006161:
A tiny RNA can tune the making of the heart by holding down a single helper protein. Gene Kim, Sadhana Samant, Judy Earley and colleagues traced that tuning in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies microRNA-130a and FOG-2, a transcriptional co-factor the team had shown to be critical for cardiac development, in cardiomyocytes, the heart's muscle cells.

MicroRNA-130a controls FOG-2 production at the translation step, the title reports, so the gene is read but its protein is rationed. Few microRNAs had been tied to heart development when this work ran. Each one named gives medicine a finer dial for a process where small timing errors become birth defects of the heart.
plos-pone-0006261:
Blood fats differ in people with high blood pressure, beyond the usual cholesterol story. Juergen Graessler and colleagues profiled the plasma lipidome of hypertensive patients in a 2009 PLOS ONE study, using a top-down approach. Obesity and insulin resistance often travel with hypertension, so the team sought effects specific to blood pressure itself.

The survey found a deficiency of ether lipids in the patients' blood plasma. Ether lipids are a less-studied fat family with roles in membranes and signalling. A specific shortfall could become a marker for hypertension risk. It may also hint at mechanisms that standard fat tests overlook.
plos-pone-0006661:
J. David Stiffler, Minhhuyen Nguyen, Ji Sohn, and colleagues mapped hepatitis C virus in infected livers in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hepatitis C virus is a plus-strand RNA virus that replicates by amplification of genomic RNA from minus strands. That leads to accumulation of many copies per cell. The team examined the focal distribution of hepatitis C virus RNA in infected livers.

Focal means the virus concentrates in patches rather than spreading evenly. Patchiness affects biopsy accuracy and treatment expectations. A small sample may miss infected zones. Mapping the distribution explains why liver samples can disagree with blood tests.
plos-pone-0006761:
Ville-Petri Friman and his team tested how hunters shape the strength of germs in PLOS ONE in 2009. A germ's strength is called its virulence. Textbooks treat virulence as a duel between germ and host. Real hosts live in webs of many species. Other species can tilt that duel in round-about ways. Hunters that eat sick hosts are one such force.

The team let predation act at more than one level of the food web. Germ strength evolved in a new way when hunters were present. A germ may grow milder or stronger when its host faces hungry hunters. The work says the full web, not just the pair, sets how germs evolve. Germ science should study hosts in their real webs, not in pairs alone.
plos-pone-0006861:
Arian D. Wallach and colleagues examined lethal control of dingoes in PLOS ONE in 2009. The dingo is Australia's top-order predator. It is also a socially complex animal. Controlling socially complex species can have deep ecological effects. Those effects stay invisible if only head counts are considered.

Killing dingoes disrupts their social stability, the authors argue. Broken social structure can change hunting, breeding, and movement. Surviving animals may behave in ways that worsen livestock conflicts. The work urges managers to count social costs, not just animals removed. It reframes predator control as an ecological intervention with hidden side effects.
plos-pone-0006961:
Vlada Melekhin, Bryan Shepherd, Samuel Stinnette, and colleagues studied HIV treatment timing in pregnancy in PLOS ONE in 2009. Pregnancy had been linked with slower HIV disease progress in the modern therapy era. What remained untested was how treatment timing around pregnancy affects the mother. The team compared women starting antiretroviral therapy before, during, or after pregnancy.

They tracked viral, immune, and clinical responses in each group. The question matters for the many women who first reach care while pregnant. Their results help clinicians decide when starting therapy gives mothers the strongest benefit.
plos-pone-0007061:
Chang-Yi Wu, Janet Steffen, and David Eide studied zinc hunger in yeast in PLOS ONE in 2009. Zinc deficiency stresses many organisms with harmful oxidation. In baker's yeast, a defender protein called Tsa1 was known to help in low zinc. It destroys hydrogen peroxide, a damaging oxidant. The team asked what another defender, the enzyme SOD1, contributes.

They found cytosolic SOD1 is critical for tolerating low zinc stress. Without it, yeast coped far worse with the oxidation. Two defenders divide the work of clearing different oxidants. The result refines the picture of how cells survive mineral shortage.
plos-pone-0007161: Elena Grigor'eva, Alexander Shevchenko, Nina Mazurok, and colleagues derived trophoblast stem cells from the common vole in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their method worked without FGF4, the growth factor normally required to grow such cells. Trophoblast stem cells build the placenta's exchange tissue. A line that grows without the standard factor gives researchers a new way to study early placental development in this rodent.
plos-pone-0007261:
