arxiv-2601-09061:
Francisco Santiago Nieto-de la Rosa, Osvaldo Guzman, and Ulises Ramos-Garcia study a class of forcing tools in set theory. Forcing is a way to build new set worlds with set traits. Laver forcing is a classic tool of that kind. Their form builds it from a co-ideal, a set of sets that codes what counts as large.

They read the traits of these tools through a rank called the Katetov order. They tell when such a tool adds a Cohen real, a type of new real line point. They also show such tools never add a random real. A reader in set theory gets a crisp split. One type of new point can come, the next can not.
arxiv-2601-09361:
Jiaying Zhang and six co-authors work on training large reasoning models at low cost. Their 2026 arXiv paper, GeoRA, adapts low-rank fine-tuning to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. In that setup, a model earns rewards only when its answers can be checked as right.

Older low-rank methods were built for supervised fine-tuning, not for this reward-based training. Used directly, they suffer spectral collapse and unstable optimization, which cap the model's skill. GeoRA is shaped to respect the geometry of the reward-based process instead. The aim is stable training that keeps the gains of full fine-tuning at a fraction of the cost.
arxiv-2601-09461:
Reemt Hinrichs and three co-authors measure the ceiling on short-term prediction of sustained speech. Their 2026 arXiv paper centers on prediction gain, a classic score in signal coding. Predictive coding stores or sends speech by guessing the next sample and keeping only the error.

A better guess means a lower bit rate for the same quality. Prediction gain links the mean-squared prediction error to the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio of a coder. The authors analyze how much gain is even possible on sustained speech sounds. Knowing the ceiling tells codec designers when better predictors stop paying off.
arxiv-2601-09561:
Hector Galindo-Silva and Paula Herrera-Idárraga ask whether civic schooling can shift a country's faith. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies religious change in Colombia after its 1991 Constitution. The new charter ended the confessional regime and ordered constitutional instruction in high schools.

The authors exploit the fact that cohorts differed in how much reform-era schooling they received. With nationally representative survey data, they run a difference-in-differences design across those cohorts. The setup lets them tie shifts in religious identification to the reform itself. The study speaks to a wider question: how much can state education reshape belief?
arxiv-2601-09861:
Roland R. Netz follows particles over energy barriers when the medium remembers. His 2026 arXiv paper studies barrier crossing and energy relaxation in non-Markovian inertial systems. Simulations show a memory-turnover: at mid-range memory times, crossing is faster than in the memory-free limit.

For long memory times, the crossing time grows with the square of the memory time, at fixed total friction. The authors reach these results with an analytical Green-Fokker-Planck approach. Barrier crossing sits at the core of chemical reaction rates. A theory that tracks memory effects sharpens rate predictions for real, sticky environments.
arxiv-2601-10361:
S. Vanderwoude and co authors test if bent radio galaxies twist their light in new ways. A radio galaxy spews jets of charged grains. In a galaxy cluster, those jets can bend. The bend is thought to come from the gas and fields in the cluster. The cause is still not firm.

A bent jet may also twist its light waves in a set way. The team ask if bent forms part from straight forms in that trait. They match bend size to twist traits in known cases. A match would tie bend cause to jet traits. It would guide how clusters shape the jets in them.
arxiv-2601-10461:
Adam Siegel and Simon Benjamin turn lost qubit states into a known kind of error. Their qubits are singlet triplet pairs in small dots. Such qubits can be shuttled fast and well in a chip. Shuttling lets a chip move states to where they are needed. That aids a shuttling based form of error fix.

Some errors hide from fix tools. Erasure conversion turns a hidden error into a flagged loss. A flagged loss is far more easy to fix. The team show how to add that step for these qubits. It lifts the grade of the whole fix chain.
arxiv-2601-11061:
Lecheng Yan and co-authors investigate a paradox in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. The method, RLVR, boosts language model reasoning by rewarding correct answers. Yet models like Qwen 2.5 gain even when rewards are spurious or wrong. The authors dig into the mechanism behind that puzzle. They name what they find the Perplexity Paradox.

Under spurious rewards, answer-token perplexity drops while the prompt side's coherence degrades. That split suggests the model bypasses reasoning in favor of memorization shortcuts. If gains can come from shortcuts, benchmark jumps may overstate true reasoning growth. The work warns trainers to audit what RLVR actually teaches, not just what scores say.
arxiv-2601-12161:
Tomoki Koike, Prakash Mohan, Mark T. Henry de Frahan, Julie Bessac, and Elizabeth Qian stream operator inference for smaller models of large dynamic systems. Projection methods shrink big systems to low-dim models that run fast. Operator Inference learns such models from data in two steps.

First, SVD compresses the data to a low-dim basis. Then a least squares fit learns the small operators, with no need for the source code. A streaming form can handle data too large to hold at once. That helps climate and fluid models at scale.
arxiv-2601-11461:
Radhika Kulkarni, Aluisio Pinheiro, Brani Vidakovic, and Abdourrahmane Atto smooth a denoising rule. Their 2026 preprint is named Smooth SCAD, for wavelet denoising. Wavelets split a signal into pieces at many scales. Thresholding kills small pieces as noise and keeps big ones.

SCAD is a known threshold rule with prized traits. It gives sparsity for small coefficients, zeroing them out. It stays near unbiased for large coefficients, a rare pair. Its flaw is a piecewise linear kink in the middle. The team swaps that kink for a raised cosine curve. The new rule is odd, continuous, and smooth off the threshold. It keeps the SCAD traits while easing numeric work.
arxiv-2601-13461:
Megan M. Kerr and Tracy L. Payne study submanifolds that hang off special subgroups in bent spaces with symmetry. Their spaces are solvmanifolds, group based spaces that solve by steps. The sub forms at stake have an odd trait next to Ricci curvature, the mean bend of space.

The work grows a study by H. Tamaru. He built such forms in symmetric spaces of non compact type from parabolic subgroups of the isometry group. He called them attached submanifolds. Kerr and Payne carry that build past symmetric spaces. For shape staff, each new host class tests if the odd Ricci trait is rare or wide.
arxiv-2601-12361:
Bernd Finkbeiner, Hadar Frenkel, and Tim Rohde study model checking for a rich logic of hyperproperties. The logic is called Hyper 2 LTL. It grows out of HyperLTL, a known logic for facts about sets of traces. The new logic adds quantification over sets of traces, a second order step.

That extra power lets one state complex facts that older logics cannot. The authors name facts about knowledge and facts about systems that do not move in lock step. The core question is cost: how hard is it to check such facts on finite structures? Work of this kind maps the price of expressive power in formal verification. It shows where checks stay feasible and where they blow up.
arxiv-2601-12461:
Jingche Chen and Han Hong prove a systolic inequality for manifolds with a curvature condition. The systole is the length of the shortest loop that cannot be shrunk to a point. A homological version of it is their focus here. Their manifolds have positive triRic curvature, a condition in higher codimension terms.

They show their inequality is optimal, meaning the bound cannot be improved. They also characterize the case of equality, when a manifold hits the bound exactly. The work extends prior results by Bray, Brendle, and Neves, and by Chu, Lee, and Zhu. Systolic results tie local curvature to global size in a sharp way. Equality cases often reveal rigid, model shapes worth study on their own.
arxiv-2601-12561:
Catriona A. Thomson and four co authors work on photonic crystal nanolasers with a tiny footprint. Photonic crystals give unmatched control over how light is confined and guided. They also shape how light interacts with matter at small scales. That control has reshaped optics and spawned many practical devices over past decades.

A nanolaser built in such a crystal can be extremely small. Small size matters for the goal named here: biointegration. A laser that can sit inside or on biological tissue opens new sensing routes. The team stress a minimal footprint design for that end. Work of this kind links photonics with medicine and life science tools.
arxiv-2601-12861:
Zhangliang Chen and six co authors launch Project FOSSO, a study of brown dwarfs in binary systems. Brown dwarfs are substellar companions, too light to burn hydrogen like stars. Their hosts here are main sequence stars that will one day become white dwarfs. What happens to the companion as the host swells and dies is the central question.

Recent discoveries found many substellar companions around white dwarfs. Those survivors constrain how the post main sequence phase treats close companions. The team investigate long term evolution and final outcomes of these systems. Some companions may be engulfed, others may drift to wider orbits. The project maps those fates across the known population.
arxiv-2601-13761:
Shengda Fan, Xuyan Ye, and Yankai Lin work on AI systems that improve themselves through self-play in 2026. In self-play, one model poses questions and an other solves them. Past setups face two flaws. The questioner's goals shift as the solver's feedback changes. And the solver learns from its own pseudo-labels, which can bake in errors.

Their method, DARC, splits the training into a decoupled, asymmetric curriculum. Separate paths for questioner and solver aim to calm the training. Stable self-play could let models grow with less human data. That path draws much hope, and much need for care.
arxiv-2601-13861: M. J. Dunwoody studies patterns in triangulated 2-spheres and 3-spheres in 2026. A triangulation splits a sphere into triangles that fit edge to edge. Patterns in such splits can encode deep facts on shape. Dunwoody gives a new proof of a lemma in Abigail Thompson's work. That lemma feeds her Recognition Algorithm for 3-spheres. The algorithm tests if a given space is in fact a 3-sphere.
arxiv-2601-14461:
Lukas Netterdon, Veronica Montanaro, Manuel Torrilhon, and Hossein Gorji improve gas simulations in this 2026 paper. The Fokker-Planck particle method speeds up rarefied-gas simulations. It replaces the binary collisions of Direct Simulation Monte Carlo with a drift-diffusion process. Like all particle methods, it is stochastic by nature.

That randomness causes statistical fluctuations in macroscopic quantities. Accurate results then need large particle numbers, which cost time. The team applies quasi-random numbers for variance reduction in the method. Quasi-random points fill space more evenly than pure random ones. The gain is clear. Runs take less time, and the noise in the end maps drops a lot. Less noise means fewer runs. That saves both time and funds on each test case. Readers get a way to calm the noise in rarefied-gas runs without simply adding more particles.
arxiv-2601-14661:
C. de León searches for dark matter signs in gamma rays in this 2026 paper. Axion-like particles are hypothetical particles and compelling candidates for cold dark matter. Their existence could be probed through conversions into photons in magnetic fields. If axion-like particles mix with light, some gamma rays from distant sources would vanish along the way.

The author searches for attenuation in the observed gamma ray spectra of galactic sources that emit at energies of hundreds of TeV. The data come from the High-Altitude Water Cherenkov Observatory, HAWC. The source is 3HWC J1908+063. Readers get constraints on axion-like particles from one of the most energetic light sources in the galaxy.
arxiv-2601-15461:
Amalendu Krishna and Subhadip Majumder work in algebraic geometry in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their topic is the Brauer group of schemes over local fields of positive characteristic. They study Kato's ramification filtration on that group. The filtration sorts elements by how wildly they ramify. A second sorting, the evaluation filtration, comes from a different route.

The authors show the two sorts agree in this setting. More precisely, the non-log version of Kato's filtration matches the evaluation filtration. The schemes in view are regular, separated, and of finite type. The result extends recent work by Bright and Newton. Their earlier result is now carried into positive characteristic. Readers in arithmetic geometry will follow the proof details.
arxiv-2601-15861:
Daniel Lokshtanov, Michał Pilipczuk, and Paweł Rzążewski hunt for large sparse patterns in graphs in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their measure is the tree-independence number. Start with a tree decomposition of a graph. Its independence number is the largest independent set inside one bag. The graph's tree-independence number is the minimum of that value over decompositions. Recent work by Lima and others set up this frame.

The authors look for large sparse induced subgraphs. They target graphs whose tree-independence number is small, but not very small. That middle zone is where the theory gets hard. Induced subgraphs keep only chosen vertices and their links. Finding big sparse ones inside structured graphs feeds algorithm design. Such results often unlock faster methods for hard graph problems.
arxiv-2601-15961:
Fengwu Sun and a large team trace dust around massive young galaxies in a 2026 arXiv paper. They use JWST NIRCam imaging and grism spectroscopy from the JADES Origins Fields. The team reports redshifts for 1,445 emission-line galaxies between redshift zero and nine. Within that sample, two galaxy protoclusters stand out. They sit at redshifts 3.47 and 3.69. Each is anchored by massive, dusty star-forming galaxies.

The title names the discovery: large reservoirs of small dust grains in the circumgalactic medium. Dust far outside galaxies, at redshift near 3.5, is hard to detect. Its presence says galaxies expel or shed material early and widely. That outflow shapes how galaxies and their surroundings evolve together.
arxiv-2601-15261:
Sophie Vo, Konstantin Y. Bliokh, and Miguel A. Alonso weigh the spin of a pulse of light with a toy model. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with spatiotemporal vortex pulses. These wavepackets carry transverse orbital angular momentum, a twist across the pulse.

How to quantify that twist has been debated in recent work. The authors build a simple mechanical model of the pulse. It is a loop of free point particles, all moving at one speed but at slightly different angles. That ray-like picture gives a clean way to compute the momentum.
arxiv-2601-16261:
Magoon and a large team show first tests of a new THz probe build. Their 2026 preprint sets out the SQUAT probe type. SQUAT stands for a transmon that boosts charge sense from split pairs. The probe ties straight to a wave line, with no ring in the path. A hit breaks pairs in the chip caps and makes loose charge grains.

Those grains cross a join and shift the chip state. The shift is the sign of the hit for read out. First tests weigh if the build sees hits as planned. A work probe of this type could sense faint far light. The work is a first proof of the build.
arxiv-2601-16361:
Philani Majozi sets out local link ideas for spaces that lack full same form. His 2026 preprint deals with spaces built on one way rules. Such spaces span quasi metrics, quasi uniform sets and modular sets. Old link and whole ideas rest on two way rules. Those rules fail to fit one way spaces with care.

Majozi gives a one way form of local link for such spaces. The form tracks links that hold in a set dir sense. New forms let teams sort such spaces by their link traits. They also aid sums of whole ends for one way spaces. The work is a base step in one way maths.
arxiv-2601-16461:
Anuj Yadav and coauthors set a loss for squeeze that keeps sense, not bits. Their 2026 preprint deals with loss based squeeze of a source. Loss is set by a log score from a fixed joint law. That law ties the source to a sense code for it. Squeeze then keeps the sense the law cares for most.

Bits that do not shift sense can be cut with low loss. Such cuts serve pics, speech and text sent at low rate. The team sums the best rates for this loss form. Firm rates guide build of sense first squeeze tools. The work joins squeeze maths to sense laws.
arxiv-2601-16661:
Monika Gupta, Ajay Meena, Anamitra Roy Choudhury, Vijay Arya, and Srikanta Bedathur study code moved across languages. Large language models now turn code from one tongue to the next. Most such models learned from code full of notes. Those notes, called comments, sit in plain words by the code. The team's 2026 preprint asks if the notes help.

The authors test the hunch that comments aid the move. Good notes can tell what a block of code should do. That clue may guide the model when syntax shifts. The study checks when notes help and when they do not. Its lessons can shape how teams write code for smooth moves.
arxiv-2601-16761:
A large team of UK astronomers sets out a plan for a new space scope. The scope, named SIRMOS, would ride on a satellite. It would split infra-red light from many space objects at once. Such split light tells what far galaxies are made of. Their 2026 preprint links that tool to big cosmic themes.

Those themes span the birth and growth of the cosmos. Star birth, galaxy growth, and dark stuff all leave marks in such light. A fleet of spectra beats one-by-one work by far. The plan shows what a mid-size craft could reap. It makes the case for funds in the years ahead.
arxiv-2601-16961:
Francesco Cesa and a team of six co-authors fake local acts in shared-drive atom grids. Atom grids trap atoms in light for quantum work. Two kinds of atoms share one grid here. All atoms feel the same drive pulse at once. Yet the team fakes acts that strike each site in turn. Their 2026 preprint shows the trick with Floquet steps.

Steps in time swap which kind feels the drive. Wide block rules for near and far pairs aid the fake. Faked local acts let plain grids run rich sims. Such sims probe new stuff states at low cost. Dual-kind grids gain a broad new use.
arxiv-2601-17061:
Dan Adler argues that facts can evolve with no genes at play. His frame is called Stability-Driven Assembly. Chance builds join bits in new forms all the time. Forms that last long pile up by that fact. No copy step or score rule is set in advance. His 2026 preprint says that bias acts like a born genetic rule set.

Lasting forms seed more joins as time runs. Fresh forms thus skew to the long-lived kinds. The frame speaks to how life first rose from raw stuff. It may also speak to how codes and tongues grow. Plain physics, in this view, can breed fit forms.
arxiv-2601-17861: Ioana Ciuclea and Cornelia Vizman study vortex loops through the lens of group geometry. Their 2026 preprint treats manifolds of such loops as coadjoint orbits of the group of area-preserving maps of the plane. A vortex loop is a closed curve carrying a vorticity density that may drop to zero at points. The result ties fluid shapes to the algebra of the group that moves them.
arxiv-2601-18061:
Kiana Jafari and co-authors test a core belief behind AI safety work in mental health. Their 2026 preprint is a preprint under review, as its note states. Learning from human feedback assumes that expert judgments, when pooled, give a valid ground truth. Mental health is a field where that truth matters most, since safety stakes are high. Three certified psychiatrists rated language model replies on their own, using a calibrated rubric.

The study checks how far the experts agree with each other. If experts diverge, then pooled feedback hides real doubt. That would shake how models are trained and tested for clinic use. The work gives safety teams hard data on the limits of expert consensus.
arxiv-2601-18161:
T. Worrakitpoonpon simulates how bars form in disk galaxies under halos of different density. His 2026 preprint uses N-body simulations. A bar is a long, straight band of stars across a galaxy's center. How a bar starts depends on the dark halo around the disk. In a highly concentrated halo, the bar's growth is limited early on. Dominant multi-arm modes, boosted by swing amplification, crowd the young disk and hold the bar back.

Other halo densities let bars grow by other routes. Comparing the routes shows how much the halo steers the disk's fate. Bars reshape galaxies and drive gas inward, so their origins matter. The work maps one control knob of galaxy evolution.
arxiv-2601-18261:
Chao-Hong Tan and co-authors present FGGM, a method that helps models learn new tasks without erasing old ones. Their 2026 preprint addresses catastrophic forgetting in large language models. The method masks gradients, blocking updates to some parameters while others learn. The mask is guided by diagonal Fisher information, a score of how much each parameter matters for past tasks. Thresholds adapt as training goes on, so critical parameters stay protected while the rest stay free to move.

The aim is balance: stability for old skills, plasticity for new ones. The method needs no replay of old data, by its design. Continual learning without old data suits privacy-bound deployments.
arxiv-2601-18961:
Uma Girish and five co-authors study proofs that pin down when and where a claim was made. Position proofs let a party show it stands at a set place, which backs claims of the form: I am at this spot. Such proofs cannot be made safe with classical tools alone, even with strong computing bounds.

Quantum tools, though, can make them work. The team gives private versions of these proofs, so a party can prove its place without giving away more than the claim needs. Private place proofs could serve location based services that must not leak a user's exact track.
arxiv-2601-19061:
Harsh Chaudhari and six co-authors show a stealthy way to poison the reasoning of language models. Models that think in chains of thought now draw on shared public data sets of reasoning traces. Some sets are downloaded tens of thousands of times a month. That sharing opens a door for quiet attacks.

Their attack, Thought-Transfer, aims poison at a chosen target in a roundabout way. Tainted traces can bend a model's chain of thought without blunt signs. The work warns data curators that popular reasoning sets need checks, since a few bad traces can steer many models at once.
arxiv-2601-19461:
Yida Lin and four co-authors grade depth sensing methods on tree branches, a hard test for drone forestry. Self flying drones in forests need sound depth estimates that travel well to new woods. Past grades focus on city and indoor scenes, leaving vegetation, the hardest case, largely unchecked.

The team runs the first systematic zero shot test of several stereo depth methods on branches. Zero shot means the methods get no practice on forest data first. Knowing which method sees twigs and gaps best guides the design of drones that must not snag or fall among trees.
arxiv-2601-19761:
Jin Huang, Fethiye Irmak Doğan, and Hatice Gunes propose a new way to think about social robots. A social robot should personalise its behaviour to each user. Current systems lean on language models that adapt replies from user data. Others learn from the user's immediate reactions in real time.

The authors argue these robots should be framed as recommender systems. A recommender picks items for a user from their tastes; a robot could pick actions and topics the same way. The paper lays foundations and a framework for that view. It also surveys applications where the framing helps. Treating robots as recommenders imports decades of research on personalisation, evaluation, and user modeling.
arxiv-2601-19961:
Huanlin Gao and colleagues speed up flow matching, a generative modeling method. Flow matching learns a velocity field that carries noise into data. Inference follows that field step by step, which costs many evaluations. Caching reuses earlier computations to skip steps, but most caches use instantaneous velocity snapshots.

That shortcut bends the trajectory, and errors pile up at high acceleration. Their framework, MeanCache, caches average velocity instead of instantaneous values. Averages track the true path more faithfully over long jumps. The method needs no retraining of the underlying model. Faster generation matters for image and video tools used interactively. The work improves the speed-quality trade-off at aggressive settings.
arxiv-2601-20061:
Dhruv Parikh, Jebacyril Arockiaraj, and Viktor Prasanna accelerate an unusual computing paradigm. Hyperdimensional computing represents data as very long, low-precision vectors called hypervectors. Learning and inference use light, noise-tolerant operations on those vectors. The catch is the dimensionality itself: huge, sparse vectors mean heavy data movement that conventional processors handle badly.

The authors build acceleration from primitive operations tailored to the paradigm. Their target is real-time image classification. If hyperdimensional methods run fast enough, they suit edge devices that need robust, low-power learning. The work treats hardware and algorithm as one design problem. It is part of a broader search for post-neural computing models. The chips are small and cheap to run. Speed is the test that counts most. A fast score here opens real use. The aim is not raw size but smart use of size. Less heat and less cost come with it.
arxiv-2601-20161:
Isadora Krsek and five colleagues study how to warn people about the privacy risk of what they share online. People often discuss sensitive topics under a sense of anonymity, yet that safety can be misjudged, which leads to over-disclosure. New language tools make it possible to estimate the risk that a post could identify its author.

The authors give design recommendations for showing users these population risk estimates. Their focus is informed self-disclosure: people should see a clear estimate before they post, not after harm is done. Good design here must be honest about risk without scaring users away from support communities.
arxiv-2601-20261:
Damian Guenzing, Dayne Y. Sasaki, and a large team demonstrate soft X-ray ptychography in reflection rather than transmission. Ptychography is a scanning method that builds high-resolution, element-specific images of nanoscale structures. Transmission setups, though, demand very thin samples, which excludes many extended or bulk specimens, above all in the soft X-ray range.

By imaging in reflection geometry, the team opens the method to samples that cannot be thinned. The work was published as a research article in an optics journal. Reflection imaging could widen soft X-ray studies to real devices and materials as they are, not only as thin slices.
arxiv-2601-20361:
Chen-Yang Dai and four colleagues present TINNs, time-induced neural networks for solving time-dependent partial differential equations. Physics-informed networks learn a smooth solution that can be read at any point in space and time. Standard versions feed time in as one input but share a single set of weights across all times.

That sharing forces the same features to represent very different dynamics at early and late times. TINNs are designed to relieve that strain. Better solvers of this kind would speed up work on heat flow, waves, and fluids, where the time evolution is the whole point.
arxiv-2601-18361:
Jean Michel de Souza Sant'Ana and three colleagues weigh new ways to link small devices that send data over the net. Ground towers serve towns well but leave gaps at sea, in fields, and in far off zones. The team looks at high platforms that float in the thin upper air. It also looks at small craft in low Earth orbit.

The study counts how often a sent signal is lost for each setup. It tests craft on their own and platforms on their own. It also tests mixed plans that join space, air, and ground links in one system. Cost counts as much as strength here, since a link that costs too much will not be built. The aim is a clear view of which mix gives firm links for the least spend.
arxiv-2601-18761:
Wout Slabbinck and three colleagues argue that web data needs a shift from who may see it to how it may be used. New laws in Europe press for data groups that can be shared across firms with trust. A right to see a file is not the same as a right to use it for each aim. Laws set terms on use that shift with the aim and with the time.

Web stores now tie their rules to files, in a tight knot. That knot makes use terms hard to state and hard to change. The team set out a path built on a shared way for users to hold and state their own terms. Such a path could let a user grant use for one aim and bar it for the next. It would bring web data rules close to the law that now binds them.
arxiv-2601-21261:
Abrar Hamed Al Barwani, Abdelaziz Amara Korba, and Raja Waseem Anwar work on catching phishing emails without flagging too many honest ones. Fake emails keep getting harder to spot, and simple rule-based filters no longer keep up. Language models read text well, but used alone they mark too many real emails as fake.

The authors pair a language model with a search step that pulls in helpful context first. The design is built around the user, not just the message. Fewer false alarms mean less wasted work for staff who must check each warning. The aim is a filter people can trust day to day.
arxiv-2601-21361:
A model-independent search looks for a new particle that decays into pairs of muons, using data from the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The search covers a low mass range where a light new particle might hide. It uses proton collisions recorded over several years of running.

Rather than assume one specific theory, the team scans for any bump in the muon-pair mass. A bump would hint at a particle no model has catalogued yet. Null results still matter, since they rule out wide classes of theories. The dataset is among the largest ever used for such a low-mass scan.
arxiv-2601-21461:
Albert Tseng and Christopher De Sa replace a popular sparsity trick in language models with simple lookup layers. Sparse models usually route each token to a few expert networks. Dynamic hard routing can waste hardware and needs extra losses to train stably.

Their large lookup layers work more like a table the model reads from. Reading a table is cheap and predictable for hardware. The design keeps the capacity gains of sparsity without the routing headaches. If it scales, future models could grow in knowledge while each token still costs little to process.
arxiv-2601-21761:
Esteban Parra, Sonia Haiduc, Preetha Chatterjee, Ramtin Ehsani, and Polina Iaremchuk chart a sustainable future for peer review in software engineering. Review is how the field vets its results. Submissions keep growing fast, while the pool of qualified reviewers does not.

The imbalance threatens the long-term growth of the whole research community. The authors examine the strain and look for paths that keep review rigorous without burning out the reviewers. Options touch incentives, tooling, and how venues match papers to expertise. The stakes are field-wide: when review fails, weak work slips through and strong work stalls.
arxiv-2601-21961:
Kuai Yu and co-authors ask how the look of a web page steers the agents that browse it. Web agents now perform tasks across many sites with strong results. Research on their weak points has focused on attacks, on whether hostile pages can fool them.

Far less is known about how ordinary design choices sway agents in benign settings. The team's 2026 preprint evaluates how visual attributes of user interfaces influence agent behavior. Colors, layouts, and emphasis may push an agent toward one element over another, much as they do with people. Designers and testers need that map, since agent-friendly design could soon matter as much as human-friendly design.
arxiv-2601-22061:
Li Zhang and Pengtao Xie make a strong image tool work on its own. The Segment Anything Model can split an image into clean parts for things it has never been taught. But it needs a prompt, a hint from a human hand, for each new image. That need blocks full use in the field.

A fast finder tool called YOLO can spot things and give those hints on its own. But when the two tools are just chained, their goals do not match. The team trains them as one team, with a two-level scheme that keeps both goals in line. Their tool is called BLO-Inst. Fast, prompt-free splitting helps in scans, farm work, and plant checks, where no hand can mark each new frame.
arxiv-2601-22161:
Anmol Guragain tests a trend in how machines read feelings from face and voice. His test uses the EAV set of clips. He asks if the new, large attention tools beat plain ones when the data set is small. He runs three groups of tools: plain Transformers, new split-attention tools, and strong CNN tools with tweaks.

The fancy tools did not win. Plain traits drawn from the clips, built with care by hand, beat the Transformers. His point is that small sets reward craft more than scale. A tool that knows the task can beat a big tool that does not. This is a warn for fields where data will stay scarce, such as care work and mood care.
arxiv-2601-20961:
Steve Hanneke provides a complete theory of optimal learning rates without hopeful assumptions. His 2026 paper concerns universal agnostic learning for binary classification. Agnostic learning makes no promise that the data follow a simple rule. The learner must still perform nearly as well as the best rule in a class. Universal rates describe the best possible speed of learning across settings. Hanneke pins down those rates in full.

The work extends an earlier realizable-case theory. That theory, by Bousquet, Hanneke, Moran, van Handel, and Yehudayoff, assumed a perfect rule exists in the class. Removing the realizability assumption is a major step. Real data are noisy, and perfect rules rarely exist. A complete agnostic theory tells practitioners what accuracy is even possible. It closes a foundational question in statistical learning theory.
arxiv-2512-01261:
Hugh McDougall and a large team share the final data from a long sky survey. The OzDES program watched active galaxy cores for years. It timed delays between core light and gas light. Those delays give the size of the gas zone near each black hole.

From size plus gas speed, the team weighs each black hole. They also test rules that link black hole mass to light output. The final set wraps up years of work on far-off cores. It gives a firm base for checks of how black holes grew with their host galaxies.
arxiv-2512-01461:
Kuangpu Guo and co-authors work on merging models trained for distinct tasks. Merging can give one model many skills with no new training. But merged models often slump on each task. They lose the traits that made each solo model good.

The team aims to keep each model's own character in the merge. Their method guards task-specific traits while skills are pooled. Kept character means less slump on each task. Good merging saves the cost of joint training. It lets teams reuse fine-tuned models they already own for fresh combined tools.
arxiv-2512-01561:
Martí Massó Moreno and co-authors link flux-rope fits to forecasts of solar storms. Coronal mass ejections hurl plasma from the Sun toward Earth. Arrival forecasts from images err by about ten hours. Sensors near Earth give great field data but warn too late.

Their X-CME frame starts from in-situ flux-rope rebuilds. It then projects how the storm will travel. Better arrival times help grid and satellite crews brace. Even a few extra hours of warning can cut damage from a strong storm's hit on Earth systems. Forecast tests use past storms with known arrival times, so gains over image-only methods show up as plain hours saved, not abstract scores.
arxiv-2512-01761:
Solal Martin, Emilie Chouzenoux, and Victor Elvira bound moments of distributions with a sequential method. Moments summarize a distribution's shape, like mean and spread. Computing them means integrals over the distribution. Many such integrals lack closed forms, so numeric methods must step in.

Their method builds upper and lower bounds step by step. Bounds certify accuracy, unlike point guesses. Sequential bounds can stop once tight enough. Certified moments serve signal processing and Bayesian learning, where downstream choices rest on those values. Sequential bounds adapt to hardness, spending steps where the integral resists and stopping early where the shape is tame and clear.
arxiv-2512-00861:
Shota Komatsu studies a string theory dual in a 2025 physics paper. Two-dimensional Yang-Mills theory is arguably the simplest gauge theory that confines, locking its charges together. Its expansion in the number of colors has the same shape as the genus expansion of string theory, hinting at a hidden string description.

That worldsheet description is still not fully understood. Komatsu studies a chiral composite linear dilaton as the string dual candidate. A dual description would let string methods compute gauge theory results, and vice versa. Progress here tests the broader idea that gauge theories and strings are two views of one thing.
arxiv-2512-01061:
Haoru Xue and a large team from NVIDIA and universities open a path from simulation to real humanoid robots in a 2025 paper. Modern GPU simulators can render photorealistic worlds and randomize physics and visuals at scale. Policies trained there can generalize beyond tidy lab settings.

The team builds a teacher-student-bootstrap learning framework for vision-based humanoid loco-manipulation. Their test case is articulated-object interaction, like opening hinged or jointed objects while moving. A strong teacher guides a student that sees only pixels, and bootstrapping improves both. Success would let humanoids learn skills in simulation that still work on real hardware.
arxiv-2601-22861:
Refael Sheffer and co-authors map the ground hidden under thick forest canopy. The terrain below the trees matters for search and rescue, trail mapping, and forest checks. Today's tools lean on costly airborne laser scans, or on thermal imaging tuned to find people.

Their method uses plain color images plus neural three-dimensional rebuilding to recover the ground shape. Cheaper mapping from normal cameras could put forest surveys within reach of small teams. It also opens a path to robots that can plan safe routes under trees. The team frames the work around applications like search and rescue, trail mapping, and forest inventory in dense woodland.
arxiv-2512-00461:
Researchers increasingly give language models synthetic personas and study how they respond. Jan Batzner and co-authors review this practice in 2025, examining sixty-three peer-reviewed studies from leading venues published over three years. They ask whose personae these experiments really represent.

The review finds a critical gap: the task and population of interest are often underspecified, even though personalization depends on exactly those criteria. Representativeness and ecological validity vary considerably between studies. The authors chart pathways to transparency so persona-based findings can be interpreted and trusted more safely. The review spans three years of rapid growth in persona-based experimentation. Transparency pathways are the constructive half of the paper's critique. For folks who run such tests, the gain is a stern check list. Say whom the fake folks stand for, say what task they face, or the claims mean little.
arxiv-2512-00661:
Central configurations are the special arrangements of bodies that collapse or expand homothetically under Newtonian gravity. A 2025 study by Alain Albouy and Jiexin Sun examines the eigenvalues of a central configuration. The n-body equations have a matrix form built from the masses and mutual distances.

That matrix appears as a factor in the equations, and its eigenvalues are real and nonnegative. Their values constrain which configurations can be central and how they behave. Central configurations underlie the few exactly understood motions of gravitating systems, so their spectral properties carry outsized weight in celestial mechanics. Eigenvalues that are real and nonnegative give the configuration a usable spectral fingerprint. For folks who track how groups of stars or rocks move as one, the gain is a clean test. The tones of the shared pull tell how the group is built.
arxiv-2512-03161:
A matrix model of physics may hold new shapes of space. Henry Liao and Reishi Maeta study the Euclidean IKKT matrix model in this 2025 work. They look at its equation of motion and seek new steady solutions, called saddles.

They find a new type of saddle that exists only as the matrix size grows without bound. Assuming the matrices match a known symmetry algebra, they identify a unique solution. From it, a geometry emerges. Such work probes how space itself might arise from matrices in quantum gravity research. Emergent geometry from matrices remains a bold idea, and each exact solution tests its reach.
arxiv-2512-01861:
How much can the simplest neural network remember? A 2025 paper by Yingying Xu, Masayuki Ohzeki, and Yoshiyuki Kabashima studies the perceptron. The perceptron is a basic model of how neurons compute. The paper asks how many patterns it can store when it may choose which inputs to use.

The question matters because real data have many dimensions. They are full of chance links that look like real structure. By adding variable selection to the classic storage problem, the authors test how picking the right inputs changes what the model can hold. The work speaks to anyone trying to sort real signal from noise in large data sets.
arxiv-2512-02161:
Text-to-image models produce striking pictures that often quietly disobey the prompt: wrong counts, wrong colors, wrong attributes. Kevin David Hayes and five co-authors introduce FineGRAIN in 2025, a framework for grading those failures in fine detail using vision-language models as judges.

The sheer variety of prompt-following errors calls for a hierarchy of checks rather than a single score. FineGRAIN compares models on how faithfully they render specified attributes in user prompts. Dependable grading matters because these generators now serve designers and advertisers whose instructions are exact, and small disobediences are real defects.
arxiv-2512-02361:
Vision-language models learn from mountains of real data, yet can still flub basic perception that ordinary vision models handle easily. Zhengzhuo Xu and five co-authors revisit in 2025 an underused remedy, visual data augmentation, and rethink it for these multimodal models under the name VACoT.

Augmentation, deliberately varying training images, is a cornerstone of robust vision training but has drawn little attention for vision-language models. The authors argue that targeted augmentation can repair weak perception without endless data collection. Stronger basic perception is a foundation skill: every higher-level visual reasoning task inherits its errors.
arxiv-2512-02461:
Peng Zhang and seven co-authors work on keeping wireless signals private at the physical level. Future systems may use fluid antennas, whose parts can shift position, inside near field links with many antennas at once. Working close to the antennas gives new ways to shape and protect a signal.

Their 2025 study adds planned noise that harms eavesdroppers more than the true receiver. Beam shaping and the added noise are designed together, for both compact and large antenna arrays. The goal is strong privacy built into the radio link itself, not just into software above it. Strong links that stay private are a key need for the next wave of phones.
arxiv-2512-02661:
Alexander Van Werde and Jaron Sanders study how fast a wandering particle mixes when walls partly block it. Brownian motion models random wandering, here inside a smooth flat region. Semipermeable barriers, drawn as closed curves, slow the crossing between zones.

The pair bounds the mixing time above and the steady distribution below, using geometric features of the domain. Barriers that are hard to cross keep the particle unevenly spread for longer. Such estimates inform models of diffusion in cells, porous media, and other spaces where membranes shape random motion. The bounds hold for a wide class of walls, so labs can use them with shapes they meet in real cells.
arxiv-2512-02861:
Oscar G. Lira, Oscar M. Caicedo, and Nelson L. S. Da Fonseca automate network setup with small, locally run language models. Modern networks keep growing in scale and complexity, so manual configuration turns slow and error prone. Large models can configure from stated intent, but they cost heavy compute and raise privacy worries in the cloud.

Fine tuned small models offer a leaner route that can stay on site. The team builds network self configuration around such models. Local automation could cut configuration errors while keeping sensitive network details inside the owner's walls. Small tools that run on site keep keys and maps at home, a trait big cloud tools can not match with ease.
arxiv-2512-03061:
Paulina Kaczyńska, Julian Sienkiewicz, and Dominik Ślęzak bring a classic explanation method to graph neural networks that predict links. Accumulated Local Effects show how one feature's value shifts a model's output, averaging over the data. Link prediction asks which missing connections a network will form next.

The authors adapt the method to visualize how node features influence link predictions. Both graph convolutional and graph attention networks serve as test models. Clearer explanations help analysts trust link forecasts used in fraud detection, biology, and recommendation systems. Plots that show which trait did the work let a team fix the trait, not just curse the tool. That counts when a call goes wrong in the field late at night.
plos-pone-0010161:
The authors were Gayla Hadwiger, Scott Dour, Swathi Arur, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper delivered a toolkit for worm research. The worm C. elegans is a major lab model, yet it lacked ready-made antibody tools. Vertebrate researchers can buy many antibodies off the shelf, while worm labs often had to make their own.

The team produced a set of monoclonal antibodies for C. elegans work. Shared, validated tools save every lab from repeating the same slow production work. A common toolkit also makes results easier to compare between research groups.
plos-pone-0010261:
The authors were Conrad Chan, Angeline Lim, Annie Chan, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study made a full antibody in ordinary lab bacteria. Antibodies are multi-part proteins that are hard to build in E. coli. Their folding is complex, and they must also be secreted, so good yields usually needed special strains or fermenter cultures.

The team tuned a common E. coli strain to express a full-length IgG1 antibody. A simple bacterial route to whole antibodies could cut production costs sharply. Cheaper antibodies matter for research tools and for antibody drugs alike.
plos-pone-0010361:
Justina Wolters and colleagues described how a bacterial transport protein grips its cargo, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein system, OpuA, imports a protective compound called glycine betaine. It switches on when salt levels around the cell pass a threshold. The authors focused on the part that first grabs the cargo. They studied it both alone and as part of the purified system.

Crystal structures showed the gripping part in fine detail. Binding tests showed how tightly it holds its target. Such detail explains how bacteria survive salty or dry conditions. It may also guide designs for hardier industrial microbes. The study is a close look at one molecular hand and what it can hold. Structure, here, explains a survival trick.
plos-pone-0009861:
Mesodermal progenitor cells are adult stem-like cells that can form tissues like bone and muscle. Simone Pacini and colleagues checked which stemness genes these cells keep switched on. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Pluripotency-associated genes are genes normally linked with embryonic stem cells. Mesoderm is the middle layer of the early embryo. The team found these genes constitutively expressed in the progenitor cells, meaning always on, not just sometimes. Steady expression hints the cells hold wider potential than expected. That potential could matter for regenerative medicine. The cells came from adult tissue, not embryos.
plos-pone-0009961:
Real brain signals come in natural bursts, not the tidy pulses labs usually use. Anja Gundlfinger and colleagues replayed those natural patterns into rodent brain synapses. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Spike trains are the sequences of electrical pulses neurons fire.

The synapses were hippocampal mossy fiber synapses, hubs in the memory circuit. Natural spike trains triggered short- and long-lasting dynamics there. Dynamics means how the synapse's strength rises and fades over time. Natural patterns reveal behavior that artificial pulses miss. The hippocampus helps form new memories. Rodents here means rats and mice in the lab.
